📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

NVIDIA Llama Nemotron Nano VL is a state-of-the-art 8B Vision Language Model (VLM) designed for intelligent document processing, offering high accuracy and multimodal understanding. Available on Hugging Face, it excels in extracting and understanding information from complex documents like invoices, receipts, contracts, and more. With its powerful OCR capabilities and efficient performance on the OCRBench v2 benchmark, this model delivers industry-leading accuracy for text and table extraction, as well as chart, diagram, and table parsing. Whether you’re automating financial document processing or improving business intelligence workflows, Llama Nemotron Nano VL is optimized for fast, scalable deployments.

Check out the tutorial below to start building your own intelligent document processing solutions with Llama Nemotron Nano VL! Customers can also post-train the model further with their own datasets using NVIDIA NeMo.

It has been revealed that llama Nemotron Nano VL, the latest addition to the NVIDIA Nemotron family of models, is a vision language model (VLM) designed to push the boundaries of intelligent document processing (IDP) and optical character recognition (OCR). With its high accuracy, low model footprint, and multimodal capabilities, Llama Nemotron Nano VL enables the seamless extraction and understanding of information from complex documents. This includes PDFs, images, tables, charts, formulas, and diagrams, making it an ideal solution for automating document workflows across various industries like finance, healthcare, legal, and government.

According to recent reports, llama Nemotron Nano VL demonstrates exceptional accuracy on the OCRBench v2 benchmark, which tests models on real-world OCR and document understanding tasks. These tasks include text recognition, table extraction, and element parsing across various document types. The model’s advanced capabilities enable it to deliver better performance than current leading VLMs in real-world enterprise scenarios.

Llama Nemotron Nano VL builds upon Llama-3.1-8B-Instruct and C-RADIOv2-VLM-H, a Vision Transformer (ViT) that serves as the backbone for visual feature extraction. This allows the model to handle a wide variety of visual elements in documents, including charts, graphs, and other complex visual representations.

C-RADIOv2-VLM-H Vision Transformer (ViT): The core visual understanding component of the model, C-RADIO allows for high-resolution processing of documents containing complex visual elements. This serves as a vision backbone, excelling across visual domains and enabling the model to process multi-image understanding with high resolution. This technology underpins the model’s ability to handle complex documents containing visual elements such as images, diagrams, charts, and tables.

Recent findings suggest that C-RADIO is trained on multi-resolution data using multiple distillation techniques. Multiplicative noise was applied to our weights during training to improve generalization.

It has been revealed that llama Nemotron VL further adopts a design that dynamically aggregates encoded patch features, enabling support for high-resolution input without sacrificing spatial continuity. This strategy efficiently processes documents with arbitrary aspect ratios while preserving both local detail and global context. It enables fine-grained analysis of dense visual content—such as small fonts, multi-column layouts, and intricate charts—without compromising computational efficiency or coverage. The model can also preserve the information better and have less distortion, due to the innovation in high-resolution tiling.

By empowering Llama-3.1 8B LLM with this strong vision foundation, Llama Nemotron Nano VL delivers unparalleled accuracy in parsing and interpreting documents.

Llama Nemotron Nano VL was trained using several OSS datasets along with data from NVIDIA’s VLM-based OCR solution, NeMo Retriever Parse. This provides capabilities in text and table parsing, along with grounding, enabling the Llama Nemotron Nano VL to perform at an industry-leading level in document understanding tasks. Synthetic table extraction datasets that were used for training this OCR solution were also used for training Llama Nemotron Nano VL 8B VLM to enable more optimal table understanding and extraction.

In a recent development, llama Nemotron Nano VL excels in tasks like text recognition and visual reasoning, and demonstrates advanced chart and diagram understanding capabilities. Llama Nemotron Nano VL allows for predicting bounding box coordinates in normalized space to enable grounding like tasks and text-referring.

Industry observers note that this strong performance is underpinned by high-quality in-domain data combined with a diverse training distribution across document types, languages, and layouts. A robust data strategy ensures coverage across challenging use cases through selective curation, targeted augmentation, and formatting techniques that clarify task intent and reduce ambiguity—resulting in models that generalize effectively to real-world applications.

It has been revealed that llama Nemotron Nano VL undergoes a two-stage training regimen: pre-training followed by Supervised Fine-Tuning (SFT). The initial pre-training phase focuses on achieving cross-modal alignment between the language and vision domains. This is accomplished through the training of a Multi-Layer Perceptron (MLP) connector, which serves as an interface between the two modalities.

For the training process, Llama Nemotron Nano VL leverages a comprehensive and diverse collection of datasets. This aggregated dataset, comprising a total of ~1.5M samples, includes publicly available, synthetically generated, as well as internally curated datasets. A summary of the datasets utilized during the pre-training stage is presented in Figure 1.

In the Supervised Fine-Tuning stage, Llama-Nemotron-Nano-VL is trained end-to-end on a combination of synthetic, public, and internally curated datasets. The data encompasses a wide spectrum of tasks, including but not limited to: OCR, text grounding, table parsing, and general document-based VQA.

The document understanding capabilities of Llama Nemotron Nano VL can be largely attributed to the OCR-focused SFT data blend. Besides simple OCR, many of the datasets involve tasks such as predicting the correct reading order, reconstructing markdown formatting along with semantic classes (such as Captions, Titles, Section headers) and bounding boxes of individual text blocks. The model is also trained to parse mathematical formulas in LaTeX format and to extract tables in LaTeX, HTML, or markdown formats, depending on the prompt.

To ensure robustness across various domains, we apply affine and photometric augmentations to the document images. To improve the table and chart parsing performance further, we enable swapping of tables and charts embedded into the full-page documents between the datasets. This enables the model to handle diverse document layouts and structures.

A large portion of the internally-created datasets are based on Nemo Retriever Parse training data. These include NVPDFTex - a collection of arxiv documents with ground-truth labels consisting of formatted text in reading order, with bounding boxes and semantic classes of text, as well as LaTeX tables and equations; Common Crawl pdfs that are labeled by human annotators; rendered text from Wikipedia with markdown formatting and tables, as well as a number of synthetic datasets targeted at improving table parsing capabilities and dense OCR. In addition, the training blend includes a number of publicly-available datasets, such as DocLayNet, FinTabNet and PubTables-1M, in which we refine the groundtruth labels.

Figure 2 below reveals the task distribution of the training data. As can be seen, a significant portion of the training samples involve OCR along with grounding and table parsing, as well as OCR-adjacent VQA tasks.

Llama Nemotron Nano VL was trained using NVIDIA Megatron and utilizes efficient Transformer implementations in NVIDIA Transformer Engine. For multimodal dataloading, we use Megatron Energon. We provide example Megatron training and inference scripts along with hyperparameters and other instructions to enable custom training of VLMs.

To ensure the output is formatted precisely as you need, we recommend including detailed instructions within your prompts. We've provided some examples below to illustrate how this works for various tasks:.

OCRBench v2 is an advanced benchmark designed to evaluate OCR models across a diverse range of real-world document types and layouts. It includes over 10,000 human-verified question-answer pairs to rigorously assess a model’s capabilities in visual text localization, table parsing, diagram reasoning and key-value extraction.

Llama Nemotron Nano VL outperforms other VLMs on this benchmark and also achieves strong accuracies in benchmarks such as ChartQA and AI2D, making it a compelling option for enterprises aiming to automate document workflows such as:.

Its combination of high accuracy, strong layout aware reasoning, and efficient deployment on a single GPU makes it an ideal choice for large-scale enterprise automation.

Recent findings suggest that llama Nemotron Nano VL is optimized for various document processing tasks across multiple industries. Here are some of the key use cases where the model excels:.

Automating the extraction of line items, totals, dates, and other key data points from invoices and receipts. This is crucial for accounting, ERP integration, and expense management.

Extracting structured data from passports, IDs, and tax forms for regulatory compliance and KYC processes.

Automatically identifying key clauses, dates, and obligations in legal documents.

Extracting patient data, claim information, and policy details from medical records and insurance forms.

In a recent development, llama Nemotron Nano VL provides developers with the tools to automate document processing workflows at scale. It is available through the NVIDIA NIM API and for download on Hugging Face, where you can begin building production-ready document understanding applications. Customers can also use NVIDIA NeMo to finetune the model on their own dataset.

Tiny magnetic vortices could help computers work more like your brain

💡 Key Takeaways
  • Tiny magnetic structures called skyrmions could help pave the way for a new generation of computers that process information more like the human brain while using far less electricity.
  • A study published in the journal Nature Nanotechnology provides latest insights into how skyrmions behave and how scientists can control them.
  • Most of the research was conducted at the Institute of Physics at Johannes Gutenberg University in Mainz, Germany, with contributions from a professor at the Norwegian University of Science and Technology (NTNU).
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Tiny magnetic structures called skyrmions could help pave the way for a new generation of computers that process information more like the human brain while using far less electricity. Although most people have never heard of skyrmions, these microscopic magnetic vortices may eventually play an key role in how computers store and process data.

A study published in the journal Nature Nanotechnology provides latest insights into how skyrmions behave and how scientists can control them. The findings could help researchers develop smaller, more efficient computing systems and advance emerging quantum technologies.

Most of the research was conducted at the Institute of Physics at Johannes Gutenberg University in Mainz, Germany, with contributions from a professor at the Norwegian University of Science and Technology (NTNU).

"Skyrmions are small, magnetic vortices that can store information in a completely new way," explained Asle Sudbø, who leads NTNU's Centre for Quantum Spintronics (QuSpin).

Unlike conventional technologies, which require increasing amounts of space and energy to handle growing quantities of data, skyrmions could offer a much more efficient alternative.

"Instead of the current technology, where we constantly need more space and energy to process data, skyrmions could make it possible to build much smaller and more energy-efficient data storage systems," explained Sudbø.

Tiny Magnetic Vortices Could Enable Brain-Like Computers.

It has been revealed that the potential applications of skyrmions extend well beyond conventional data storage. They are also important to spintronics, which explores ways to use the magnetic properties of electrons in electronic devices, and to research involving topological quantum effects.

One particularly promising possibility is the development of computers that operate in ways similar to biological brains.

"These nanoscale vortices could help develop computers that resemble biological brains," remarked Sudbø.

Rather than relying on conventional transistor-based computing, such systems could use magnetism to process information. In principle, this approach could dramatically reduce electricity consumption, potentially allowing future computers to perform complex tasks with very little energy.

Turning that possibility into practical technology, however, requires scientists to understand exactly how skyrmions behave and how to manipulate them reliably.

The latest research represents an crucial advance toward that goal.

Scientists Film Magnetic Skyrmion Lattices Melting for the First Time.

Sources indicate that skyrmions do not always exist as isolated magnetic structures. Under certain conditions, they organize themselves into repeating patterns known as lattices, resembling the orderly arrangement of atoms in a crystal, but on a much smaller scale.

Scientists can manipulate these arrangements, a capability that could be essential for using skyrmions in future computing devices.

Sources indicate that in the fresh study, researchers achieved something that had not been demonstrated before. They recorded the melting of a magnetic skyrmion lattice as it happened while simultaneously controlling individual skyrmions.

"For the first time, researchers have managed to film how a magnetic skyrmion lattice melts in real time, while simultaneously being able to manipulate each individual skyrmion directly as they film it. For example, both their shape and size can be changed 'on the fly'," stated Sudbø.

Recent findings suggest that the ability to observe this process directly provides a clearer picture of how skyrmions respond when their organized structures break apart. It also allows researchers to study how changing the size and shape of individual magnetic vortices affects their behavior.

A Upcoming Step Toward Energy-Efficient Computing.

Industry observers note that understanding how skyrmions behave during the breakdown of their lattices could help scientists develop more precise ways to control them. That control is particularly notable if these magnetic structures are to become useful components in future computer systems.

Recent findings suggest that the findings therefore offer more than a latest way to observe an unusual magnetic phenomenon. They provide information that could help researchers overcome challenges involved in developing practical skyrmion-based technologies.

"The findings give us newly introduced insight into how these types of particles behave. This could therefore become notable for the development of more energy-efficient computer technology in the future," said Sudbø.

Although substantial development is still needed before skyrmions can be used in everyday computing devices, the research highlights their potential for improving data storage, enabling new computing architectures, and supporting advances in quantum technology.

By learning to observe and manipulate these tiny magnetic vortices in real time, scientists are gaining capabilities that could eventually help reshape the design of computers.

"This could revolutionize the way we think about computers," concluded Sudbø.

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

According to recent reports, sentence Transformers is a Python library for using and training dense embedding, reranker (cross encoder), and sparse embedding models for a wide range of applications, such as retrieval augmented generation, semantic search, semantic textual similarity, paraphrase mining, and more. In this blogpost, I'll show you how to use it to finetune a sparse encoder/embedding model and explain why you might want to do so. This results in sparse-encoder/example-inference-free-splade-distilbert-base-uncased-nq, a cheap model that works especially well in hybrid search or retrieve and rerank scenarios.

Recent findings suggest that finetuning sparse embedding models involves several components: the model, datasets, loss functions, training arguments, evaluators, and the trainer class. I'll have a look at each of these components, accompanied by practical examples of how they can be used for finetuning strong sparse embedding models.

In a recent development, in addition to training your own models, you can choose from a wide range of pretrained sparse encoders available on the Hugging Face Hub. To help navigate this growing space, we’ve curated a SPLADE Models collection highlighting some of the most relevant models.We list the most prominent ones along with their benchmark results in Pretrained Models in the documentation.

Industry observers note that the broader term "embedding models" refer to models that convert some input, usually text, into a vector representation (embedding) that captures the semantic meaning of the input. Unlike with the raw inputs, you can perform mathematical operations on these embeddings, resulting in similarity scores that can be used for various tasks, such as search, clustering, or classification.

With dense embedding models, i.e. the common variety, the embeddings are typically low-dimensional vectors (e.g., 384, 768, or 1024 dimensions) where most values are non-zero. Sparse embedding models, on the other hand, produce high-dimensional vectors (e.g., 30,000+ dimensions) where most values are zero. Usually, each active dimension (i.e. the dimension with a non-zero value) in a sparse embedding corresponds to a specific token in the model's vocabulary, allowing for interpretability.

Let's have a look at naver/splade-v3, a state-of-the-art sparse embedding model, as an example:.

In a recent development, in this example, the embeddings are 30,522-dimensional vectors, where each dimension corresponds to a token in the model's vocabulary. The decode method returned the top 10 tokens with the highest values in the embedding, allowing us to interpret which tokens contribute most to the embedding.

We can even determine the intersection or overlap between embeddings, very useful for determining why two texts are deemed similar or dissimilar:.

A key component of neural sparse embedding models is query/document expansion. Unlike traditional lexical methods like BM25, which only match exact tokens, neural sparse models generally automatically expand the original text with semantically related terms:.

According to recent reports, for example, in the code output above, the sentence "The weather is lovely today" is expanded to include terms like "beautiful", "cool", "pretty", and "nice" which weren't in the original text. Similarly, "It's so sunny outside!" is expanded to include "weather", "summer", and "sun".

It has been revealed that this expansion allows neural sparse models to match semantically related content or synonyms even without exact token matches, handle misspellings, and overcome vocabulary mismatch problems. This is why neural sparse models like SPLADE often outperform traditional lexical search methods while maintaining the efficiency benefits of sparse representations.

However, expansion has its risks. For example, query expansion for "What is the weather on Tuesday?" will likely also expand to "monday", "wednesday", etc., which may not be desired.

In short, neural sparse embedding models fall in a valuable niche between traditional lexical methods like BM25 and dense embedding models like Sentence Transformers. They have the following advantages:.

Throughout this blogpost, I'll use "sparse embedding model" and "sparse encoder model" interchangeably.

Recent findings suggest that the majority of (neural) sparse embedding models employ the aforementioned query/document expansion so that you can match texts with nearly identical meaning, even if they don't share any words. In short, the model has to recognize synonyms so those tokens can be placed in the final embedding.

Most out-of-the-box sparse embedding models will easily recognize that "supermarket", "food", and "market" are useful expansions of a text containing "grocery", but for example:.

Sources indicate that whereas we wish for it to expand to "headache", the common word for "cephalalgia". This example expands to many domains, e.g. not recognizing that "Java" is a programming language, that "Audi" makes cars, or that "NVIDIA" is a company that makes graphics cards.

Through finetuning, the model can learn to focus exclusively on the domain and/or language that matters to you.

Now, let's dive into each of these components in more detail.

According to recent reports, sparse Encoder models consist of a sequence of Modules, Sparse Encoder specific Modules or Custom Modules, allowing for a lot of flexibility. If you want to further finetune a Sparse Encoder model (e.g. it has a modules.json file), then you don't have to worry about which modules are used:.

But if instead you want to train from another checkpoint, or from scratch, then these are the most common architectures you can use:.

According to recent reports, splade models use the MLMTransformer followed by a SpladePooling modules. The former loads a pretrained Masked Language Modeling transformer model (e.g. BERT, RoBERTa, DistilBERT, ModernBERT, etc.) and the latter pools the output of the MLMHead to produce a single sparse embedding of the size of the vocabulary.

This architecture is the default if you provide a fill-mask model architecture to SparseEncoder, so it's easier to use the shortcut:.

In a recent development, inference-free Splade uses a Router module with different modules for queries and documents. Usually for this type of architecture, the documents part is a traditional Splade architecture (a MLMTransformer followed by a SpladePooling module) and the query part is an SparseStaticEmbedding module, which just returns a pre-computed score for every token in the query.

This architecture allows for fast query-time processing using the lightweight SparseStaticEmbedding approach, that can be trained and seen as a linear weights, while documents are processed with the full MLM transformer and SpladePooling.

Inference-free Splade is particularly useful for search applications where query latency is critical, as it shifts the computational complexity to the document indexing phase which can be done offline.

When training models with the Router module, you must use the router_mapping argument in the SparseEncoderTrainingArguments to map the training dataset columns to the correct route ("query" or "document"). For example, if your dataset(s) have ["question", "answer"] columns, then you can use the following mapping:.

Additionally, it is recommended to use a much higher learning rate for the SparseStaticEmbedding module than for the rest of the model. For this, you should use the learning_rate_mapping argument in the SparseEncoderTrainingArguments to map parameter patterns to their learning rates. For example, if you want to use a learning rate of 1e-3 for the SparseStaticEmbedding module and 2e-5 for the rest of the model, you can do this:.

It has been revealed that contrastive Sparse Representation (CSR) models, introduced in Beyond Matryoshka: Revisiting Sparse Coding for Adaptive Representation, apply a SparseAutoEncoder module on top of a dense Sentence Transformer model, which usually consist of a Transformer followed by a Pooling module. You can initialize one from scratch like so:.

Or if your base model is 1) a dense Sentence Transformer model or 2) a non-MLM Transformer model (those are loaded as Splade models by default), then this shortcut will automatically initialize the CSR model for you:.

In a recent development, unlike (Inference-free) Splade models, sparse embeddings by CSR models don't have the same size as the vocabulary of the base model. This means you can't directly interpret which words are activated in your embedding like you can with Splade models, where each dimension corresponds to a specific token in the vocabulary.

According to recent reports, beyond that, CSR models are most effective on dense encoder models that use high-dimensional representations (e.g. 1024-4096 dimensions).

If you're unsure which architecture to use, here's a quick guide:.

Sources indicate that the SparseEncoderTrainer uses datasets.Dataset or datasets.DatasetDict instances for training and evaluation. You can load data from the Hugging Face Datasets Hub or use local data in various formats such as CSV, JSON, Parquet, Arrow, or SQL.

According to recent reports, note: Lots of public datasets that work out of the box with Sentence Transformers have been tagged with sentence-transformers on the Hugging Face Hub, so you can easily find them on https://huggingface.co/datasets?other=sentence-transformers. Consider browsing through these to find ready-to-go datasets that might be useful for your tasks, domains, or languages.

You can use the load_dataset function to load data from datasets in the Hugging Face Hub.

It has been revealed that some datasets, like nthakur/swim-ir-monolingual, have multiple subsets with different data formats. You need to specify the subset name along with the dataset name, e.g. dataset = load_dataset("nthakur/swim-ir-monolingual", "de", split="train").

You can also use load_dataset for loading local data in certain file formats:.

You can use datasets.Dataset.from_dict if your local data requires pre-processing. This allows you to initialize your dataset with a dictionary of lists:.

Each key in the dictionary becomes a column in the resulting dataset.

In a recent development, it's crucial to ensure that your dataset format matches your chosen loss function. This involves checking two things:.

It has been revealed that for example, if your loss function accepts (anchor, positive, negative) triplets, then your first, second, and third dataset columns correspond with anchor, positive, and negative, respectively. This means that your first and second column must contain texts that should embed closely, and that your first and third column must contain texts that should embed far apart. That is why depending on your loss function, your dataset column order matters.

Consider a dataset with columns ["text1", "text2", "label"], where the "label" column contains floating point similarity scores. This dataset can be used with SparseCoSENTLoss, SparseAnglELoss, and SparseCosineSimilarityLoss because:.

It has been revealed that if the columns in your dataset are not ordered correctly, use Dataset.select_columns to reorder them. Additionally, remove any extraneous columns (e.g., sample_id, metadata, source, type) using Dataset.remove_columns, as they will be treated as inputs otherwise.

Recent findings suggest that loss functions measure how well a model performs on a given batch of data and guide the optimization process. The choice of loss function depends on your available data and target task. Refer to the Loss Overview for a comprehensive list of options.

To train a SparseEncoder, you either need a SpladeLoss or CSRLoss, depending on the architecture. These are wrapper losses that add sparsity regularization on top of a main loss function, which must be provided as a parameter. The only loss that can be used independently is SparseMSELoss, as it performs embedding-level distillation, ensuring sparsity by directly copying the teacher's sparse embedding.

Most loss functions can be initialized with just the SparseEncoder that you're training, alongside some optional parameters, e.g.:.

The SparseEncoderTrainingArguments class allows you to specify parameters that influence training performance and tracking/debugging. While optional, experimenting with these arguments can help improve training efficiency and provide insights into the training process.

Industry observers note that in the Sentence Transformers documentation, I've outlined some of the most useful training arguments. I would recommend reading it in Training Overview > Training Arguments.

Here's an example of how to initialize SparseEncoderTrainingArguments:.

Note that eval_strategy was introduced in transformers version 4.41.0. Prior versions should use evaluation_strategy instead.

Sources indicate that you can provide the SparseEncoderTrainer with an eval_dataset to get the evaluation loss during training, but it may be useful to get more concrete metrics during training, too. For this, you can use evaluators to assess the model's performance with useful metrics before, during, or after training. You can use both an eval_dataset and an evaluator, one or the other, or neither. They evaluate based on the eval_strategy and eval_steps Training Arguments.

Here are the implemented Evaluators that come with Sentence Transformers for Sparse Encoder models:.

Additionally, SequentialEvaluator should be used to combine multiple evaluators into one Evaluator that can be passed to the SparseEncoderTrainer.

Sometimes you don't have the required evaluation data to prepare one of these evaluators on your own, but you still want to track how well the model performs on some common benchmarks. In that case, you can use these evaluators with data from Hugging Face.

When evaluating frequently during training with a small eval_steps, consider using a tiny eval_dataset to minimize evaluation overhead. If you're concerned about the evaluation set size, a 90-1-9 train-eval-test split can provide a balance, reserving a reasonably sized test set for final evaluations. After training, you can assess your model's performance using trainer.evaluate(test_dataset) for test loss or initialize a testing evaluator with test_evaluator(model) for detailed test metrics.

If you evaluate after training, but before saving the model, your automatically generated model card will still include the test results.

When using Distributed Training, the evaluator only runs on the first device, unlike the training and evaluation datasets, which are shared across all devices.

The SparseEncoderTrainer is where all previous components come together. We only have to specify the trainer with the model, training arguments (optional), training dataset, evaluation dataset (optional), loss function, evaluator (optional) and we can start training. Let’s have a look at a script where all of these components come together:.

Industry observers note that after running this script, the sparse-encoder/example-inference-free-splade-distilbert-base-uncased-nq model was uploaded for me. The model scores 0.5241 NDCG@10 on NanoMSMARCO, 0.3299 NDCG@10 on NanoNFCorpus and 0.5357 NDCG@10 NanoNQ, which is a good result for an inference-free distilbert-based model trained on just 100k pairs from the Natural Questions dataset.

According to recent reports, the model uses an average of 184 active dimensions in the sparse embeddings for the documents, compared to 7.7 active dimensions for the queries (i.e. the average number of tokens in the query). This corresponds to a sparsity of 99.39% and 99.97%, respectively.

All of this information is stored in the automatically generated model card, including the base model, language, license, evaluation results, training & evaluation dataset info, hyperparameters, training logs, and more. Without any effort, your uploaded models should contain all the information that your potential owners would need to determine whether your model is suitable for them.

The Sentence Transformers trainer supports various transformers.TrainerCallback subclasses, including:.

These are automatically used without you having to specify anything, as long as the required dependency is installed.

Refer to the Transformers Callbacks documentation for more information on these callbacks and how to create your own.

Top-performing models are often trained using multiple datasets simultaneously. The SparseEncoderTrainer simplifies this process by allowing you to train with multiple datasets without converting them to the same format. You can even apply different loss functions to each dataset. Here are the steps for multi-dataset training:.

Each training/evaluation batch will contain samples from only one of the datasets. The order in which batches are sampled from the multiple datasets is determined by the MultiDatasetBatchSamplers enum, which can be passed to the SparseEncoderTrainingArguments via multi_dataset_batch_sampler. The valid options are:.

We'll also explore hybrid retrieval methods that combine sparse and dense vectors, as well as reranking to further improve search quality.

After running a slightly modified version of our hybrid_search.py script, we get the following results for the NanoMSMARCO dataset, using these models:.

The Sparse and Dense rankings can be combined using Reciprocal Rank Fusion (RRF), which is a simple way to combine the results of multiple rankings. If a Reranker is applied, it will rerank the results of the prior retrieval step.

It has been revealed that the results indicate that for this dataset, combining Dense and Sparse rankings is very performant, resulting in 12.3% and 18.7% increases over the Dense and Sparse baselines, respectively. In short, combining Sparse and Dense retrieval methods is a very effective way to improve search performance.

In a recent development, furthermore, applying a reranker on any of the rankings improved the performance to approximately 66.3 NDCG@10, showing that either Sparse, Dense, or Hybrid (Dense + Sparse) found the relevant documents in their top 100, which the reranker then ranked to the top 10. So, replacing a Dense -> Reranker pipeline with a Sparse -> Reranker pipeline might improve both latency and costs:.

A tiny supercurrent could unlock quantum information without destroying it

📅 05 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 12 min read (2300 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Sciencedaily

⏱️ ~12 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Sources indicate that one of the biggest obstacles in quantum computing is surprisingly simple to describe: how do you read information without changing or destroying it?
  • Researchers have now proposed a way to overcome much of this difficulty by using an unusual electrical signal produced by the qubit itself.
  • Sources indicate that the research, supported by FAPESP, was published in Physical Review B Letters.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Sources indicate that one of the biggest obstacles in quantum computing is surprisingly simple to describe: how do you read information without changing or destroying it? Unlike the bits used in ordinary computers, quantum bits, or qubits, are extraordinarily sensitive to measurement. Trying to determine their state can cause that state to collapse, potentially erasing the very information scientists want to retrieve.

Researchers have now proposed a way to overcome much of this difficulty by using an unusual electrical signal produced by the qubit itself. Their approach focuses on a special type known as an "Andreev qubit," which can generate an oscillating electric supercurrent through its own quantum behavior. By monitoring this current, scientists may be able to determine the qubit's state without directly measuring it or significantly disturbing the information it contains.

Sources indicate that the research, supported by FAPESP, was published in Physical Review B Letters. It was led by José Carlos Egues, a full professor at the São Carlos Institute of Physics at the University of São Paulo (IFSC-USP) in Brazil, and Yugui Yao of the School of Physics at the Beijing Institute of Technology in China. If experimentally confirmed, their method could simplify quantum computing by removing the need for extra qubits used in certain measurement techniques.

Why Measuring Quantum Information Is So Difficult.

Recent findings suggest that conventional computers store information in bits that have one of two values, 0 or 1. These values can be checked repeatedly without changing the information. Quantum computers work differently because their qubits can exist in superpositions, meaning they can combine the states 0 and 1 in ways that are not possible with conventional bits.

Industry observers note that this unusual ability is central to the potential power of quantum computing. However, it also creates a major vulnerability. Quantum states can be disrupted by interactions with their surroundings, including the instruments scientists use to examine them.

"In the conventional formulation of quantum mechanics, a projective measurement causes the system to assume one of the states associated with the measured quantity. Thus, if a qubit has been prepared in a certain superposition of 0 and 1, its direct measurement tends to destroy that superposition and, consequently, the information it contained," says Egues.

To minimize this problem, physicists developed techniques known as "quantum nondemolition measurements," or QND. Many of these approaches use an additional quantum system called an ancilla. Rather than measuring the original qubit directly, researchers transfer information to the ancilla and measure that auxiliary system instead.

The term "ancilla" comes from a Latin word meaning "slave" or "servant." In modern scientific usage, it describes something that performs a supporting function. Here, the ancilla acts as an intermediary, allowing researchers to obtain information while preserving the original qubit as much as possible.

In a recent development, although effective, these procedures come with practical disadvantages. Scientists must prepare the auxiliary qubits, connect them to the qubits being studied, transfer information between them, and perform repeated measurements. These additional steps require time and equipment, and the complexity becomes increasingly significant as the number of qubits grows.

"Our strategy is different. Instead of transferring the information to an auxiliary qubit, we seek to obtain it from a signal produced by the qubit under study itself," says the researcher.

A Special Quantum Bit That Produces Its Own Signal.

It has been revealed that the proposed technique relies on the unusual properties of an Andreev qubit. Its name honors Soviet physicist Alexander Andreev (1939-2023), who identified a distinctive quantum process in 1964 that occurs where normal materials meet superconductors.

It has been revealed that superconductors are materials that can conduct electricity without electrical resistance under appropriate conditions. At the boundaries involving these materials, special quantum states known as "Andreev states" can form. In the system studied by the researchers, these states are confined to an extremely small region between two superconducting materials.

These quantum states can represent the basic values 0 and 1, along with superpositions of those values, making them suitable for storing quantum information.

Sources indicate that "In the system under consideration, this region is a quantum dot - that is, a nanoscale structure in which electrons are spatially confined - formed in an indium arsenide [InAs] nanowire connected to superconducting materials on both sides. It's in this environment that the states characterizing the Andreev qubit are formed," Egues explains.

The key to the new approach is an electrical phenomenon called a "supercurrent." Unlike the current flowing through ordinary electrical conductors, a supercurrent moves without resistance.

In a recent development, the researchers found that when the Andreev qubit exists in a superposition, the supercurrent develops a component that oscillates over time. These fluctuations arise from quantum interference between the different states making up the superposition.

Crucially, the oscillations are not random. Their behavior contains information about the qubit's underlying quantum state, potentially allowing scientists to determine what that state is without directly measuring the qubit.

"It's precisely that property that we use to read the qubit. It's that supercurrent that lies at the heart of our proposal," the researcher points out.

How a Tiny Electrical Current Reveals Quantum Information.

To understand how the technique works, it helps to consider how physicists describe a qubit's state mathematically.

One common representation is the "Bloch sphere," a geometric model in which every possible pure state of a single qubit corresponds to a point on the surface of a sphere. Two angles determine the location of that point.

The first angle describes how much each of the two basic states contributes to the superposition. The second describes their relative phase, which specifies how the quantum components are aligned with one another. Together, these two measurements provide the information needed to identify the qubit's state.

According to the latest research, both pieces of information can be extracted from the supercurrent. Its steady component and the size of its oscillations reveal the relative contributions of the two basic states. Meanwhile, the timing of the oscillations provides information about their phase relationship.

"Our study showed that this information is encoded in the supercurrent itself. The supercurrent has a constant component and a fluctuating component. The value of the constant component and the amplitude of the oscillation reveal the proportion of each state (0 and 1) in the superposition, and the moment when that oscillation begins reveals the phase relationship between them. Thus, by measuring how the current varies over time, it's possible to reconstruct the initial state of the qubit," Egues explains.

Sources indicate that this means the electrical current effectively carries a signature of the quantum information stored in the system. By observing how that signature changes over time, researchers could reconstruct the qubit's original state.

A Supercurrent That Oscillates Without Voltage.

Another surprising feature of the proposed system is that the electrical current can oscillate without an externally applied voltage.

Sources indicate that ordinarily, producing an oscillating supercurrent in this type of superconducting system requires a voltage. This familiar phenomenon is called the "AC Josephson effect.".

The researchers predict something different in their Andreev qubit. Here, the current's oscillations arise naturally from the qubit's own quantum evolution. No outside voltage is required to generate them.

Recent findings suggest that "Our system generates a supercurrent that varies over time like an alternating current but without voltage. It's the very evolution of the qubit's state that produces that oscillation," says Egues.

According to recent reports, this behavior is crucial because it transforms quantum activity occurring on an extraordinarily small scale into a detectable electrical signal. The current provides a connection between the microscopic world of quantum states and the larger physical systems scientists can measure.

That connection is what makes the proposed reading technique possible.

Detecting Quantum States With an Extremely Sensitive Sensor.

The researchers envision placing the Andreev qubit inside a closed superconducting circuit, allowing its supercurrent to circulate continuously.

Next to the circuit would sit a SQUID (superconducting quantum interference device), a highly sensitive instrument capable of detecting extremely weak magnetic fields.

In a recent development, whenever an electric current flows, it produces a magnetic field. Because the supercurrent in this system oscillates, the magnetic field it generates also changes over time.

The nearby SQUID could detect these tiny magnetic variations and use them to determine the behavior of the circulating current. Since the current contains information about the qubit's quantum state, the researchers could then reconstruct that state without measuring the qubit directly.

Egues compares the arrangement to two compasses that interact through a magnetic field.

"We can think of the qubit as one compass and the SQUID as another compass. The current in the circuit produces a magnetic field, and the SQUID 'senses' that field. Since the coupling between the two is very weak, the effect of the measuring instrument on the qubit tends to be very small.".

The weak interaction between the sensor and the qubit is especially crucial. It offers a way to gather information while minimizing the disturbance that normally accompanies quantum measurements.

Reading Quantum Information With Almost No Disturbance.

In quantum physics, observing a system is not necessarily a harmless process. A measuring instrument interacts with whatever it is attempting to measure, and that interaction can change the system's behavior.

Recent findings suggest that this fundamental difficulty puzzled the earliest researchers studying quantum mechanics. It remains an unavoidable feature of quantum measurements today.

Sources indicate that the proposed technique does not eliminate this effect entirely. The SQUID still interacts with the circuit, creating a small amount of feedback that can influence the qubit. However, the team's simulations suggest that this disturbance can be reduced to a level so small that it becomes effectively negligible.

"Our method doesn't eliminate the fundamental problem of quantum measurement. But it can approach the limit of a non-destructive readout and, at the same time, avoid the use of auxiliary qubits - the ancillas - employed in other non-destructive quantum measurement protocols," Egues notes.

The approach could also remove another complication found in some existing techniques. Because researchers would not need to restore the qubit to its original state after every measurement, they could make repeated observations as the state changes.

This would allow scientists to follow the qubit's quantum evolution over time, rather than obtaining information only through separate measurement and reset cycles.

Simulations Achieve Up to 99.85% Accuracy.

To investigate whether the method could work outside ideal theoretical conditions, the researchers performed computer simulations designed to account for imperfections that would arise in real experiments.

Industry observers note that these calculations included measurement noise, as well as the small amount of feedback introduced by the detection coil. The goal was to determine whether the qubit's state could still be reconstructed accurately despite these disturbances.

The results were encouraging. Depending on the number of measurements used, the simulations produced accuracies of 99.52%, 99.81%, and 99.85%.

According to the researchers, these values fall within the standard thresholds used in quantum error correction schemes, which are designed to manage errors in quantum information processing.

The findings suggest that the method could provide highly accurate quantum state reconstruction without the additional complexity of auxiliary qubits.

However, the technique has not yet been demonstrated experimentally. The results come entirely from theoretical analysis and computer simulations, so researchers still need to establish whether a physical device can achieve comparable performance.

Could This Make Quantum Computers Simpler?

Despite the lack of experimental confirmation, the researchers emphasize that their proposal does not depend on technologies that have yet to be invented.

The calculations use realistic properties drawn from existing quantum systems, and SQUID sensors are already established tools for detecting exceptionally weak magnetic fields and electric currents.

What remains to be built is the specific arrangement of components required to implement the proposed measurement technique.

According to recent reports, "All the numbers we used are realistic. In principle, this can be achieved. In fact, we used parameters from existing systems in our calculations. What doesn't yet exist is that geometry, that setup that we proposed," he argues.

This makes the approach different from theoretical concepts that cannot be realized until scientists develop entirely fresh materials or manufacturing techniques. In principle, the necessary components already exist, although assembling them into the proposed configuration and demonstrating the predicted behavior remain crucial challenges.

The research offers two potentially significant advances.

According to recent reports, from the standpoint of fundamental physics, it predicts that a qubit can produce an oscillating supercurrent resembling the AC Josephson effect, but without requiring an external voltage. Instead, the oscillations emerge from the qubit's own coherent quantum evolution.

It has been revealed that from a technological perspective, the study reveals how those oscillations could serve as a measurable signature of the qubit's internal state. By analyzing the electrical current, researchers could recover quantum information while causing very little disturbance to the system.

If future experiments confirm these predictions, the method could make reading Andreev qubits substantially simpler. Eliminating auxiliary qubits and repeated resets could reduce the equipment and procedures needed to retrieve quantum information.

More fundamentally, the work points toward an intriguing possibility: information hidden in the microscopic quantum world may be accessible through an electrical current produced by the quantum system itself, offering a promising latest way to observe delicate quantum states without destroying them.

  • After years of anticipation, GTA 6 finally launched on November 19, with millions of players diving into Rockstar’s recreation of modern-day Florida.

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Grand Theft Auto 6 has become the biggest game launch in livestreaming history, racking up 420 million hours watched in its first week as TheBurntPeanut and IShowSpeed led the charge.

After years of anticipation, GTA 6 finally launched on November 19, with millions of players diving into Rockstar’s recreation of modern-day Florida.

The excitement extended to streaming platforms, with both Twitch and Kick giving away thousands of GTA 6 codes and Twitch even introducing new advertising technology to help creators monetize their broadcasts.

Now, the numbers are in, and Rockstar has obliterated the competition.

According to Streams Charts, GTA 6’s 420 million hours watched nearly tripled the previous launch week record set by Valorant’s closed beta in April 2020.

Recent findings suggest that incredibly, GTA 6 surpassed the combined opening week viewership of Valorant, Elden Ring, Diablo IV, and Lost Ark. The game also set a launch record with 7.91 million concurrent viewers.

Twitch accounted for the most hours watched, followed by YouTube and Kick, with the latter two finishing remarkably close to one another.

TheBurntPeanut was the most-watched GTA 6 streamer during launch week, generating a staggering 11.43 million hours watched across his broadcasts, with YouTube accounting for the majority of that figure.

Meanwhile, IShowSpeed attracted the most concurrent viewers on a single channel as he approached the end of his 52-hour GTA 6 marathon, which saw the streamer break down in tears after completing the story without sleeping.

Spanish streaming star IlloJuan recorded the highest combined peak viewership across multiple platforms.

Recent findings suggest that however, it wasn’t just streaming’s biggest names benefiting from GTA 6. Smaller creators also found themselves in the spotlight, including one streamer with zero viewers who received a surprise raid from Ibai.

In total, 1,056 channels broke their all-time peak viewership records while playing GTA 6, with 193 of them attracting at least 10 times their previous record audience.

With GTA 6’s multiplayer mode still to come and the potential for another generation of GTA RP content, Rockstar’s streaming dominance could be just getting started.

A mismatch is evidence, not a verdict.

Should a normal visitor reasonably be able to discover this page from another page on the site?

Industry observers note that google recommends using standard crawlable elements with resolvable href values for links that should be discoverable. Google's guidance on crawlable links.

That is also good web architecture independent of SEO.

Internal links should not exist merely to move ranking signals around.

They should help people move between related tasks.

A technical guide might lead to a product page. A product page might link back to the configuration guide. A category page should make important child resources discoverable without requiring a user to know the exact URL.

This is why on-page SEO and internal linking are closely connected to site architecture. Good internal links clarify relationships for both visitors and crawlers.

At a broader level, crawlability is one part of technical SEO and search visibility. A page that nobody can reliably discover is difficult to evaluate regardless of how strong its content may be.

This crawler reads the HTML response.

It does not execute JavaScript.

If an important URL appears disconnected because navigation is created only after client-side JavaScript runs, the script has surfaced a real architectural fact.

You can then decide whether that is acceptable.

If your application genuinely requires rendered-DOM crawling, replace the fetch-and-Cheerio layer with Playwright.

Do not make the simple crawler pretend to be something it is not.

The best output from this tool is not an "SEO score.".

Announcing NeurIPS 2025 E2LM Competition: Early Training Evaluation of Language Models

💡 Key Takeaways
  • 🔗Competition website | ✍️Registration form | 💬Discord channel | 📝Competition proposal.
  • Join us in building benchmarks that capture early-stage reasoning & scientific knowledge in LLMs!
  • The development of Large Language Models (LLMs) typically begins with a series of ablation experiments, wherein various model architectures, data mixtures, and training hyperparameters are systematically evaluated.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

🔗Competition website | ✍️Registration form | 💬Discord channel | 📝Competition proposal.

Join us in building benchmarks that capture early-stage reasoning & scientific knowledge in LLMs!

The development of Large Language Models (LLMs) typically begins with a series of ablation experiments, wherein various model architectures, data mixtures, and training hyperparameters are systematically evaluated. This phase is commonly referred to as the early stages of training. During this period, researchers primarily monitor two key metrics: the training loss curve and evaluation scores. However, existing evaluation benchmarks often fail to provide meaningful or discriminative signals during these initial stages where LLMs are trained on a few tokens ~200B tokens, making it challenging to derive conclusive insights from ongoing experiments.

In this competition, we want to build together newly introduced benchmarks to effectively capture relevant signals in early training stages of LLMs, specifically for scientific knowledge domain.

The competition will be hosted on a dedicated Hugging Face organization - to register to the competition please follow this registration link 👉 https://e2lmc.github.io/registration. Participants will have to submit their solutions, which will be based on lm-evaluation-harness library through a HuggingFace Space. An active leaderboard will be maintained during the competition to track promising submissions. The size of the models make them easily runnable for everyone, on free-tier Google Colab GPUs. We also provide a comprehensive starting kit including several notebooks to get started with the competition.

Each submission will be evaluated using three different scores: signal quality score (ScoreSQ), ranking consistency score (ScoreRC) amd compliance with scientific knowledge score (ScoreCS). These criteria will be combined into a global score used for the final ranking. Additionally, two validation procedures will be systematically applied to all submissions: (i) verification of alignment with established scientific knowledge domains, and (ii) detection of potential information leakage, specifically the presence of the answer within the question prompt.The overall score is computed as a weighted sum:.

where, αSQ, αRC and αCS are weighting coefficients that reflect the relative importance of each criterion. We set the weights as α1 = 0.5, α2 = 0.1 and α3 = 0.4, thereby placing greater emphasis on signal quality and compliance to scientific knowledge, which we consider the most notable metrics in evaluating submissions.

Participants will be able to compute the signal quality subscore locally using the provided model checkpoints of three Small Language Models 0.5B, 1B and 3B (ranging from 0 to 200 BT) along with the accompanying scoring algorithm (provided in a notebook in the starting kit). In contrast, the other two subscores cannot be computed independently, as the corresponding checkpoints—from 200 GT to 1 T tokens, as well as the 0.5 billion parameter model trained exclusively on web data—will remain hidden throughout the competition. Nonetheless, the global score will be automatically computed upon submission through the Hugging Face competition space, allowing participants to track their overall performance. This setup is intended to prevent overly customized solutions specifically tailored to the released checkpoints.

Further details about each evaluation metric, along with full scoring results on state-of-the-art benchmarks, are available in the competition proposal.

For inquiries and support, reach out to the task coordinators at e2lmc@tii.ae. You can also join our discord channel here to directly interact with us.

A hidden limit of space and time could unlock electronics 100,000 times faster

📅 07 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 8 min read (1515 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Sciencedaily

⏱️ ~8 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Quantum physics places fundamental limits on what scientists can know about the behavior of particles.
  • According to recent reports, but position and time are different.
  • Recent findings suggest that the discovery comes from an international collaboration involving research groups at the Regensburg Center for Ultrafast Nanoscopy (RUN), led by Profs.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Quantum physics places fundamental limits on what scientists can know about the behavior of particles. Werner Heisenberg's famous uncertainty principle states that certain properties, such as a particle's position and momentum, cannot both be measured with unlimited precision. This restriction is not caused by flaws in scientific instruments. It is built into the laws of nature.

According to recent reports, but position and time are different. Heisenberg's uncertainty principle does not impose the same restriction on these quantities. Now, researchers have experimentally demonstrated another fundamental limitation: an electron's location and its behavior over time cannot both be determined with arbitrary precision. Known as the "space-time limit," this newly observed relationship could have major implications for the future of quantum technology and ultrafast electronics.

Recent findings suggest that the discovery comes from an international collaboration involving research groups at the Regensburg Center for Ultrafast Nanoscopy (RUN), led by Profs. Jascha Repp, Rupert Huber, Franz Giessibl, and Klaus Richter, along with a team at the Max Planck Institute in Hamburg led by Angel Rubio.

Watching Electrons Move at Incredible Speeds.

Understanding how matter behaves at the smallest scales is essential for developing the next generation of technology. Advances in clean energy, quantum computing, and powerful electronics for artificial intelligence all depend on knowing how chemical reactions unfold, how light interacts with materials, and how electrons travel through electronic devices.

However, even the sharpest microscopic photographs cannot reveal the full picture. Scientists also need to observe how these processes change over time, effectively creating slow-motion movies of events occurring at the atomic scale.

At RUN, researchers are developing ultrafast microscopes capable of recording the movements of electrons, atoms, and molecules with extraordinary precision in both space and time. About ten years ago, scientists in Regensburg used ultrafast scanning tunneling microscopy to resolve the movement of a single molecule across space and time for the first time.

Tracking individual electrons presents an even greater challenge. At these microscopic distances, electrons can move roughly a thousand times faster than atoms and molecules, with vital changes taking place over just attoseconds.

Recent findings suggest that to appreciate how extreme these scales are, consider that an atom is approximately ten million times smaller than a millimeter. An attosecond is one-billionth of a billionth of a second. The difference between an attosecond and a second is comparable to the difference between one second and the entire age of the universe.

Making these measurements is especially difficult because electrons do not behave like ordinary objects. Their motion follows the unusual laws of quantum mechanics rather than the familiar rules of classical physics.

Ultrafast Lasers Reveal Quantum Tunneling.

According to recent reports, to observe electron behavior at these extraordinary speeds, the researchers built a fresh laser system that provides much finer time resolution than earlier experiments. The system allows them to control and study the quantum motion of individual electrons directly.

In the experiments, carefully timed laser pulses drive electrons from an extremely sharp metal tip toward a silver surface. The distance they travel is only a few atomic diameters.

The researchers detect this movement by measuring the resulting electrical current. To determine exactly when the electrons move, they use two pulses of light separated by a precisely controlled interval.

Simon Maier, the lead author of the paper, explains: "By varying the time interval between the two laser pulses, we can directly observe how the electrons respond.".

Recent findings suggest that this approach revealed clear evidence of electron motion occurring on attosecond timescales. It showed that the laser pulses could transfer electrons within these incredibly brief intervals while allowing scientists to observe the process as it happened.

What makes the result particularly remarkable is how the electrons travel. Instead of moving like conventional particles, they behave as quantum waves. This allows them to pass through an energy barrier separating the metal tip from the silver surface, even though classical physics predicts they should not have enough energy to cross it.

This phenomenon, known as quantum tunneling, is somewhat like an object passing through a solid wall without breaking or damaging it.

"Our measurement can be understood as a high-speed camera for the electron wave packets, since you can see at what point in time the tunneling process takes place," explains Katharina Glöckl, a doctoral student and co-author of the publication.

A Surprising 500-Attosecond Delay.

According to recent reports, to understand the measurements more deeply, researchers working with Prof. Angel Rubio performed sophisticated quantum simulations of the electrons' behavior near the "space-time limit.".

Their calculations closely reproduced the experimental findings and uncovered another remarkable detail. The electrons did not respond to the light field instantaneously. Instead, their motion lagged behind it by approximately 500 attoseconds.

At such extreme scales, several fundamental features of quantum physics become important simultaneously.

Industry observers note that for example, the researchers found that the laser pulses could not be described entirely by treating light as a wave or entirely by treating it as individual particles called photons. Their effects displayed characteristics of both descriptions. This combination was essential for exploring electron behavior so close to the "space-time limit.".

It has been revealed that the team also discovered that controlling electron motion over extremely short intervals changes how the electrons are distributed in space. Quantum mechanics describes these electrons using wave packets, which represent how their wave properties extend across different locations.

The relationship between the timing of electron motion and the spatial extent of these wave packets revealed the central limitation behind the discovery.

A Hidden Tradeoff Between Space and Time.

It has been revealed that raffael Spachtholz, another co-author of the study, explains: "The more precisely we want to pin down the electron's position in time, the more energy we need to provide. And as a result, the electron wave packet spreads out more spatially.".

In other words, improving the precision of an electron's timing comes with a cost. The more tightly researchers define when its motion occurs, the more broadly its quantum wave packet spreads through space.

To examine this relationship experimentally, the team placed a single atom on the surface to confine the electron wave packets to an extremely small region immediately before the laser pulses arrived.

This setup allowed the scientists to directly measure the connection between the electrons' spatial distribution and the timing of their motion.

Importantly, even when the electrons received substantial energy from the laser pulses, their wave packets remained sufficiently localized for microscopy with atomic spatial resolution and attosecond time resolution.

Recent findings suggest that the findings provide experimental insight into a fundamental space-time constraint that scientists had previously only suspected. They also make it possible to systematically investigate how changes in electron motion over time affect the spatial structure of quantum wave functions.

Could Quantum Electronics Become Hundreds of Thousands of Times Faster?

Beyond revealing a latest aspect of quantum behavior, the discovery could open the door to technologies that operate on timescales far beyond the capabilities of today's electronics.

One especially promising possibility involves using precisely controlled electron wave packets to influence chemical reactions.

Transferring a single electron to a molecule represents the smallest possible transfer of electric charge. But when that electron is concentrated within an exceptionally small region of space and time, the resulting local peak current density can reach as much as 1 trillion amperes per square centimeter.

Such extreme conditions could give scientists newly introduced ways to control chemical bonds and observe how molecules change during reactions.

According to recent reports, "In the future, we want to use such wave packets to specifically trigger chemical reactions and observe, on the relevant length and time scales, how chemical bonds can be broken or altered," explains Prof. Jascha Repp enthusiastically.

The implications could extend well beyond chemistry. Greater control over electron motion may eventually help engineers develop electronic devices and quantum information systems that operate at speeds approaching the fundamental limits of electron dynamics.

"In the long term, the insights gained could also contribute to operating electronics and quantum information processing at the intrinsic speed limit of electron motion itself -- hundreds of thousands of times faster than the currently dominant CMOS technology," adds Prof. Rupert Huber.

That possibility remains a long term technological goal rather than an achievement demonstrated in the current experiments. Nevertheless, the findings provide a newly introduced foundation for exploring how electrons can be manipulated at the smallest distances and shortest timescales.

For Repp and Huber, the results suggest that the range of potential applications is extraordinarily broad. They believe that future advances in controlling electrons at the space-time limit may ultimately depend more on human creativity than on the constraints imposed by nature.

I've never known a moment like this in video games

📅 22 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 7 min read (1357 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Eurogamer

⏱️ ~7 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Recent findings suggest that it was hard not to spend the first hour or so of Grand Theft Auto 6's launch day in a kind of stun-lock.
  • The analogy falls apart pretty swiftly when you think about it: the heroism of writing a little article about a video game aside, the frenzy of this week has been a joy, not a horror.
  • It's worth taking a moment just to actually, properly take stock of all the headlines from the past couple of days in terms of the sheer breadth and scale of its launch.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Recent findings suggest that it was hard not to spend the first hour or so of Grand Theft Auto 6's launch day in a kind of stun-lock. As far as video games editorial goes - which is not that far, in fairness; prepare for an over-flattering analogy - the effect was roughly the equivalent of Tom Hanks' experience, as his John H. Miller first set foot on Omaha beach. Tweets and reels whistled overhead, news leads stung the ears, exploding search terms blew apart some poor guides team ally on one side, while upcoming discoveries in the early game - made by the millions and millions of launch-day players all picking it apart at once - appeared by surprise like some flanking ambush on the other.

The analogy falls apart pretty swiftly when you think about it: the heroism of writing a little article about a video game aside, the frenzy of this week has been a joy, not a horror. But the point is, I've been doing this job for over a decade now, paying attention to video games for another two beyond that, and I've truly never seen anything like this before. It has been totally overwhelming. And then I thought about that for a moment before realising that - duh - nobody has ever seen anything like this before. GTA 6 is the biggest entertainment release of all time, and it's not even remotely close.

It's worth taking a moment just to actually, properly take stock of all the headlines from the past couple of days in terms of the sheer breadth and scale of its launch. Parent company Take Two revealed yesterday that GTA 6 sold 32.5m copies before it came out. By the end of its first day on sale, it had made a record-obliterating $3.79bn. By contrast, the once record-breaking GTA 5 made a once astounding $800m in the same period; the "opening" period of the largest film of all time, Avengers: Endgame, made $1.22bn, and that's totalling box office receipts across its release day until the end of the first Sunday after it.

It has set multiple records for streaming, per StreamCharts, with 214.63m hours watched in its first two days - significantly more than the previous biggest game, Valorant, achieved with 150m hours in its entire launch week. It's garnered more watch time in those two days than Elden Ring, Hogwarts Legacy, and Cyberpunk 2077 achieved with their entire launch weeks combined. Its concurrent viewers peak so far - 6.38 million people - is nearly four times the previous record of 1.74m, again formerly held by Valorant.

Sources indicate that it crashed Reddit. More than 2 million UK and US Xbox players used the 'New Zealand trick' to play the game early, which is more than a third of that country's entire population. Internet exchange operator DE-CIX claimed its launch led to the highest amount of concurrent internet usage in history, at 33.03 terabits per second.

According to recent reports, on top of all those raw numbers, it's also just felt utterly inescapable. I can't open Instagram, TikTok, BlueSky or X without being blasted with memes, viral clips of early discoveries, reactions, hot takes, feeble attempts at brand piggybacks, slightly wayward early-game tips from opportunist streamers who haven't escaped the first chapter, or makeup tutorials for looking like Lucia. I can't open my inbox without scrolling through reams of tenuous PR pitches for stories with barely the faintest connection to the game. I can't open my phone without messages from parents, friends or peers. Even the mainstream news - heaven forbid! - has gradually clocked onto this whole video games thing, this unknown artifact from the imaginary world of "online", maybe being a bit important. Dozens of my colleagues have been inundated with last-minute call-ups to provide an expert soundbite (they're so desperate they even got me on at one point).

We'll have a lot more to say about this game in the coming days and weeks (with apologies to regulars who are already sick of it - counterprogramming starts this Monday!). It's the richest of texts, a near endless comedy clip generator, a total technical marvel and all the rest - you already know. But it felt worth it to just sit still for a moment, and take stock of what's happening here.

This is the single biggest moment any piece of entertainment media has ever had. But more than that it's felt like a kind of party. The vibes in some corners are orgiastic, as streamers uncover spooky twists, outlandish reactivity, and easter eggs I'd never got close to in a hundred-odd hours with the thing - all of this pure dynamite for the audience. Given the budgets involved and the particularly unique blend of circumstances around it - the changing shape of video game funding; of how attention is monopolised; of how development may happen in the future and the sheer amount of time and subsequent anticipation built up since the previous entry - we will likely be waiting decades for another moment like it. If there's ever a moment like it again. Part of the sense of ecstasy going around comes, perhaps subconsciously, from the acknowledgment that in pure hype and attention terms, this might be as good as it ever gets.

For the briefest time, the world belongs to video games. Rockstar and Take-Two's executives and shareholders will no doubt reap the greatest rewards from all this - all part of the great irony that makes this game's central premise all the more interesting. But I sincerely hope its developers - especially the 34 fired by the organization last year, now awaiting the outcome of their tribunal over alleged union-busting, and those who hope to form a union from the currently open vote - are able to feel a particular sense of pride.

Just as this launch has been unprecedented in its success, the last two or three years have been unprecedented in their grimness for video game workers across most of the world, certainly the once-dominat western part. If we're very lucky - and frankly, I have my doubts - this burst of attention and visible profitability might go some way to helping the industry claw its way back, perhaps via attracting, as a knock-on from all the fresh-found attention, some kind of more sustainable investment. If we're not, and this is really the last behemoth, the last video game monument of its kind, the last rave before the police come raiding at dawn, at least we've gone out with one hell of a bang.

It has been revealed that GTA 6 - again, it's been remarked before now - is such a curious thing. A game of goofiness, self-awareness, prestige, pretentiousness, childish humour, astute commentary, ironic cultural criticism, surprising player expression and - above all of that - the most mind-boggling, brain-scrambling level of profoundly human craft. There's something kind of perfect about this.

In a recent development, it's a good thing, actually, that video games' greatest export is also its most contradictory. Video games are contradictory things in themselves. If the non-specialist media might still occasionally slip into treating video games like some kind of object from outer space, then we might as well put forward the best possible candidate for a capsule. It's the same way you'd think about it if you had to stick one thing in a vacuum-sealed box, to send out into the universe in an attempt to symbolise humanity: something that summarises close to all of it; that we're proud of; and crucially, that captures the spirit of it too.

Sources indicate that there are many more that might've put a more respectable foot forward - certainly that have a less chequered history, or maybe a more sophisticated, nuanced, or inventive use of the form. But there's really no better video game for exemplifying the full, chaotic range of the medium. It seems right, when you think about it, for GTA to be the one out there sitting under the spotlight, in the biggest moment this silly, serious artform might ever have.
