Industry observers note that power BI, Microsoft's reporting and dashboard tool, now lets an AI agent work on the data model behind a report. If you ask one to add a year-on-year revenue measure (a measure is Power BI's name for a saved calculation) with Microsoft's MCP server connected, it can write the formula and save it to the model without you opening the formula bar. When we tried this on a sample model, an agent inspected the model, wrote the measure, tested it and saved it in under four minutes.

Recent findings suggest that the agent did a careful job, but its formula didn't follow the same rules the finance team uses to count revenue. Nobody had told it what "revenue" meant in this business, so it had to decide for itself. We then gave another agent a short brief that set out finance's rules for what counts as revenue and which date to count it by. The agent wrote the formula from those rules, and the result matched finance's figure exactly. The two results show how much difference it makes in how you brief an AI agent to build accurate measures.

Industry observers note that we wanted to find out what an agent can see in a Power BI model and how to brief it so the measure matches the business's own definitions, with the setup arranged so that every change can be checked. Developers will know the principle from agents that write SQL or API code, where the brief ends up doing the job of a specification.

Because MCP (Model Context Protocol) is an open standard, the same server can be used from different AI clients, GitHub Copilot in VS Code and Claude among them, although some clients need extra sign-in setup for the hosted version.

Power BI has two current MCP servers, plus an older one, the Power BI Consumption MCP server, kept for existing integrations. The first of the current pair is the Power BI Authoring MCP server, which you may still see under the name of its package, powerbi-modeling-mcp. It lets an agent create and change the objects inside a semantic model, which is the layer of a Power BI report that holds the tables, the relationships between them and the calculations, kept separate from the charts on the page. It comes in two forms. The hosted version, still in preview, needs nothing installed. The local version is generally available and runs on your own machine, which makes it the one to use when the model is a file you hold yourself, whether that's open in Power BI Desktop, the free Windows app used to build reports, or saved as a project folder. Macs aren't supported by the local version, so on a Mac it has to be the hosted one, which works only with models published to Microsoft's cloud (a Fabric workspace).

The second is the Fabric IQ MCP server. Fabric IQ is part of Microsoft Fabric, the wider data platform that Power BI now sits within. It gives an agent read-only tools for finding published reports and models and running queries against them, within the permissions already set, so the agent can answer questions about the data but can't change a model.

In a recent development, which one to use follows from the job. Anything that changes a model goes through the authoring server, whether that's a new measure, a relationship or a set of descriptions, and it has to be the local version if the model is a Desktop file or a project folder under source control. Fabric IQ is for agents that only need answers from models other people maintain.

In a recent development, an agent connected to a semantic model can see its metadata (table and column names, data types, relationships, existing measures and any descriptions someone has written) and can run queries against the data. Everything it produces is inferred from those clues. A model that has served a business for years carries names that made perfect sense to the people who built it, and a column called Amt on a table called Sales_v2 tells an agent far less than it tells them.

Recent findings suggest that names carry a lot of the meaning. A column called Amount could hold the value with VAT (the UK's sales tax) or without, before credit notes or after, and an agent asked for "revenue" has to pick one. If the model holds several revenue measures built for different reports, the agent has to choose between them, and the one it picks may have been built for a different purpose.

In a recent development, the formulas depend on context as well. Power BI measures use a syntax of their own called DAX, which stands for Data Analysis Expressions. A DAX result shifts with whatever the person viewing the report has filtered or clicked on, which is known as filter context. A developer might think of a measure as a function that reads implicit state set by its caller. The same measure can be right as a single total on a card and need different handling once it's split by product in a table or filtered by a date slicer (the on-page date filter), depending on how CALCULATE (the DAX function that changes which filters apply) is used. Which behaviour is correct depends on how the business wants the number to respond, and that's something the agent has to be told.

In a recent development, relationships work the same way. Plenty of models have more than one date column on the sales table, say order date and dispatch date, with only one relationship active at a time. A DAX measure uses the active relationship unless it's written to switch to the other one, and the agent has no way of knowing which date your monthly reporting runs on unless something tells it.

In a recent development, in each case the agent can write a valid measure. Which of two valid measures matches the business's own definition is the part it can't see from the model.

To see this in practice, we built a small sales model in a Power BI Desktop file, working through the server itself, with invented data: 5,266 order lines, with order dates from January 2025 to October 2026. We gave the Sales table an Amt column holding each line's value after discount with 20% VAT added, next to LineTotal and Discount columns that excluded VAT, and an existing [Revenue] measure that summed Amt. There were two date columns, with the active relationship to the Date table on dispatch date and the order date relationship inactive. Orders stop at the end of October 2026, which made the current year a part year, a deliberate test. Nothing in the model had a description. In this made-up business, finance reports revenue net of VAT and discounts, by order date.

Sources indicate that on 12 November 2026 we connected an AI agent (Anthropic's Claude Fable 5.2) to version 1.0.1 of the local server through a small Node.js script that speaks MCP over stdio. In all three runs the agent had the server's tools only, without Microsoft's powerbi-authoring plugin, which adds modelling guidance on top of them. It was also told that nobody was available to answer questions, so each measure was saved exactly as the agent wrote it, with no review in between. The first prompt was one sentence: "Add a year-on-year revenue measure.".

Recent findings suggest that before writing anything, the agent listed the tables, relationships and columns, read the existing measure, sampled some rows and checked the date ranges. It worked out for itself that 2026 was a part year and limited the comparison to the same dates in 2025, which avoided a misleading result of -6.7%. From 15 sample rows it also spotted that Amt looked like the net figure plus 20%.

The measure it saved reused the existing [Revenue] measure and followed the active relationship. This is the core of it, with the date handling and blank checks left out. CurrentDates is defined in those lines as the dates up to the last order:.

It returned growth of 21.5% for 2026, which is correct for revenue counted by dispatch date. On finance's definition, by order date, the answer is 18.6%, and the whole difference came from that choice of date. The VAT question made no difference to a percentage, because Amt was already net of discount and every line carried the same rate, although it would have overstated any figure in pounds by 20%.

We reset the model and repeated the run with a fresh agent, which made the same two choices and returned the same 21.5%. Both choices were reasonable readings of the model as it stood, and the DAX was sound. In their reports, both agents flagged the date basis and the VAT treatment as open questions, and both worked out that an order-date basis would give 18.6%. That's what a good analyst would do, and with those two answers they would have had everything they needed.

It has been revealed that think of a capable analyst on their first morning, someone who knows DAX well but has never seen your business before and knows nothing (or not a lot) about it. You wouldn't say "add a revenue measure" and walk off. You'd tell them which table holds the trusted figures, whether revenue includes VAT, which date drives the reporting calendar, and what they shouldn't touch. An agent needs that briefing for the same reasons, and getting good work out of it draws on the skills you'd use with any new starter. Developers do the same thing when they write a good ticket. A request for a measure is a requirement, and it needs the same definitions and constraints, plus a way to check the result.

Sources indicate that before you send a prompt, ask yourself whether you could do the task properly if you were given only the words in that prompt and the model itself. If the answer is no, then the agent is in the same position, and it will make its own assumptions.

For the detailed run we cleared the earlier measure from the model and gave a fresh agent this brief:.

It has been revealed that this time the measure summed LineTotal minus Discount and used USERELATIONSHIP, the DAX function that switches a calculation to an inactive relationship, to work from order date. It returned 18.6% from that one brief, with no follow-up prompt, which is the figure we had calculated separately from the source data. This is the full measure as the agent saved it:.

Each line of the brief answered a question the agent would otherwise have had to settle alone. It also made some sensible decisions the brief hadn't covered. It left the grand total blank, for instance, where a plain total across both years would have shown a meaningless growth figure of 151.2%. The final line of the brief, asking to see the DAX before anything is saved, is there so that a person can see choices like that. In the test we approved that step in advance, to keep the run unattended.

Recent findings suggest that one detail needs adjusting before this measure is reused on other data. Its guard checks that each comparison period starts on or after the first order date, which works here because the sample data has an order on 1 January 2025. When we swapped that date for 2 January 2025 in a copy of the measure, January 2026 and the 2026 row came back blank. Comparing against the first date in the Date table, as the first agent's measure did, brought the 2026 figure back, since the Date table starts on 1 January. That version doesn't confirm that sales exist for the whole comparison period, though, so the right check depends on whether the business wants growth shown only where a complete prior period exists. That's a decision for whoever reviews the measure.

We ran the one-sentence prompt twice and the detailed brief once, all with the same AI model and one small set of data, which is enough to illustrate the pattern but too little to say how often it happens.

Good briefs help, but you'll be writing the same definitions into prompts again and again unless they live in the model itself. Descriptions on tables, columns and measures are part of the metadata the agent reads, so filling them in is one of the cheapest ways to put business definitions in front of it every time. In our test, where nothing had a description, both agents given the one-sentence prompt noted that nothing confirmed what Amt contained. A description such as "Net sales value in GBP, excluding VAT, after credit notes" stays in the model, where the agent reads it without anyone retyping it.

Industry observers note that naming deserves the same attention. Spelling out abbreviated column names, hiding technical keys that no report needs, gathering measures into a single measures table, and removing measures that are no longer used all give the agent fewer things to choose between. These are the same habits that make a model easier for a newly introduced colleague to pick up, so asking someone outside the team to find a figure in it is a fair test of the result.

In a recent development, microsoft has also added a set of Prep data for AI features (in preview) to Power BI Desktop and the service. They let you choose which fields Copilot, Microsoft's AI assistant, should consider and write AI instructions that explain your business terms, with verified answers available for common questions. They're aimed at Copilot, but deciding and writing down your definitions is the same work whichever AI tool reads them.

An agent working through the authoring server has the same access as the person signed in, so anything that person can change, the agent can change. Sign in with an account that has no more access than the job needs, and take a copy of the model first, as you would before any bulk edit.

Recent findings suggest that start with read-only mode. The local server takes a --readonly flag that blocks all write operations, which is the right setting while you're learning how the agent behaves on your models. When we tried to create a measure in this mode, the server refused and mentioned it was running read-only. In VS Code, the configuration looks like this (other clients use a similar structure, sometimes under an mcpServers key instead of servers):.

You'll need Node.js installed for the npx command. The server won't run other tools until its licence terms (the EULA) have been accepted. Once you've read them, you can either tell the agent to accept for you or add --accepteula to the args list.

Industry observers note that the --readonly flag belongs to the local server. On a Mac the route is the hosted server and a copy of the model in a Fabric workspace, once a Fabric administrator has switched on the tenant setting that allows the MCP endpoint, and there the copy is the safeguard. For an enforced limit, sign in with an account that holds only Build permission on the model, which lets the agent read and query it and nothing more.

Industry observers note that read-write is the default, so check how confirmation behaves in the version you install. Version 1.0.1 skips confirmation prompts by default, which the project's README hasn't caught up with, and has a --require-confirmation flag to turn them on. The flag is listed in the server's own --help output. In our runs every edit went through without a prompt. When we added the flag to the args list, the server asked for confirmation before the first write, with a message beginning "Are you sure you want to perform operations that will modify your database", and answering no blocked the change.

Recent findings suggest that version control is the other safeguard. Saved in the Power BI Project format (PBIP), a report and its model become folders of text files instead of one binary .pbix file. Commit those before the agent starts and its work arrives as an ordinary diff, which you can review and revert like any other change.

It has been revealed that whatever the agent reads, including table and column names and the rows returned by any query, is passed on to the AI provider behind your client, which may sit outside Microsoft's compliance commitments. For a model holding customer or payroll data, check that the provider is approved under your data policies before you connect.

In a recent development, an agent can draft and test a measure in minutes, and someone still has to read what comes back. For a developer fresh to Power BI, that takes enough DAX to see what a measure's filters will do in a table broken down by month or product, and enough knowledge of the business to confirm the agent used the right column and the right date. Writing the brief takes the same knowledge. Ours could only have come from someone who knew the model had an inactive relationship and which columns carried VAT.

These are data modelling and DAX skills, which many learners find the hardest part of Power BI. If the person reviewing agent output hasn't had that grounding yet, it helps to know how to judge whether a Power BI course covers enough DAX and data modelling, because courses vary a great deal in how much time they give to those two subjects compared with building charts.

In a recent development, take a copy of a model you know well and connect the local server to it in read-only mode. Ask the agent to describe every table and measure in its own words, then check those descriptions against what you know the model does. Wherever the two differ, the model needs a clearer name or a written description, and the corrected text can go straight into the description fields. With those in place before you allow any writes, the agent starts its first real task with the same definitions your finance team uses.

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

A football referee has denied accusations of being drunk after being removed from a match at halftime following a bizarre incident in which he showed a yellow card to a goalkeeper nearly half the pitch away from a foul.

Syrian referee Hanna Hattab was officiating an AFC Champions League Two match between the United Arab Emirates’ Al Jazira and Iran’s Gol Gohar when his decision-making raised eyebrows.

In the 32nd minute, Hattab awarded a free kick following a foul by Al Jazira’s Felicio Milson and approached the winger with a yellow card in hand.

However, as reported by the Daily Mail, the referee appeared to receive a message through his earpiece before suddenly changing direction and walking toward Al Jazira goalkeeper Ersin Destanoglu.

Despite being nowhere near the foul, the stunned goalkeeper was shown a yellow card.

Hattab eventually overturned the decision after consulting his fourth official, while Milson avoided receiving what would have been his second yellow card of the match.

Gol Gohar manager Mehdi Rahmati was reportedly seen shouting “he’s drunk” at Hattab, while the club’s sporting director, Heydar Afsari, revealed the team had threatened to boycott the second half.

#218362. Warhammer 40,000: Boltgun 2 captures the franchise's bloody absurdity like nothing else

📅 24 Nov 2026 • ⏱️ 5m • 📚 Deep Dive (1028 w)
📖 Baca
General ⚖️ Neutral 🌐 Eurogamer ↗ Open Full Page

Warhammer 40,000: Boltgun 2 captures the franchise's bloody absurdity like nothing else

📅 24 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 5 min read (1028 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Eurogamer

⏱️ ~5 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • According to recent reports, warhammer 40,000 is a universe of two distinct moods.
  • Perhaps the best praise I can give Boltgun 2 - which, like its 2023 predecessor, is developed by Auroch Digital - is that it honours 40k's sillier side wonderfully.
  • Like its predecessor, Boltgun 2 adopts the style of a retro first-person shooter.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

According to recent reports, warhammer 40,000 is a universe of two distinct moods. On the one hand, it's a grimdark future of serious, solemn stories where trillions die in galactic wars of attrition; of tragedies and insurmountable threats. But there's also the other side of Warhammer 40,000, where goofy hilarity and gory absurdity lies. Where Orks paint their cars go-faster red, and where chainaxe-wielding Khorne Berserkers indulge in gleeful hyperviolence.

Perhaps the best praise I can give Boltgun 2 - which, like its 2023 predecessor, is developed by Auroch Digital - is that it honours 40k's sillier side wonderfully. It's unashamedly gory, over-the-top, and, most crucially, fun. Its creators understand that after a long day at work, sometimes all you want to do is shred a guy or five.

Like its predecessor, Boltgun 2 adopts the style of a retro first-person shooter. It's a little bit Doom, a little bit Duke Nukem, as you blast through its low-poly environments and its sprite-based enemies, hoovering up - and using up - ammo and health as you go. I jumped in right as I was starting World of Warcraft: Forever. And in contrast to that game's slow burn beginning, Boltgun 2 is a full-throttle roar right from the word go that rarely lets up. Just moments in, you're belting down corridors - either playing as a Space Marine or a Sister of Battle, depending on your mood - and unloading endless rounds into cultists and Chaos dregs.

I should note that while I'm a Warhammer fan, the original Boltgun passed me by, so this sequel has been something of a revelation. It truly revels in its violent delights, indulging in its hunger for spectacle. As your bullets turn lesser goons into raspberry jam, strong animation work and excellent audio design bring its cartoonish brutality to life. And it's paired with some brilliantly over-the-top weaponry too. Take your basic Boltgun: when you pull the trigger, this beefed-up rifle's fist-sized projectiles erupt with a weighty bang. Weaker enemies get minced in their path, and for the Space Marine, this is the first gun.

As a Space Marine, you've also got a devastating cool-down-based rush attack known as the Obliterating Charge. It's handy for repositioning in a pinch, but it also bursts through enemies with the power of a speeding lorry. The Space Marine has his chainsword for slice-and-dicing too, and tougher enemies really require some elbow grease - you really have to mash that melee button - to get through 'em. Is all this the height of video game sophistication? Absolutely not, but it got me grinning, and it's a visceral thrill that still hasn't lost its sheen.

I also love that the two selectable characters aren't just cosmetic swaps. If you opt for the Sister of Battle, she comes with her own distinct weapons and abilities. I adore her Flamer and the close-quarters havoc it can cause; the way fire roars from its nozzle as sparks fly and black smoke spews. And while she doesn't have an Obliterating Charge, she does get a slide move that's a fantastic way to maintain forward-momentum. Both characters have their own quirks and appeal - the Space Marine is slower and heavier, but offers punchier gunplay, while the Sister of Battle is swifter but lighter in combat - and both, I reckon, warrant their own playthroughs.

It'd also be remiss not to mention Boltgun 2's dedicated 'taunt' button. Both characters have their own voice lines and many are context-specific. It's a fun thing to spam mid-fight, or to hit when celebrating moments of especially grisly victory. I remembered hearing you could get some extra ammo or healing items if you threw a taunt at the floating servo skull that flies beside you throughout the game and, yup, it's true. Little details like that, alongside the smaller secrets hidden around each mission, create an FPS that's so far been a real joy to mess around in.

It's occasionally all a bit floaty, perhaps, but the combination of speed and action is a winner. What elevates it even further, though, are those Warhammer 40,000 flourishes. I've been amazed how swiftly levels introduce latest enemies, and how lovingly they're depicted here. Basic Black Legion Chaos Space Marines take centre stage early on, but as you progress, new subfactions are introduced with their own unique quirks. Khorne-loving Berserkers thunder toward you at speed for painful melee strikes, while devilish Bloodletters lurch at your blind spots with giant swords in-hand. In a later mission things are flipped, and the melee-focused enemies are replaced by menacing ranged forces. Noise Marines carry giant sonic weapons that shoot from afar and disrupt your movement, all while their own daemon allies leap in.

It has been revealed that there's also something to say about the variety of the missions you'll encounter. Often, you're given a choice of paths through the game, each with their own planets and battlegrounds. These can be snow-laden ruins, unruly jungles, or cities under siege, and things get even wilder the further you go into the game. And while it's not the sort of experience that encourages you to stand still, if you do you'll see some striking views.

It has been revealed that there's a moment, not too far into Boltgun 2, when you find yourself in the bowels of a Khorne-controlled world. Here, literal rivers of blood flow, and you can't go two steps without someone or something rushing in. So I whip out a shotgun and charge on in, properly exhilarated by the chaos of it all as I blast stray enemies into mist. It takes a lot to stave off fatigue in a game with this sort of relentless action but Auroch manages it here.

Sources indicate that warhammer 40,000 is, I think, the sort of setting you can't do half-heartedly, and Boltgun 2 feels like a total embrace of the series' wilder, more absurd side. So far, around five hours in, it's a damn good FPS, retro or otherwise. You can grab it for just over £20, and it's even on sale as of writing. For that price it's a no-brainer.

#218361. SmolLM3: smol, multilingual, long-context reasoner

📅 08 Jul 2025 • ⏱️ 20m • 📚 Deep Dive (4040 w)

General ⚖️ Neutral 🌐 Hugging Face ↗ Open Full Page

SmolLM3: smol, multilingual, long-context reasoner

📅 08 Jul 2025 | ⏱️ 20 min read (4040 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Hugging Face

⏱️ ~20 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Industry observers note that small language models are becoming increasingly key as users seek capable models that can be deployed efficiently.
  • SmolLM3 sits in the efficiency sweet spot.
  • Sources indicate that the complete recipe: We're releasing SmolLM3 with our engineering blueprint.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Industry observers note that small language models are becoming increasingly key as users seek capable models that can be deployed efficiently. The community has produced a fascinating range of capable small models, each pushing the boundaries of what's possible at this scale. With SmolLM3, we're excited to contribute a new competitive fully open 3B model:.

SmolLM3 sits in the efficiency sweet spot. Our 3B model outperforms Llama-3.2-3B and Qwen2.5-3B while staying competitive with larger 4B alternatives (Qwen3 & Gemma3). Beyond the performance numbers, we're sharing exactly how we built it using public datasets and training frameworks.

Sources indicate that the complete recipe: We're releasing SmolLM3 with our engineering blueprint. It includes architecture details, exact data mixtures showing how we progressively boost performance across domains in a three-stage pretraining approach, and the methodology for building a hybrid reasoning model. Usually, achieving these results would require months of reverse engineering. Instead, we're providing the full methodology.

Whether you're building your own models or want to understand what drives performance at this scale, this blueprint indicates the engineering story behind competitive 3B performance.

Let’s have a look at the pretraining stage.

SmolLM3 both changed the architecture and data mixture over its predecessors. Let’s have a look at the architecture and training configurations first!

SmolLM3 follows a transformer decoder architecture with tied embedding similar to SmolLM2, building on Llama architecture with some key modifications optimized for efficiency and long context performance.

According to recent reports, grouped Query Attention (GQA): We replaced multi-head attention with grouped-query attention using 4 groups. Our ablations on a 3B model trained with 100B tokens from FineWeb-Edu revealed that GQA matches the performance of multi-head attention while significantly reducing the KV cache size during inference.

It has been revealed that noPE: We implemented NoPE from "RoPE to NoRoPE and Back Again: A Fresh Hybrid Attention Strategy" (Yang et al., 2025), selectively removing rotary position embeddings from every 4th layer. This approach improves long context performance without affecting short context capabilities, as confirmed by our ablations.

In a recent development, intra-Document Masking: Following "Analysing The Impact of Sequence Composition on Language Model Pre-Training", during training, we use attention masking to ensure tokens from different documents in the same training sequence don't attend to each other. Similar to Llama 3, this helps with faster and more stable long context training while maintaining short context performance.

Industry observers note that training Stability: Following OLMo 2, we remove weight decay from embedding layers to improve training stability. This modification contributed to more stable training dynamics, with embedding norms naturally stabilizing at healthier values during training without impacting overall performance in our ablations.

All these changes were validated through ablations using the same 3B architecture trained on 100B tokens from FineWeb-Edu, ensuring each modification either improved performance or maintained it while offering other benefits.

Training Configuration: We use a global batch size of 2.36M tokens with 4096 sequence length, a learning rate of 2e-4, and the AdamW optimizer (beta1: 0.9, beta2: 0.95) with weight decay of 0.1 and gradient clipping of 1. We use the WSD (Warmup-Stable-Decay) scheduler, with 2000  warmup steps, and a linear decay to 0 in the final 10% training steps. We use nanotron framework for the training, datatrove for data processing and lighteval for evaluation. The model was trained on 384 H100 GPUs for 24 days. You can see the distributed training setup in the following figure.

Sources indicate that in addition to architecture changes we also ablated and improved the training recipe. Let’s have a closer look.

Sources indicate that following SmolLM2's multi-stage approach, we train SmolLM3 on 11.2T tokens using a three-stage training strategy that mixes web, math, and code data with evolving proportions. We conducted extensive ablations on 3B models trained on 50B to 100B tokens to determine the data mixture and ratios.

The pretraining consists of these stages, also shown in the figure above:.

In a recent development, with these stages and mixtures we achieved very competitive performance for the base model. More on that in the evaluation section. The nanotron training configs with exact data weights can be found here. We will also share our training logs along with intermediate checkpoints.

After the main pretraining we improved the model in a mid-training stage for long context and reasoning.

Sources indicate that we call the long context adaptation and reasoning adaptation “mid-training”. They are much shorter than the main pretraining but still somewhat general and aimed at improving the model in those two domains. Let’s first have a look at long context training.

According to recent reports, after the main pretraining, we trained SmolLM3 on an additional 100B tokens to extend its context length. We sequentially extended the context window in two stages for 50B tokens each: first transitioning from 4k to 32k context with RoPE theta increased to 1.5M, then from 32k to 64k context with RoPE theta increased to 5M. Both stages upsampled math, code, and reasoning data. During ablations, we found that upsampling specific long context data such as code repositories, books, and long web pages (beyond the naturally long samples in our mixture) didn't further boost performance on RULER and HELMET benchmarks. Using NoPE and training on the decay mixture with longer sequences and increased RoPE theta values was sufficient to achieve competitive long context performance up to 64k.

In a recent development, following Qwen2.5, we use YARN to extrapolate beyond the training context length. During inference, the model can handle up to  128k context (2x extension beyond the 64k training length).

After extending the context length of the model, we trained it at a mid-training stage to incorporate reasoning capabilities. The main difference between the mid-training stage and the pre- and post-training stages is that we targeted a general capability without yet focusing on a specific domain. In our case, we wanted to train the model to reason without targeting a particular domain, such as mathematics or computer code.

It has been revealed that our mid-training dataset contained 35B tokens sourced from Open Thought’s OpenThoughts3-1.2M and a subset from NVIDIA’s Llama-Nemotron-Post-Training-Dataset-v1.1 with reasoning traces from R1. We used the ChatML chat template and wrapped packing to avoid providing too much structure to the model. We trained the model for 4 (~140B tokens) epochs and used the checkpoint for subsequent SFT stages.

The release of reasoning models like DeepSeek R1 and Qwen3 has demonstrated the powerful capabilities that emerge when models can engage in explicit reasoning. However, the community still lacks fully open recipes with public datasets to build dual instruction models that support both reasoning and non-reasoning modes. Most existing approaches involve complex reinforcement learning processes and proprietary datasets, making it difficult for researchers to reproduce and build upon these results.

Industry observers note that in this section, we explain how we tackled these challenges and share our complete recipe for building a dual instruction model. We detail how we balance performance between reasoning and non-reasoning modes through a carefully designed training pipeline that includes mid-training for general reasoning capabilities, supervised fine-tuning with synthetic data generation, and alignment using Anchored Preference Optimization (APO) - a recent variant of DPO.

Sources indicate that before diving into the training methodology, it's essential to establish how customers interact with our dual-mode model. The chat template serves as the interface that enables seamless switching between reasoning and non-reasoning modes, and its design directly impacts both our training data format and model behavior. SmolLM3's chat template allows users to control the reasoning mode during a conversation. Users can activate reasoning or non-reasoning modes by including the /think and /no_think flags, respectively, in the system prompt. In non-reasoning mode, we pre-fill the model's response with empty think blocks, similar to Qwen3, to ensure direct answers without explicit reasoning.

Sources indicate that smolLM3 supports tool calling, and its chat template incorporates two distinct sections for tool descriptions: XML Tools and Python Tools. This specific categorization proved beneficial in our experiments for the model's accurate interpretation of tool definitions in each format.

According to recent reports, the chat template provides a default system message for both reasoning modes, along with a metadata section that includes the date, knowledge cut-off date, and current reasoning mode. Customers can replace the default system message by providing one with the system role. The metadata section can be excluded by using the /system_override flag in the system prompt, offering flexibility for specific use cases.

It has been revealed that following the reasoning mid-training stage, where we trained the model on 140B tokens of general reasoning data, we proceed with Supervised Finetuning (SFT) to incorporate capabilities across both reasoning and non-reasoning modes for math, code, general reasoning, instruction following, multilinguality, and tool calling. Training a dual-mode model requires carefully balancing the data mixture to maintain strong performance in both modes across all target domains. To evaluate SmolLM3’s performance throughout training, we tracked the following domains: math, code, general reasoning, instruction following, and multilinguality.

The primary challenge we encountered when building the reasoning mode dataset was the scarcity of datasets containing reasoning traces for certain domains. To address this gap, we generated synthetic data by prompting Qwen3-32B in reasoning mode with prompts from existing non-reasoning datasets. This allowed us to improve performance in domains where the model initially struggled in reasoning mode, such as multi-turn conversations, multilinguality, and everyday conversations.

Recent findings suggest that our final data mixture was the result of extensive ablations examining the optimal ratio of reasoning to non-reasoning tokens and the composition within each mode. The resulting SFT dataset contains 1.8B tokens: 1B in non-reasoning mode and 0.8B in reasoning mode, comprising 12 non-reasoning datasets and 10 datasets with reasoning traces. We trained for 4 epochs (~8B tokens) using BFD (best-fit decreasing) packing with the loss masked on user turns and the results from tool calls.

We will release this data mixture along with our full training scripts to enable the community to reproduce and build upon our work.

After the SFT step, we performed a round of model alignment using a combination of the Tulu3 preference dataset for non-reasoning mode and new synthetic preference pairs for reasoning mode, that we generated from Qwen3-32B and Qwen3-0.6B. To ensure full coverage of all domains in the non-thinking dataset, we generated complementing thinking mode preference pairs. We selected generations from Qwen3-32B as “chosen” and responses from Qwen3-0.6B as “rejected” for alignment with Anchored Preference Optimization.

In a recent development, anchored Preference Optimization (APO) is a variant of Direct Preference Optimization (DPO) that provides a more stable optimization objective. In DPO, the reward function r_θ(x,y) measures the log-ratio of the probability of the sequence during training compared to the model at the start of training, the reference model:.

Here β controls how much the model being optimized can change relative to the reference model. The DPO loss optimizes triplets of prompts x, chosen y_w and rejected y_l responses:.

The APO objective has been shown to be more stable, and we also observed higher downstream performance in our internal ablations.

In a recent development, while downstream evaluations highlighted improvements across mathematics, science, instruction following, coding, chat, and multilingual tasks, we observed performance degradation on long context benchmarks like RULER. We traced this degradation back to the reasoning mid-training stage, where the focus on reasoning capabilities impacted long context performance. Additionally, the APO training data was limited to 24k tokens since the vast majority of our reasoning dataset fell below this length.

To mitigate this performance drop, we explored model merging as a solution.

In a recent development, model merging is a popular and powerful technique that allows combining the strengths of different models without the computational overhead of ensembling or the need for additional training. We used the MergeKit library to perform the model merging, as it includes several merging methods, including linear and non-linear merging.

Our merging recipe consists of two steps:.

The resulting model is the checkpoint we are releasing today. It maintains performance across a wide range of tasks. So let’s turn to the evaluation result both of this model as well as the base model.

Sources indicate that we evaluate base models and the instruct model both in reasoning and non-reasoning mode. Let’s first cover the base model’s performance!

In a recent development, the plot below shows SmolLM3's win rate across 12 popular benchmarks evaluating knowledge, reasoning, math, and coding capabilities. SmolLM3 consistently outperforms other 3B models and achieves competitive performance with larger 4B models including Qwen3-4B and Gemma3-4B.

Evaluation benchmarks used for the win rate: HellaSwag, ARC, Winogrande, CommonsenseQA, MMLU-CF, MMLU Pro CF, PIQA, OpenBookQA, GSM8K, MATH, HumanEval+, MBPP+.

SmolLM3 achieves first or second place on knowledge and reasoning benchmarks (HellaSwag, ARC, BoolQ), demonstrating strong performance in these core capabilities. Math and coding performance is competitive within the 3B class. Long-context performance on Ruler 64k indicates the model can handle extended sequences effectively.

Industry observers note that the model demonstrates strong multilingual performance across five major European languages when evaluated on multilingual benchmarks including Global MMLU, MLMM HellaSwag, Flores-200, Belebele, testing knowledge, commonsense reasoning, text understanding, and translation. This shows SmolLM3 maintains consistent performance beyond English.

In summary, the base model shows very strong performance across many domains. Let’s see how this translates to the instruct model’s performance.

Since SmolLM3 has both an instruct and reasoning mode we need to evaluate the model in both modes and compare to models with same capabilities.

Recent findings suggest that we evaluate SmolLM3 against other 3B non-reasoning models and compare it to Qwen3 reasoning models in no thinking mode across multiple benchmarks. As shown in the performance chart, SmolLM3 outperforms other 3B non-reasoning models including Llama3.2 3B Instruct and Qwen2.5 3B Instruct and sits at an efficiency sweet spot between reasoning models, significantly outperforming Qwen3 1.7B while getting close to the 4B model performance at a lower computational cost.

According to recent reports, so the instruct model sits right at the pareto front of performance and cost. Let’s see how the reasoning model does!

It has been revealed that when evaluating SmolLM3's reasoning capabilities with extended thinking enabled, the model shows substantial improvements across most benchmarks compared to its non-reasoning counterpart. We observe notable gains in challenging tasks like AIME 2025 (36.7% vs 9.3%), competitive programming on LiveCodeBench (30.0% vs 15.2%), and graduate-level reasoning on GPQA Diamond (41.7% vs 35.7%).

While Qwen3 4B generally achieves the highest scores across both thinking and non-thinking modes, SmolLM3 demonstrates competitive performance within the 3B parameter class, particularly excelling in mathematical reasoning and complex problem-solving tasks. The model's dual-mode capability allows people to choose between faster inference without reasoning or more thorough analysis with extended thinking.

So the last question is: how can you use the model?

According to recent reports, the modeling code for SmolLM3 is available in transformers v4.53.0, so make sure to upgrade your transformers version. You can also load the model with the latest vllm which uses transformers as a backend.

We recommend setting temperature=0.6 and top_p=0.95 in the sampling parameters.

It has been revealed that we enable extended thinking by default, so the example above generates the output with a reasoning trace. For choosing between enabling, you can provide the /think and /no_think flags through the system prompt as shown in the snippet below for extended thinking disabled. The code for generating the response with extended thinking would be the same except that the system prompt should have /think instead of /no_think.

It has been revealed that smolLM3 supports tool calling! Just pass your list of tools under the argument xml_tools (for standard tool-calling), or python_tools (for calling tools like python functions in a  snippet).

We release SmolLM3, a small, long-context, multilingual, reasoner with up to 128k context. In addition to the model checkpoint we release the full training recipe including pre-training, mid-training, post-training, and synthetic data generation as well as the datasets (coming shortly). We hope this model proves useful to the community and the recipe will allow other groups to improve upon it.

Congratulations to the team on the release of SmolLM3! This is a really impressive piece of work, and the detailed ablations on GQA, NoPE, and the other architectural tweaks are super valuable for the community.

According to recent reports, your focus on pushing the boundaries of long-context performance is fascinating. It reminded me of a recent paper that tackles the same challenge from a completely different architectural angle.

I was just reading about ATLAS from Google Research (arXiv:2505.23735), which proposes replacing the standard attention mechanism with a modern recurrent "long-term memory module".

Recent findings suggest that the core idea is to overcome the limitations of both Transformers and older RNNs by creating a memory that explicitly "learns to memorize the context" instead of just individual tokens. They introduce a concept called the Omega Rule, which updates the memory based on a sliding window of the past, rather than the "online" token-by-token enhancement that can lead to concerns like the "lost in the middle" problem.

The results they show are compelling, especially its ability to scale effectively to a 10M context length on the BABILong benchmark.

It has been revealed that it's exciting to see two powerful—and very different—approaches for scaling context length. One path is perfecting the Transformer architecture (like SmolLM3), and the other is designing latest memory-centric recurrent models (like ATLAS).

I'm curious to hear your thoughts on the future of these alternative architectures and if you envision a future where hybrid models might combine the best of both worlds!

Latest Update: Tiny flaws in diamonds could unlock a quantum computing revolution

📅 13 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 6 min read (1175 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Sciencedaily

⏱️ ~6 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • A new computational technique could accelerate the search for diamond materials capable of powering future quantum computers and highly sensitive sensors.
  • The approach has already revealed new candidates for quantum computing and sensing applications.
  • It has been revealed that one of the biggest challenges in developing quantum technology is finding materials that can maintain delicate quantum states under practical conditions.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

A new computational technique could accelerate the search for diamond materials capable of powering future quantum computers and highly sensitive sensors. Developed by a researcher at the U.S. Department of Energy's (DOE) Princeton Plasma Physics Laboratory (PPPL), the method makes it much easier to identify promising materials for quantum technology, potentially opening the door to advances across many areas of science.

The approach has already revealed new candidates for quantum computing and sensing applications. The findings were recently published in ACS Central Science and have attracted attention from other researchers in the field.

It has been revealed that one of the biggest challenges in developing quantum technology is finding materials that can maintain delicate quantum states under practical conditions. Many candidates require extremely low temperatures to function reliably. Diamond materials stand out because certain quantum properties can remain useful even at room temperature.

This capability could help advance technologies that are important to national research priorities and the development of next-generation computing. Quantum sensors promise levels of sensitivity and precision beyond those of conventional instruments, while quantum computers could eventually solve certain extraordinarily complex problems much faster than today's most powerful supercomputers.

Why Imperfect Diamonds Could Be the Key to Quantum Computing.

Sources indicate that although diamonds are made of carbon atoms, a flawless diamond crystal is not enough to create a useful quantum computing system. The key lies in tiny irregularities within the crystal structure.

Industry observers note that these imperfections, known as defects, can occur when a carbon atom is absent from its normal position, when another element replaces a carbon atom, or when both changes occur together. The atoms surrounding these defects can form qubits, the basic units used to store and process quantum information in quantum computers and sensors.

Finding the most useful defects, however, has been difficult. Accurately modeling their quantum behavior traditionally requires enormous computational resources, making it challenging to evaluate large numbers of possible candidates.

A Simpler Way to Discover Better Diamond Qubits.

Sources indicate that mark Martirez, a staff research scientist at PPPL, developed a way to dramatically reduce the complexity of these calculations. Instead of simulating a much larger diamond structure, he isolates a small region containing just 16 to 30 atoms around a defect.

It has been revealed that by "carving out" this tiny atomic cluster and treating it like a separate molecule, Martirez can use powerful computational methods that chemists have spent decades refining. These established techniques make it possible to analyze the quantum properties of diamond defects much more efficiently without sacrificing the high level of accuracy needed for the calculations.

Sources indicate that "Because we're treating the qubits as molecules, the cost of calculating these defects is equivalent to the cost of just modeling a simple molecule," Martirez mentioned. "This method really opened the floodgates" in terms of how qubits can be assessed.

It has been revealed that the upcoming technique allows researchers to calculate how different qubits respond to laser light and microwave pulses far more promptly than before. Using this approach, the team identified promising defects involving boron and oxygen that could serve as new types of qubits.

Newly introduced Diamond Defects Reveal a Spectrum of Quantum Colors.

Light plays an key role in how scientists interact with diamond qubits. Researchers use lasers and microwave pulses to manipulate their quantum states and retrieve stored information.

Much of the previous work in this area has centered on a defect known as the nitrogen-vacancy center. This structure forms when a nitrogen atom takes the place of a carbon atom in a diamond crystal, while an adjacent position that would normally contain another carbon atom remains empty.

Under laser illumination, this type of defect can emit red light when it occupies a particular quantum state.

Sources indicate that the newly investigated defects offer different optical properties. Oxygen defects can produce blue light, while those involving boron emit ultraviolet light.

Industry observers note that these differences could make it possible to combine several types of qubits within a single quantum device. Because each type responds differently to light, researchers might be able to interact with one group of qubits without disturbing another.

"One could imagine, then, combining different qubits of different responses, so you can basically probe one qubit but not the other," Martirez said.

Industry observers note that beyond identifying fresh candidates, the findings suggest a broader change in how researchers approach quantum technology. Diamond qubits have traditionally been studied primarily through physics, but understanding their underlying chemistry could provide additional ways to design them.

Martirez believes that researchers could eventually engineer qubits for particular functions using principles similar to those applied when chemists create specialized molecules, including compounds designed for new medications.

How Quantum Chemistry Could Transform Future Research.

Industry observers note that the potential benefits extend well beyond the development of quantum computers themselves. Martirez sees an intriguing possibility in which advances made possible by quantum chemistry eventually lead to quantum technologies that help improve the field of chemistry.

In other words, quantum chemistry could develop the very tools needed to "enrich itself" in the coming decades.

A practical quantum system containing multiple qubits could make molecular calculations substantially more accurate. That would allow scientists to study increasingly complex chemical structures, including large biological molecules and proteins, with a level of detail that is difficult to achieve using conventional methods.

"We could describe larger molecules, biomolecules, proteins and everything like that in a more accurate way, and that could improve all the chemical-adjacent industries, such as pharmaceutical science and materials science. Even our fundamental understanding of molecular systems could be enriched.".

Such improvements could have far-reaching implications for pharmaceutical development, materials research, and the fundamental study of how molecules behave.

According to recent reports, martirez also hopes the research will encourage more chemists to explore solid-state physics. Although building advanced quantum computers is often viewed as a challenge primarily for physicists, he argues that chemistry offers valuable expertise that could help accelerate progress.

"At this moment in time, there's a great emphasis on building the first state-of-the-art qubit computer," he noted. "But it's not just physicists who should be participating in this research. Chemists have decades of developed intuition about chemical systems that could be easily translated into understanding defects in solids as well.".

By bringing these disciplines together, scientists may be able to develop more effective ways to discover, understand, and eventually engineer the quantum materials needed for future technologies.

The research was funded through PPPL's Laboratory Directed Research and Development program under prime contract number DE-AC02-09CH11466, with additional support from the DOE Office of Science, Office of Fusion Energy Sciences.

General ⚖️ Neutral 🌐 Sciencedaily ↗ Open Full Page

Quantum computers are getting too powerful to check. Scientists have a solution

📅 17 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 5 min read (962 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Sciencedaily

⏱️ ~5 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • As quantum computers grow more powerful, researchers face a troubling question: How can they know whether the results are correct when conventional computers can no longer verify them?
  • Industry observers note that the technique uses experimental measurements to reconstruct how a quantum system behaves, then calculates how uncertainties in that reconstruction affect the results.
  • Industry observers note that quantum systems are expected to become capable of solving increasingly complex problems that traditional computers struggle with or cannot handle at all.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

As quantum computers grow more powerful, researchers face a troubling question: How can they know whether the results are correct when conventional computers can no longer verify them? Scientists have now developed a promising new method that could help overcome this challenge by measuring the accuracy of quantum simulations and identifying how much uncertainty their predictions contain.

Industry observers note that the technique uses experimental measurements to reconstruct how a quantum system behaves, then calculates how uncertainties in that reconstruction affect the results. Researchers successfully demonstrated the approach using a quantum simulator with up to 51 qubits in Innsbruck, Austria.

Industry observers note that quantum systems are expected to become capable of solving increasingly complex problems that traditional computers struggle with or cannot handle at all. However, this progress creates a verification problem. When a simulation is small enough, scientists can compare its results with calculations performed on a conventional computer. As quantum systems grow beyond those limits, that direct comparison becomes impractical, making alternative ways to assess their reliability essential.

A Latest Way to Measure Quantum Computing Accuracy.

The breakthrough comes from an international research team led by Tristan Kraft at the Technical University of Munich and Peter Zoller at the University of Innsbruck and the Institute for Quantum Optics and Quantum Information of the Austrian Academy of Sciences, working alongside Barbara Kraus of the Technical University of Munich. The researchers developed a method for experimentally determining how a quantum simulator operates and translating uncertainties in its behavior into measurable limits on the accuracy of its results.

Sources indicate that quantum simulators are specialized physical systems designed to reproduce the behavior of other quantum systems. They are especially useful for investigating situations involving large numbers of interacting particles, where the calculations required can quickly overwhelm even powerful conventional computers.

But quantum experiments are never entirely free from errors. "But no real experiment is perfect," states Tristan Kraft. "Interactions may turn out differently than expected, the system is influenced by its environment, and measurements are also subject to uncertainties.".

Rather than assuming a quantum simulator behaves exactly as intended, the new approach examines experimental data to determine what is actually happening inside the system. This allows researchers to identify important interactions and account for disturbances such as fluctuations and noise.

According to recent reports, "From this data, we determine the relevant interactions as well as key influences from fluctuations and noise. We then calculate how the uncertainties in this model affect the simulation results," explains Tristan Kraft. "The quantum simulator thus provides not just a single value, but a result with error margins that quantify its accuracy.".

Successfully Tested on a 51 Qubit Quantum Simulator.

To evaluate the method, the researchers began with a relatively small quantum system containing ten trapped ions. Because conventional computers can still calculate the behavior of a system of this size, the team could test its reconstructed models and calculated error limits against independent measurements.

After this initial validation, the researchers expanded their experiments to a chain of 51 trapped ions. The larger demonstration, carried out by a team led by Manoj Joshi and Christian Roos using an ion trap quantum simulator, showed that the technique could also work with substantially more complex quantum systems.

This represents an notable step toward establishing how trustworthy quantum simulation results are, particularly as quantum devices advance into territory where direct verification with traditional computing methods becomes increasingly difficult.

Extending the Breakthrough to More Complex Quantum Systems.

Sources indicate that the next challenge is to bring the technique to two-dimensional quantum simulators. These systems can model more complicated interactions among particles, making them valuable for exploring quantum physics. At the same time, their growing complexity makes their results particularly difficult to confirm using conventional calculations.

Industry observers note that "This is particularly crucial because classical calculations for such systems become significantly more difficult as the number of particles increases," explains quantum computing pioneer Peter Zoller. "This also makes independent verification of the results increasingly complex, making the question of experimentally determined error limits all the more important.".

The researchers are now adapting their method for the newest generation of two-dimensional quantum simulators, which offer improved precision and can investigate systems containing larger numbers of particles.

Looking further ahead, the approach could help scientists establish a more meaningful way to measure quantum advantage, the ability of quantum systems to outperform conventional computers. Instead of comparing machines based only on their processing speed or the size of the problems they can handle, researchers could also examine how accurately each system produces its answers.

"After all, when a classical computer and a quantum simulator tackle the same problem, it's not just a matter of which one delivers a result faster. What's also crucial is which one can solve the problem with a smaller, verifiable margin of error," states Peter Zoller.

According to recent reports, this shift could change how progress in quantum computing is evaluated. Future breakthroughs may be judged not simply by how many particles a simulator can model or how rapidly it performs calculations, but by its ability to solve increasingly difficult problems with demonstrably reliable results.

The findings were published in Physical Review X. The research received support from the Austrian Science Fund (FWF), the German Ministry of Research, Technology and Space, the European Union, BMW, and other funding organizations.

  • "Do you know the closest ATM?" and "I was charged twice, the refund never arrived, and now my card is blocked" are both customer messages.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Stay up to date with AI tools, model releases, and developer workflows that matter.

Industry observers note that 7 Day Free Trial. Cancel Anytime.

"Do you know the closest ATM?" and "I was charged twice, the refund never arrived, and now my card is blocked" are both customer messages. Most AI apps send both to the same large model and pay large-model prices for each one.

Model routing fixes that. A router looks at each request and sends it to the cheapest model that can handle it, and keeps the expensive model for the requests that need it.

Recent findings suggest that in this guide we'll cover what model routing is, how routers decide, and what it saves. Then we'll build a small router in about 60 lines of JavaScript and run it over 200 customer messages. At one setting it matched a large model's accuracy for about a third of the cost. At another it came within a point and a half for 89% less.

According to recent reports, model routing in AI is the practice of sending each request to the model best suited to it, instead of sending every request to one model. A router sits between your app and a pool of models, reads each request, and picks a model based on what you care about: cost, speed, or quality.

Recent findings suggest that you'll also see it called AI model routing, LLM routing, or LLM model routing. They all mean the same thing. The pool might be a small and a large model from one provider, or models from several providers behind one API.

The idea rests on one observation: most requests are easy. A small model answers them as well as a large one, in a fraction of the time and for a fraction of the price. The router's whole job is finding the hard ones.

The diagram below demonstrates a typical AI model routing architecture.

Model routing works in three steps: the router reads the request, decides which model should answer it, and forwards the request to that model. The middle step is where routers differ. Routing tools decide which model to use in one of four ways.

Sources indicate that rule-based routing uses rules you write by hand. Requests from free-plan users go to a small model. Anything tagged as code goes to a coding model. Prompts over a certain length go to a model with a bigger context window. It's simple, predictable, and free to run, but the rules only know what you thought of in advance.

Industry observers note that intelligent model routing uses a model to make the decision. A small, fast classifier reads each request and predicts which model in the pool will answer it well. You'll also see it called smart or dynamic model routing.

Two more terms come up here. Task-aware routing picks a model by the kind of job, like summarising, coding, or answering a support question. Context-aware routing also looks at what surrounds the request, like the conversation so far, the user, or the tools available.

The big platforms work this way. Microsoft describes its Foundry model router as "a trained language model" that picks a model for each prompt in real time. Google claims Gemini Notebook uses its upcoming Decisions API as a real-time router, serving everyday queries with up to 40% lower latency. I've tested the Google Decisions API against Jev on the same messages we'll use below.

Cascade routing tries the cheapest model first and only moves up when the answer isn't good enough. The usual test is confidence: if the cheap model is sure, keep its answer. If it isn't, send the request to a stronger model. It's also called confidence-based routing, and it's what we'll build below.

A cascade needs no separate classifier, because the first model's own confidence does the routing. The trade-off is that escalated requests pay for two models and wait for both.

Fallback routing is about staying up, not saving money. If a model times out, hits a rate limit, or its provider has an outage, the router sends the request to the next model on a list. Most production routers combine fallbacks with one of the three methods above.

The main benefits of model routing in AI systems are lower cost, faster responses, and fewer outages, without giving up quality on the hard requests.

Recent findings suggest that we'll build a cascade router for a job every support tool has: sorting customer messages. Each message gets one of ten labels, like atm support or request refund.

The test set is 200 messages from Banking77, a public set of banking support messages: ten labels, 20 messages each. They're the same 200 messages from my zero shot classification test, which is where the single-model numbers below come from.

Put both keys in a .env file and run the examples with node --env-file=.env. It's the same setup as in my guide to getting a YouTube API key.

Create router.mjs. The first function sends the message to Jev with one multiple-choice question, and returns the label Jev picked along with its confidence:.

Confidence runs from 0 to 1. When nearly all the probability sits on one label, it's close to 1. When Jev is torn between two labels, it drops.

The second function asks Claude Opus 5.5 the same question. The output_config block limits the answer to one of our labels, so there's no free text to parse. SitePoint's guide to LLM structured output with JSON Schema explains how that works.

The router itself is about a dozen lines:.

According to recent reports, if Jev is at least 80% confident, its answer goes straight back. If not, Claude answers instead. And if Claude fails, the router falls back to Jev's answer, because a shaky answer beats an error page.

Try it on an easy message and a harder one:.

Sources indicate that jev was sure about the lost card. On the ATM question it leaned towards card acceptance with a confidence of 0.64, so the router asked Claude, which got it right.

Because cheap, strong, and threshold are options, the same function routes between any two models.

In a recent development, model routing reduces AI costs by keeping easy requests on a cheap model and paying for the expensive one only when it's needed. Here's what that looked like on our 200 messages, starting with each model on its own:.

Opus gets six more messages right out of 200, and costs more than 120 times as much.

Now the router, at four confidence thresholds:.

Speed improved too. At the 0.8 threshold, the messages Jev kept came back in a median of 227 ms. The ones that escalated took about 2.1 seconds, because they waited for both models.

A note on method: I ran every message through both models once and saved the answers, then replayed the router over them at each threshold. That's how you compare thresholds without paying for the same test four times.

In a recent development, then I ran the router live to check. At 0.95 it scored the same 95.0% and sent 61 messages to Opus. At 0.8 it scored 93.5% and sent 20, a point under the replay. Two answers moved: one of Jev's confidence scores landed at 0.82 instead of 0.78, just over the line, and Opus changed its answer on one message. Scores near the threshold shift a little between runs, so leave yourself a margin.

Recent findings suggest that the choice of cheap model matters less than you'd think. With Google's Gemini Decision 1 in first place instead of Jev, a 0.7 threshold reached the same 95% for US$0.28 per 1,000 messages.

Recent findings suggest that model routing can cost a little quality, and the threshold decides how much. In our test the gap to Opus ranged from nothing at 0.95 to two points at 0.7.

In a recent development, the loss comes from one place: answers the cheap model got wrong while feeling sure. At the 0.8 threshold, Jev kept five wrong answers because its confidence was above the line. Opus got four of those five wrong as well, so only one was a real loss: "Do all ATMs take this card?", which Jev filed under card acceptance with a confidence of 0.91.

Industry observers note that escalating isn't risk-free either. On one message, Jev had the right label with a confidence of 0.44, and Opus overruled it with the wrong one.

To optimize costs using AI model routing, measure first, route second, and keep measuring. These six steps cover LLM model routing cost optimization for any pair of models:.

The return is easy to estimate once you know the split. If nine in ten requests stay on a model that costs 1% as much, the bill drops by about 89%, which is what we measured.

In a recent development, several inference providers have multi-model routing built in, and most AI gateway platforms support model routing too, so you don't have to write your own. As of November 2026, these are the top model routing solutions for AI apps. Each name links to the tool's model routing docs:.

Hosted model routing platforms for large language models decide for you, which is the fastest way to start. A hand-built router like ours takes more work, but you choose the signal and you can see why every request went where it did.

An LLM router is the component that does model routing for large language models. It can be a function in your own code, like the one in this guide, a hosted model such as Microsoft Foundry's model router, or a feature of an AI gateway.

Industry observers note that smart model routing is another name for intelligent model routing: a model, not a hand-written rule, decides where each request goes. Dynamic model routing means the same thing.

Recent findings suggest that the ROI of AI model routing depends on how much of your traffic a cheaper model can handle. In our test, a 0.8 threshold kept 89.5% of messages on the cheap model and cut the cost per 1,000 messages from US$1.96 to US$0.22, for about a point of accuracy. The build was about 60 lines of code.

OpenRouter's auto model routing works through its Auto Router. You set the model to openrouter/auto, and a decision model picks a model and a reasoning effort for each request. You pay the standard rate of whichever model it selects, with no extra fee.

It has been revealed that openClaw model routing is a primary model plus an ordered list of fallbacks. In the OpenClaw model routing configuration you set agents.defaults.model.primary and agents.defaults.model.fallbacks, and an agent can override the fallback list. When a model fails, OpenClaw first rotates auth profiles on the same provider, then moves to the next model on the list, as its model failover docs describe. That makes it fallback routing, not cost-based routing.

An AI gateway simplifies model routing by putting every model behind one API, one set of keys, and one place for logs. Your app calls the gateway, and the routing rules live in config instead of code, so changing a model doesn't need a deploy.

Sources indicate that mid-stream failover is when a router switches models after a streamed response has already started, because the first model failed partway through. It's the hardest kind of failover, because the user has already seen part of an answer. Many routers only fail over before the first token arrives and return an error after that, so check what your gateway does.

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Sources indicate that upskill your LLMs With Gradio MCP Servers Have you ever wanted your favorite Large Language Model (LLM) to do more than just answer questions? What if it could edit images for you, browse the web, or organize your email inbox?

In a recent development, well, now it can! In this blog post, I'll show you:.

The Model Context Protocol (MCP) is an open standard that enables developers to build secure, two-way connections between an LLM and a set of tools. For example, if you create an MCP server that exposes a tool capable of transcribing a video, then you can connect an LLM client (such as Cursor, Claude Code, or Cline) to the server. The LLM will then know how to transcribe videos and use this tool for you depending on your request.

It has been revealed that in short, an MCP server is a standard way to upskill your LLM by granting it a newly introduced ability. Think of it like the apps on your smartphone. On its own, your smartphone can't edit images, but you can download an app to do this from the app store. Now, if only there were an app store for MCP servers? 🤔.

Hugging Face Spaces is the world's largest collection of AI applications. Most of these spaces perform a specialized task with an AI model. For example:.

Recent findings suggest that these spaces are implemented with Gradio, an open source python package for creating AI-powered web servers. As of version 5.28.0, Gradio apps support the MCP protocol.

That means that Hugging Face Spaces is the one place where you can find thousands of AI-powered abilities for your LLM, aka the MCP App Store!

Want to browse the app store? Visit this link. Manually, you can filter for MCP Compatible in https://hf.co/spaces.

Sources indicate that flux.1 Kontext[dev] is an impressive model that can edit an image from a plain text prompt. For example, if you ask it to "dye my hair blue" and upload a photo of yourself, the model will return the photo but with you having blue hair!

Let's plug this model as an MCP server into an LLM and have it edit images for us. Follow these steps:.

Recent findings suggest that using a popular public space as a tool may mean you have to wait longer to receive results. If you visit the space, you can click "Duplicate This Space" to create a private version of the space for yourself. If the space is using "ZeroGPU", you may need to enhancement to a PRO account to duplicate it.

Industry observers note that this blog post has walked you through the exciting new capabilities that the Model Context Protocol (MCP) brings to Large Language Models. We've seen how Gradio apps, particularly those hosted on Hugging Face Spaces, are now fully MCP compliant, effectively turning Spaces into a vibrant "App Store" for LLM tools. It’s been nearly three years since Best Buy decided to ditch selling physical copies of movies, stripping its inventory from both its brick-and-mortar stores and its online catalog. But with the growing rise of 4K Blu-ray collections as a vinyl-esque collector’s item, the electronics giant has slowly begun dipping its toes back into the physical media game.

Sources indicate that as spotted by TheHDRoom on Twitter and on the 4K Blu-ray subreddit, Best Buy is now selling 14 different 4K Blu-rays on its website, marking another step in the brand’s slow return to selling physical media. These films include:.

Technically, Blu-ray returned to Best Buy’s online storefront in August of 2025, when it opened a third-party marketplace similar to Amazon or Walmart. These titles, however, are shipped and sold by Best Buy. Everything’s still online-only, unfortunately, save for The Odyssey, which introduced in-store shelf displays alongside yesterday’s release date. It shouldn’t come as too much of a surprise that The Odyssey is getting some special treatment; in addition to its status as a box office juggernaut, Nolan’s previous movie, Oppenheimer, initially sold out of physical copies in its first week of release in 2023.

Outside of these 14 titles, additional Blu-rays continue to be sold through Best Buy’s third-party marketplace.
