Creating custom kernels for the AMD MI300

📅 09 Jul 2025 | ⏱️ 32 min read (6413 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Hugging Face

⏱️ ~32 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Industry observers note that more than a billion per day: that’s a low estimate of how many requests ChatGPT handles daily, a number which is unlikely to go down soon.
  • Industry observers note that but where might that gain come from?
  • It has been revealed that kernels are essential for running operations in neural networks—without a kernel, an operation effectively can't be used.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Industry observers note that more than a billion per day: that’s a low estimate of how many requests ChatGPT handles daily, a number which is unlikely to go down soon. For each request and each generated token, we run an inference of a multi-billion parameters model. This is why model optimization is paramount at each and every level: when one deals with these kinds of scale, even a 1% latency or power gain can bring huge savings.

Industry observers note that but where might that gain come from? Model architectures are already well established, and popular models have had quantized weight for a long time now. However, a crucial level at which we can optimize model inference remains: the kernel level. Kernels are the algorithms executed when you do any operation in your network: there are matrix multiplication kernels, convolution kernels, batch normalization kernels, etc. Kernels are low-level, highly-optimized algorithms, often tailored for the device they will be running on. They are notoriously long and hard to write, and require a good understanding of the inner working of the GPU.

It has been revealed that kernels are essential for running operations in neural networks—without a kernel, an operation effectively can't be used. Because of this, new innovations often launch with a "day 0" kernel, typically optimized only for the latest Nvidia hardware. This approach excludes many other devices, particularly AMD GPUs, which, despite offering comparable or superior specs, are often overlooked by kernel developers. Hugging Face collaborated with AMD to deliver state-of-the-art performance on AMD platforms and make it benefit the open source community. As part of this partnership, we decided with AMD to focus on delivering open-source optimized kernels to improve the performance of serving Llama 3.1 405B in FP8 on a node of 8 MI300X using VLLM.

It has been revealed that in this blog post, we'll explore how we optimized performance for the MI300X and how each kernel was individually fine-tuned. But first, let’s look at the performance gains achieved using our custom kernels. By combining the following three optimized kernels:.

we achieved significant speedups when running VLLM on a node powered by MI300X GPUs.

Measures were taken with input size 1 and output size 128 to mimic decoding regime. We measure decoding latency using the median over 30 iterations.

Those performance gains were measured in VLLM, but you may also use the kernels separately, as described in the “How to” section that follows.

Industry observers note that all kernels described previously are available on the hf-rocm-kernels repository located here. In it, you will find instructions on how to install the package, the source code for each kernels, their respective python bindings, various benchmarking scripts and a test suite. Using benchmarking scripts and a MI300X, you may even reproduce from this blog post. To ensure same results for Torch or VLLM, you can use the same container as we did. You can also use the repo as a base to build your own kernels: it has instructions on how to bind a CUDA-style kernel to python and a simple sample kernel. You may even have a look at branches under development for fresh kernels, like a compute-and-communicate kernel as described here.

The kernels described will soon be integrated in the AMD fork of the VLLM project, but if you want to have a look at how you might do something like that yourself, you may check out this branch and this document.

Sources indicate that we are first going to do a quick refresher on the architecture of the device we are working on: the MI300X. Then, we are going to take a look at the state of our model’s inference before optimizing it. This will allow us to identify bottlenecks and know which custom kernels we need to write. Then, we will take a look at each kernel we have written, which will give us an opportunity to explore how kernel optimization is conducted through many angles.

According to recent reports, before we dive into optimizing GPU code, we need to know how a GPU works. There are a lot of resources out there that already do a great job of explaining the inner workings of your GPU, which I will link right here, here and here. We are still going to run through the different levels of the GPU, as a quick refresher. If you want to skip the refresher and get directly into the details of our custom kernels, click here!

The smallest unit of work in the GPU is the thread. Any time any work is done on a GPU, it’s because a thread executed an instruction. Instructions are basic operations like additions, multiplication, conversion from one data type to another, or loads and stores. Each thread has its own memory, called registers (or VGPRs), which only it can access. A thread can have a maximum of 256 registers, each 32-bit wide. Below is represented a thread with access to its 256 VGPRs.

Recent findings suggest that threads, except when using load or store instructions, can only execute instructions on their own registers. For instance, to add two vectors A and B together, each thread is going to 1) load in its registers an element from A and 2) another from B, then 3) perform the addition and store the result in another register, and finally 4) store the value from that register in memory. That’s a total of 4 instructions.

The next unit of work is a warp: each warp is composed of 64 threads. Warps don’t have their own memory, but they are of interest to us because all threads in a warp must execute the same instruction at the same time. This is both a guarantee and a constraint.

Warps also allow for different threads to exchange information coming from their registers with other threads in the same warp. Although different threads in a warp have access to different data, the fact that they all have to execute the same instructions means that when writing a kernel, warp-level behavior is what you need to think about.

Warps are bundled together into thread blocks: thread blocks are software abstractions, but run on a hardware component called a compute unit (CU). A single compute unit can run multiple thread blocks at once, but it can only fit 16 warps. Each compute unit has a dedicated L1 cache and shared memory. L1 cache cannot be controlled or allocated and helps with data reuse of all warps situated on the CU. Conversely, shared memory can be allocated and used as a storage shared by all warps. For instance, when we want all warps (and thus threads) in a compute unit to access the same buffer, we allocate it in shared memory. Both shared memory and L1 cache are fast to access because they are “close” to the threads.

Thread blocks also offer the ability to synchronize all threads running inside: this is quite useful when dealing with operations that impact shared memory, like initializing an array in shared memory to zero or reduction operations. In general, when writing a kernel, thread blocks are the highest level to take into consideration: it’s very hard to synchronize different thread blocks or make them interact in any way whatsoever. Kernel throughput is tightly linked to the number of compute unit present on the GPU: the more CUs there are, the more thread blocks can be run at the same time, which increases throughput if you manage to use all CUs.

Compute units are then grouped into accelerator complex dies (XCDs), which hold 38 compute units each. Although CUs may not interact with each others, they all share a L2 cache which you can’t control but still may prove useful when re-using data. For instance, when accessing memory, having two compute units located on the same XCD access the same data will reduce loading latency by a lot. L2 cache is quite large: it has a size of 4MB, while shared memory has a size of 64kB and L1 cache contains 32kB.

By assembling 8 XCDs (which gives us 8 * 38 = 304 CUs) and adding a last level of cache (called infinity cache, with 256MB) and a huge quantity of video ram (192GB) we get the MI300X.

All XCDs, and thus all threads, have access to the VRAM, but getting there is quite slow. As you get further away from thread-level, memory becomes slower to access but has a larger size and larger scope, meaning it serves more threads. When optimizing a kernel, there is always a balance to strike between doing lots of operations or loading lots of data, but in general, you want to access the VRAM (commonly referred to as global memory) as little as possible.

According to recent reports, when looking at this figure, we can see why GPUs are referred to as “massively parallel”: here, we have 304 compute units, which can each run 16 warps, each with 64 threads. This means that we can have up to 311296 threads running at the same time, each executing an instruction of its own. Keep in mind an instruction is something basic like an addition, so simple routines like Newton’s method can be quite long to run for a single thread. GPUs are not optimized for instructions to run fast, i.e. for the latency of each instruction to be low: that would be a latency-oriented device. They are optimized for many threads to be run together, consuming and outputting a large quantity of data: it is a throughput-oriented device. When optimizing a kernel for the GPU, we adapt in consequence: it is better to have an algorithm running a few instructions on many threads at once, than having it run many instructions on a few threads. Hence calling algorithms running on GPUs “parallel”.

What can get in the way of such algorithms running in an optimized manner are three things: when there is a lot of data to load (memory bound), when there are many operations to performs (compute bound) or when threads have to work together (synchronization overhead).

Recent findings suggest that when optimizing a workload, the first thing to do before writing a single line of code is to profile the current state of the workload. In our case, we are going to profile the model inference in VLLM to get an idea of how much time each operation is taking up. This can help identify major bottlenecks and which kernels we can tackle first for maximum speedup. For instance, here is the breakdown for batch size 32:.

We can see the different parts of the network through each slice:.

Already we can see that most of the latency comes from GEMMs and communications, but also that attention and the operations surrounding it are not a major contributor to latency. This can come as a surprise, because a lot of papers focus on attention and reducing its cost, but it seems that through a combination of KV caching and FlashAttention, which has already been optimized in VLLM, this part may no longer be a top priority. Surprisingly, the two calls made to the “RMS norm” kernel are quite costly, so there might be a large benefit to optimizing that kernel. Along with the SwiGLU kernel, they represent 15% of the total latency, which is not negligible. All in all, working on those two kernels, plus trying to gain a small speedup on GEMMs may be our best course of action. To check that this performance breakdown is not a fluke, we can take a look at other batch sizes:.

In a recent development, we can see the pattern that emerged for batch size 32 holds up for other batch sizes, albeit with the latency contribution of GEMMs and communications becoming greater as the batch size increases. Also, it seems that batch size 32 is an outlier when it comes to the latency of GEMMs: it’s probably because the GEMMs chosen when batch size is 32 have been manually tuned or because batch size 32 presents good memory alignment patterns, so GEMMs for batch size 32 are faster than for batch size 24 or 28.

Now that we have identified some hot spots to optimize, let’s take a look at the first kernel we wrote: the RMS norm kernel.

Industry observers note that in each decoder block, we have two main parts: an attention block and an MLP block. Both begin with a residual connection between two inputs: the current hidden states x x x and the residual r r r . Both have the same shape, which is n n n rows (as many as there are tokens) and d d d columns. After they are added together, we apply a row-wise Root Mean Square (RMS) norm to x x x and, since the model is in FP8, we quantize x x x to FP8 using a scale s s s . Simply fusing those three operations into a single kernel can deliver a nice performance boost. Mathematically, the operations we have to perform are the following:.

i+j+kx←x+rr←xV=∑i=1dxi2x←xV+ϵxQ=Qfp8(s∗x∗w) \begin{align} \phantom{i + j + k} &\begin{aligned} x &\leftarrow x + r\\ r &\leftarrow x \end{aligned}\\ &\begin{aligned} V &= \sum_{i=1}^{d} x_i^2 \end{aligned}\\ &\begin{aligned} x &\leftarrow \frac{x}{\sqrt{V + \epsilon}} \\ x_Q &= Q_{\text{fp8}} \left( s * x * w\right) \end{aligned} \end{align} i+j+k​xr​←x+r←x​V​=i=1∑d​xi2​​xxQ​​←V+ϵ​x​=Qfp8​(s∗x∗w)​​​.

where w w w is a d d d -sized weight vector. Steps (1) and (3) are pretty basic. For step (1), we just need to position each thread to a different location in the tensor, load some elements of x x x and r r r , add them and store back r r r . For step (3), each thread performs some scalar operations (addition, square root, division) and a conversion to FP8. All of this, each thread can do on its own: this is perfectly suited to the parallel nature of the GPU. The step to watch out for is (2): we need to sum over d d d , which means either each thread is going to visit each of the d d d columns, or we need to exchange data between threads. The greater d d d is, the more data we would have to load for the first option, so the less viable it becomes. We are going to pick the second option: synchronize threads at the block level, and they will exchange data using the shared memory. Each thread is going to accumulate a part of V V V on its own and then we are going to sum all of those parts across the thread block, which is what we call a reduction. Since V V V is computed across an entire row, we are going to assign a thread block for each row.

When compared to out-of-the-box pytorch, the bare bones version of this kernel brings about a 10x speedup. But this is not enough: there are still many optimizations we can add on top of this.

In terms of latency, one of the most costly operation is accessing VRAM, also called global memory. Luckily, there are some easy-to-follow principles that can dramatically reduce the cost of loading data.

First, we can take a look at how much data a single thread can load in a single instruction: using the MI300X instruction guide, we see that the largest load we can make from global memory is 128 bits wide. Since we are loading FP16 data, we are going to load 128b / 16b = 8 elements per load. For fp32 elements, it would correspond to 4 elements per load.

Recent findings suggest that secondly, we make sure memory accesses are coalesced. Since each thread is part of a warp, when one thread reaches a “load” instruction, all other threads in the warp do too. For efficiency’s sake, these “load” instructions are then bundled together across the warp. The warp then collectively fetches the data needed and each thread gets the data it requires. Maximum efficiency is reached when the warp fetches a single chunk of data without any gap in it: this is what we call contiguous data. An matter arises when we need to load more data that can be loaded in one “load” instruction, and is illustrated below.

In this hypothetical scenario, we have two threads in the same warp. They need to collectively load 16 fp32 elements, without constraint on which thread loads which element. This is a typical “reduction” situation. Since a thread can only load 4 fp32 elements per instruction, we have at least two ways of reading the data, represented in scenario (a) and (b). To decide which scenario is best, we need to look at this from warp perspective, not thread perspective. In scenario (a), the first load fetches elements 0,1,2,3,8,9,10,11 : we see that the data is not contiguous, because there is a gap between elements 3 and 8. While in scenario (b), the first load fetches elements 0,1,2,3,4,5,6,7 : we load contiguous data. Same goes for the second load. Thus scenario (b) is better. Although in scenario (a) we end up with 8 contiguous elements per thread, this does not matter: what matters is whether or not the warp loads contiguous data. This matters because if the warp can only load 8 contiguous elements in one cycle, then each load of scenario (a) is processed in two cycles, while in scenario (b), each load only needs the one cycle.

It has been revealed that third, we reduce the number of stores: when we look at steps (1) and (3) we can see that there are only two stores needed: one for r r r and one for xQ x_Q xQ​ . After step (1) we can already store r r r and be done with that. But we still need to access the modified version of x x x after step (2) is done. To do that, we can store the modified version of x x x in global memory and reload it after step (2) is done and rely on cache hits when reloading it. Or, if x x x is small enough, we can store its modified version in shared memory: if x x x is in FP16 and we only have one thread block per CU, then we can store 64KB / 2B = 32 * 1024 elements in shared memory per thread block. In the case of Llama 405B, d d d is equal to 16384, so that fits. Using shared memory provides a nice speedup over relying on cache hits, especially when many thread blocks are active at once: if the L1 cache is not big enough to fit the whole of x x x, then we have to rely on L2 cache, which is shared by 38 CUs.

Apart from memory access, we can also optimize computational efficiency, but we are going to leave that for the next kernel, as they will be similar in both cases.

When we apply the optimizations discussed above, we get the following results:.

with a [X, 16384] shaped FP16 input tensor. The most basic version of our kernel, referred to as “Pointwise”, has no memory-related optimization and already indicates at least a x4 speedup over torch. It is less optimal than VLLM’s implementation of the kernel, but our “Vectorized” implementation beats both “Pointwise” and VLLM. This is the version of the kernel that implements coalesced 128 bits loads, which is only surpassed by the “Vectorized + SMEM” (SMEM stands for shared memory) implementation, that offers a notably better speedup ratio than VLLM for both low and high batch sizes.

In the MLP block, after the kernel we have just written about, comes a projection which we have referred up to this point as “Gate / Up” projection. The reason we call it that way is because the “Gate / Up” projection is actually a concatenation of two projections with the same input: “Gate” and “Up”. Thus, we will write the result x x x of the “Gate / Up” projection as x=xG∣xU x = x_G | x_U x=xG​∣xU​ where ∣ | ∣ is the concatenation operator applied along the column axis. xG x_G xG​ and xU x_U xU​ have the same dimensions. The reason we need those two projections is the SwiGLU activation function that comes right after, which results y y y is defined by equation (4). The SwiGLU activation function is followed by the “Down” projection, which in our case is in FP8, so we also need to quantize y y y as shown in equation (5):.

i+j+ky=σ(xG)⋅xUyQ=QFP8(s∗y) \begin{align} \phantom{i + j + k}& \begin{aligned} y = \sigma \left( x_G \right) \cdot x_U \\\end{aligned}\\ &\begin{aligned} y_Q = Q_\text{FP8} \left( s * y \right) \end{aligned} \end{align} i+j+k​y=σ(xG​)⋅xU​​yQ​=QFP8​(s∗y)​​​.

Industry observers note that where σ \sigma σ is the sigmoid function: σ(x)=e−x/(1+x) \sigma (x) = e^{-x} / (1 + x) σ(x)=e−x/(1+x) . We are going to write a fused kernel that takes care of all of this. For this kernel, optimizations described for the RMS kernel are still relevant with the expection of the shared memory buffer. We will focus here on computation-related optimizations.

There are two ways we are going to increase the speed of our kernels: increase the volume of work done for each instruction executed and use faster instructions.

To increase the amount of work done per instruction, we can use packed instructions. Packed instruction are useful when we want to apply the same operator on several elements: rather than executing one instruction per element, we execute one instruction over a vector of element. In a CPU, packed (or vectorized) instructions are the bread-and-butter of single-threaded optimization, as the AVX family of instruction can attest to. There are a few packed instructions on GPU, but they can be quite useful in the right place. On the MI300X there is, among others, packed instruction for FP16 addition and multiplication, which we will use for both steps. There also exists packed conversion from FP32 to FP8, which can provide a nice boost in performance when compared to non-packed conversion. As a matter of fact, there is no conversion from any other data type than FP32 to FP8, so for the RMS norm kernel and this one, we have to go to FP32 precision in order to convert to FP8.

However this is not an issue in this kernel: the sigmoid function σ \sigma σ require us to compute an exponent, which is an operation that greatly benefits from FP32 precision. And this is in an instance where we can optimize computation by using a faster instruction: instead of using the exp instruction, we scale the input by log(2) \text{log}(2) log(2) and use the exp2 instruction, which is much faster. We suffer an almost negligible loss in precision but also reduce latency.

We get the following table for a [X, 16384] shaped FP16 input tensor:.

With memory and compute optimizations tailored for the MI300X, we get a kernel that is more than 14 times faster than Torch on average and from 27% to 100% faster than VLLM’s kernel.

According to recent reports, as we have seen earlier, about 60% of the model’s inference latency comes from projections, which rely on GEMM kernels. GEMM kernels are heavily optimized in dedicated libraries such as hipBLASLT rocBLAS on AMD, so writing a custom kernel that performs better in all cases is quite hard. But if we focus on some edge cases that are relevant to us, and write a GEMM kernel for those specific cases, then there is a chance our custom kernel may be faster than the ones in the dedicated libraries.

According to recent reports, in both prefill and decoding, the input of any of the network’s projection has as many rows as there tokens being processed. And during decoding, the number of tokens being processed is equal to the batch size. So during decoding, the number of input rows of all GEMM kernels is equal to the batch size, which for our purposes ranges between 1 and 256. We are going to take an interest with very low batch sizes. When we have a GEMM A∗B=C A * B = C A∗B=C such that A A A has few rows and many columns, we say that the GEMM is skinny. The reason we have a specific term for such GEMMs is that they are ill-fitted for the classic GEMM algorithm we run on GPU. Usually, the efficiency of GEMM kernels comes from tiling: we divide the result matrix in many sub-matrices, called tiles, and we assign each tile to a different compute unit (CU). If we have many tiles, we can use many CUs and GPU usage is high. This is illustrated in the figure below.

But if the input A A A has very few rows, then only a few tiles can be formed, which results in only a few compute units active, hence low GPU utilization:.

It has been revealed that skinny GEMMs are fundamentally inconvenient for the GPU. In the next part, we are going to see how through a custom kernel that assumes we are in a skinny GEMM context, we can make them more convenient.

Recent findings suggest that since the main glitch of skinny GEMMs is that we use too few compute units, the first thing we can do is figure out a way to use more. To do this, we can exploit the following mind-breaking formula:.

cij=∑k=1Kaikbkj=(∑k=1K/2aikbkj)+(∑k=1+K/2Kaikbkj) c_{ij} = \sum_{k=1}^K a_{ik} b_{kj} = \left( \sum_{k=1}^{K/2} a_{ik} b_{kj} \right) + \left( \sum_{k=1+K/2}^{K} a_{ik} b_{kj} \right) cij​=k=1∑K​aik​bkj​=​k=1∑K/2​aik​bkj​​+​k=1+K/2∑K​aik​bkj​​.

Sources indicate that thanks to the associativity of the sum, we can split the main GEMM along the shared axis (commonly referred to as the K axis) and replace one GEMM with several sub-GEMMs that are executed concurrently. Each sub-GEMM is going to use as many CUs as the main one would have, so the number of CUs used is multiplied by the number of times we split the K axis. This is shown in the figure below:.

Here, we set split K equal to 2 and thus double the amount of CU used at once. Since we get partial results, we need to add them up after the both sub-GEMMs are done. What may seem counter-intuitive is that we are adding an operation, summing the partial results, yet we claim to reduce the latency of the overall process. But since each CU needs to go through the entire K axis to compute the result, because we are cutting it in two, the amount of work done by each CU is also cut in two. If the amount of work saved this way counter balances the amount of work added by the summing up of the final results, then we have an overall optimization. This is generally true as long as K is large and the original GEMM uses less than 50% of the GPU.

If we assume that through split-K, most compute units are busy with their own tile, we can focus the scope of optimization at the compute unit level. We are going to take a look at how the actual matrix multiplication is done, and how we can accelerate it.

In state of the art GPUs like the MI300X, matrix multiplication is handled by a dedicated hardware unit called tensor cores. Tensor cores only perform matrix multiplications, but they do so at very high speed. The format of tensor core instruction is mfma_MxNxK... where mfma stands for matrix fused multiply-add, M is the number of rows of the left-hand matrix, N the number of column of the right-hand matrix, and K is the shared dimension of both. We illustrate a hypothetical instruction mfma_2x2x4 below:.

In a recent development, there are only a few tensor core instructions, but for any triplet MxNxK using the dedicated tensor core instruction is much faster than any other alternative. Tensor core instruction also come in two flavours: “dense” and “sparse”. Dense instruction correspond to standard matrix multiplication. Sparse instructions assume that the left-hand side matrix A A A has a 4:2 structured sparsity pattern, which means that two out of every 4 elements along the matrix K axis are zero. Mathematically, for any i,j i, j i,j such that ai,4j+3 a_{i, 4j+3} ai,4j+3​ is an element of A A A , we have at least two zeros in (ai,4j,ai,4j+1,ai,4j+2,ai,4j+3) \left( a_{i,4j}, a_{i,4j+1}, a_{i,4j+2}, a_{i,4j+3} \right) (ai,4j​,ai,4j+1​,ai,4j+2​,ai,4j+3​) . Below is an example of a sparse matrix.

Let’s get back to our model, Llama 405B in FP8. For FP8, we only have two dense tensor core instruction: 16x16x32 and 32x32x16 . We also have one sparse instruction of size 16x16x64 . For an input with 8 rows, using even the smallest dense instruction 16x16x32 means that we have to add 8 rows of padding to our input, which is a waste of compute resources. One can wonder if we can use the sparse instruction instead: after all, if half of a 16 rows matrix is 4:2 sparse, we can fully describe its non-zero coefficients using a dense 8 rows matrix. Conversely, if we have an 8 rows dense matrix, we can fit all of its data into a 16 rows matrix with 4:2 sparsity. And the benefit of using the sparse instruction is obvious: the dense instruction has K=32 while the sparse instruction has K=64 . For the same amount of cycles, the sparse instruction has twice the depth. We illustrate this sparsity trick in the figure below with a 1 row input and the 2x2x4 dense instruction and its sparse 2x2x8 counterpart.

Using this trick, we can notably speed up our GEMM for any input with 8 or less rows, which results in a reduction in per-token latency for any decoding batch that has less than 8 requests.

We have seen that in a skinny GEMM, the fact we have a little number of rows limits the number of output tiles, which in turns limit the GPU utilization. But the small number of rows also limits the number of rows each output tiles has, which in turns reduces what we call arithmetic intensity. Simply put, arithmetic intensity is the amount of work done divided by the amount of data loaded to do that work. Let us compare two examples:.

sn=∑i=1nxitn=∑i=1nyi=y (1+tn−1) s_n = \sum_{i=1}^{n} x_i \\ t_n = \sum_{i=1}^n y^i = y ~( 1 + t_{n-1}) sn​=i=1∑n​xi​tn​=i=1∑n​yi=y (1+tn−1​).

Industry observers note that where x x x is an n n n -sized vector and y y y is a scalar. To compute sn s_n sn​ , we load n n n elements and perform n−1 n-1 n−1 additions. To compute tn t_n tn​ , we load 1 element and perform 2n−1 2n-1 2n−1 additions and multiplications. So the “arithmetic intensity” of computing sn s_n sn​ is n−1n \frac{n-1}{n} nn−1​ while tn t_n tn​ is 2n−1 2n - 1 2n−1 : the computation of tn t_n tn​ is more “arithmetically intensive” than the computation of sn s_n sn​ . What we see here is that when the lower arithmetic intensity is, the more data we need to load to perform work.

Why does this matter to us? Well, we have seen that loading data from VRAM has a high latency cost, which is not great for the GPU. In other words, workloads with low arithmetic intensity are ill-suited for the GPU, and it turns out skinny GEMMs have lower arithmetic intensity than their non-skinny counterparts. This becomes intuitive when looking at the figure below: we can see that when we divide the amount of data loaded by two, we divide the number of output coefficients by 4, due to the quadratic nature of the GEMM’s dimensions.

According to recent reports, in a skinny GEMM the number of rows of the output tile is limited and so is the arithmetic intensity. Already this means that we are going to need to load a lot of data to compute an output tile. Furthermore, since we are using FP8 arithmetic, computation is quite fast, so we cannot rely on computation time to hide the latency of data loading. All in all, it would be ideal to have more threads in charge of loading data than threads in charge of computing the result.

Recent findings suggest that to achieve this, we are going to use a technique called warp specialization. Instead having all warps in the thread block execute the same instructions, we are going to dedicate some warps to loading data only and some to computing the results only. The warps in charge of loading data are called producers and the ones that compute the results are named consumers. Producers and consumers work asynchronously: producers first load data from the VRAM, which is slow, and make it available to the consumers by storing it in a shared memory buffer. Until data is available in shared memory, the consumer is idle. After it data is made available, the consumer loads it from shared memory, which is fast, and computes the result. Coordination of producers and consumers is achieved through a queue stored in shared memory. When a producer finishes storing data in a shared memory buffer i i i , it changes the state of the i i i th variable of the queue to signal data is available there. The consumer is watching out for this, and begins loading data afterwards. When it is done, it changes the i i i th variable of the queue to signal that data can be written over in buffer i i i . In the figure below, we represent the steps involved in a simple asynchronous GEMM with one producer, one consumer and a queue of size 2.

What makes the whole process work is that once buffer 0 0 0 is filled by a producer, it can start working on buffer 1 1 1 without waiting for the consumer to have loaded the data from buffer 0 0 0. The goal is to have a queue large enough for the producers to be constantly filling buffers and consumers constantly consuming them. The size of queue is constrained by the size of the shared memory.

According to recent reports, we also need to tune the ratio of producers to consumers: we have said that we have a low arithmetic intensity, so we need to load a lot of data to do a relatively fast computation. Hence, we are going to have a lot of producer warps (typically 8 or 10) for a few consumer warps (something like 2 or 3). Furthermore, we can exploit the fact the GEMM is skinny by having separate producers for the input (the skinny matrix) and the weights (the non-skinny matrix). To make the output tile bigger in the dimension in which it is not constrained in, which is the columns dimension, we allocate more producers for the weights.

For a more in-depth blog post about asynchronous GEMMs, I encourage you to check out this blog post. A lot of its contents are not applicable in our case though: the MI300X has no warp-level barriers, only a single thread block-level barrier. This led to “fun” shenanigans like ASM to ensure warps waited at their barriers, shared memory loads and stores were resolved before checking the barrier state, and careful handling of the modular nature of the queue. All this would be out of place here, but I encourage you to check out the code or ask away in the comments. A deep dive on the details of async handling might be coming in the future.

Through warp specialization and asynchronous work, we can adapt our kernel to the low arithmetic intensity workload, but is that enough to come ahead of libraries like hipBLASLT? The answer is yes, in some cases.

Since Torch already binds a highly optimized GEMM taken from AMD’s linear algebra library, we are not going to get speedups in the same range as for the two last kernels. We are first going to take a look at the three GEMM dimension that are of interest to us: namely, the GEMMs dimensions associated with the QKV projection, the Gate / Up projection and the Down projection. The Output projection is being left out because its dimensions do not correspond to the skinny GEMM case.

In a recent development, measures are taken after 500 warmups iterations, over 2000 profiling iterations, using CUDA graph and multiple weights to avoid cache hits. In order, the GEMM dimensions shown above correspond to QKV projection (N = 2304 and K = 16384), Gate / Up projection (N = 13312 and K = 16384) and Down projection (N= 16384 and K = 6656). We can see that for those dimensions, which have been tuned for, there is a notable speedup for low number of rows (M = 1, 8, 16) but less so for more rows (M = 32). Especially for dimensions in which we can use our sparsity trick (M = 1, 8) we see a notable speedup over Torch, which probably pads everything to 16 rows to use the smallest MFMA instruction.

In a recent development, in this post, we explored just a handful of the many kernel optimization techniques available. If you're interested in experimenting with them, feel free to dive into the hf-rocm-kernels repository and start tinkering! And if you develop a kernel you like of and want to distribute it, be sure to check out kernel-builder and kernels — two Hugging Face packages designed to help kernel builders make their work widely available and more impactful.

How does the async handling work?

It has been revealed that we use an int16 variable in the shared memory (a semaphore), which can be looked up by any warp on the SM. The thing you have to be carefull about is to have all instructions related to SMEM or GMEM finished before changing the state of the semaphore. For instance, you have to explicitly wait for SMEM stores to be over before switching the semaphore.

According to recent reports, one of the most annoying things about playing Ocarina of Time right now is that everyone in my home is at a different point in their save file. This makes it tough to be in the same room with others and not spoil something for them, but plugging in a pair of Viture glasses makes this much easier since no one else can see the screen inside the glasses I’m wearing.

Native spatial tracking means that you can pin the virtual monitor in space and move around as if it were a TV mounted on a wall. Beast doesn’t have diopters, so you’ll need to order prescription lenses if you need myopia adjustment.

The biggest discount of all is on Viture Luma Pro, which is down to $339 ($160 off). Luma Pro is Viture’s “Goldilocks” pair with excellent image quality and RGB lighting along the frames for some extra style, and even includes myopia adjustment diopters. Pair any of these Viture glasses with the Mobile Dock Mini for Switch 2 compatibility, making them the only pair of smart glasses with official Switch 2 support.

Recent findings suggest that lastly is Viture Luma Ultra, down to $449 ($150 off). Luma Ultra sports the best image quality of all Viture glasses and includes myopia-adjusting diopters. These are the only pair that support 6DoF tracking when using the Viture Spacewalker app thanks to the cameras on the front, but there’s no native 3DoF support like Beast has, so this functionality is limited to content you view through the app.

Weekly. Free. One click to leave.

Elementor made your site easy to build. It may also be making it slow. Here's how to move a site onto the Block Editor without breaking URLs, losing content or dropping out of Google.

Industry observers note that page builders solved a real problem. Before the Block Editor matured, they were the easiest way to give clients drag-and-drop layouts. Many of those sites are still running today, and a lot of them are slow on phones.

Sources indicate that the data backs that up. According to the HTTP Archive Core Web Vitals Technology Report for June 2026, 36.8% of Elementor sites pass Core Web Vitals on mobile. Sites built with the Block Editor pass 53.0% of the time. That's correlation, not proof, since hosting and setup matter too. But in my experience, it matches what happens when you remove the builder from a slow site.

According to recent reports, my reason for migrating sites off Elementor is simple: **page builders make websites heavy. **Having mentioned that, Elementor has improved a lot. Its performance settings, Flexbox Containers, and asset-loading options cut much of the bloat, and a carefully tuned Elementor site can pass Core Web Vitals. But tuning only goes so far. You’re still shipping the builder’s framework, wrapper markup and scripts, and every plugin or Elementor update is a chance for the speed to slip again.

For small business sites that don’t need drag-and-drop editing, rebuilding the same design on the WordPress Block Editor (Gutenberg) removes that weight at the source, without changing what the client sees.

This guide follows the order I use. It assumes you're comfortable with WordPress admin, WP-CLI and a staging site. If you need to set those up first, SitePoint's guide to the ultimate WordPress development environment covers the tooling.

In a recent development, not every Elementor site needs to move. Migration makes sense when:.

Sources indicate that it's harder to justify when the site leans on Elementor Pro features you'd need to replace, such as complex popups, dynamic loops or WooCommerce templates. Those can all be rebuilt, but the job gets bigger fast.

You can't prove a migration worked without "before" numbers. Capture these on the live site first.

Recent findings suggest that crawl the site with a tool such as Screaming Frog, and export every indexable URL with its title, meta description, H1 and canonical tag. You can also pull published pages and posts with WP-CLI:.

It has been revealed that run Google PageSpeed Insights, which uses Lighthouse for its lab scores, on the homepage and two or three key templates. Save the mobile lab scores and, if the site has enough traffic, the field data from real customers.

Export the last three months of pages and queries from Google Search Console. That's what you'll compare against after launch.

Sources indicate that elementor stores each page's layout as JSON in the elementordata post meta field, and marks builder pages with elementoredit_mode. This command lists every page that uses the builder:.

Then list everything else Elementor controls, which is easy to miss:.

On the small business sites I've migrated, the inventory usually turns up more than the owner expects. The pages are the easy part. The surprises are saved templates nobody remembers creating, a popup still running on every page, add-on widgets from plugins that were installed once and forgotten, and contact forms that live inside Elementor Pro rather than a form plugin. Finding those before the rebuild saves a broken launch.

According to recent reports, work on a staging copy. Install a block theme, such as Twenty Twenty-Five or a lightweight starter theme, and move the Elementor global styles into theme.json. That way colors, fonts and spacing are defined once, instead of in every widget.

Copy the hex values and font names from Elementor's Site Settings so the new site matches the old one. Rebuild the header and footer as template parts in the Site Editor. If you'd rather write a theme yourself, SitePoint's series on building a WordPress theme from scratch covers the basics.

Most Elementor sites repeat the same few sections: a hero, a services grid, testimonials and a call to action. Build each one once as a block pattern, then reuse it on every page. Patterns are plain block markup, so you don't need React to write them, whatever you may have heard about React and WordPress development.

In a block theme, any PHP file in the /patterns folder with a header comment is registered automatically:.

It has been revealed that for page content, there's a useful shortcut. Elementor saves a plain HTML copy of each page into post_content. Open a page in the Block Editor, and the old content usually appears in a Classic block. Choose Convert to blocks, then delete the leftovers and rebuild the layout with your patterns. It keeps the copy and images, so you only redo the design.

The difference demonstrates up in the page source. Here's typical front-end markup for a single heading on an Elementor page, using the older section and column layout:.

And the same heading as a block:.

Newer Elementor versions with Flexbox containers and the optimized markup settings trim some of those wrappers, but most older sites still carry all of them. Multiply that by every element on every page, and the weight adds up.

To speed up this step, I built a free Elementor to Gutenberg converter. Paste in a page's elementordata JSON from Step 2, and it returns block markup you can paste into the Block Editor's code editor. It handles headings, text, images, buttons, spacers, dividers and column layouts, and lists anything it can't convert, such as forms and popups, for you to rebuild by hand. It runs entirely in your browser, so the page data never leaves your computer.

In a recent development, the code is rarely what holds a migration up. Content is. Once clients see their site being rebuilt, many decide it's time to rewrite their pages too, and the project ends up waiting on copywriters and approvals. My fix is to separate the two: migrate the existing content as it is, launch, then update the copy afterwards. That keeps the speed and SEO gains on schedule, and it means any ranking change can be traced to either the migration or the upcoming copy, not both at once.

This is the step that decides whether rankings hold.

To spot-check a redirect or a status code from the command line:.

Industry observers note that when staging matches the live site, deploy it. Then:.

Recent findings suggest that leave the old elementordata meta in place for a few weeks, in case you need to roll back. Once you're confident, take a backup and remove it to shrink the database.

It has been revealed that run PageSpeed Insights again straight away for lab scores. Field data takes longer: the Chrome UX Report uses a rolling 28-day window, so give it a month before judging real-user results. Compare Search Console clicks for the same period before and after launch.

In my migrations, the biggest change is usually page weight and loading time, because the builder's CSS, JavaScript and wrapper markup are gone. What doesn't always improve is server response time. If the site is on slow shared hosting, the first byte still arrives late, and that needs a hosting fix, not a rebuild. Search traffic should hold steady if the URLs and metadata were protected. If it drops, the Step 5 crawl comparison is the first place to look.

In a recent development, moving off Elementor isn't a one-click job, but it isn't a full redesign either. Record a baseline, inventory what the builder controls, rebuild with patterns, and protect every URL. Most of the speed gain comes from removing code the site never needed. For what to tackle after that, see these practical web performance techniques. Most of the risk comes from rushing the SEO checks. Done carefully, the client gets the same site, a faster one, and an editor that comes with WordPress itself.

According to recent reports, when using the out-of-the-box Gemini Enterprise web application, identity and access management happen behind the scenes. Employees sign in through Google Identity or Workforce Identity Federation (such as Microsoft Entra ID or Okta), search results automatically respect per-user access controls (ACLs), and third-party login prompts for Federated Connectors or custom agents appear automatically in the chat UI.

Recent findings suggest that in practice, however, many enterprises build their own Customer UI to embed Gemini Enterprise into an internal portal, intranet, or line-of-business application. To do this, Customer BE calls the Gemini Enterprise StreamAssist API.

The moment an application builds a custom UI and calls the StreamAssist API directly, the three authentication flows that the built-in web app handled automatically become the responsibility of Customer UI and Customer BE:.

This guide walks through the architecture, component flows, and runnable code for all three layers (Figure 1):.

Building the Hugging Face MCP Server

📅 10 Jul 2025 | ⏱️ 7 min read (1431 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Hugging Face

⏱️ ~7 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Sources indicate that TL;DR: The Hugging Face Official MCP Server offers unique customization options for AI Assistants accessing the Hub, along with access to thousands of AI applications through one simple URL.
  • We've learned many things about building a useful MCP server in the last month - we'll describe our journey here.
  • The Model Context Protocol (MCP) is fulfilling its promise of being the standard to connect AI Assistants to the outside world.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Sources indicate that TL;DR: The Hugging Face Official MCP Server offers unique customization options for AI Assistants accessing the Hub, along with access to thousands of AI applications through one simple URL. We used MCPs "Streamable HTTP" transport for deployment, and examine in detail the trade-offs that Server Developers have.

We've learned many things about building a useful MCP server in the last month - we'll describe our journey here.

The Model Context Protocol (MCP) is fulfilling its promise of being the standard to connect AI Assistants to the outside world.

At Hugging Face, providing access to the Hub via MCP is an obvious choice, and this article shares our experience developing the hf.co/mcp MCP Server.

According to recent reports, the community uses the Hub for research, development, content creation and more. We wanted to let people customize the server for their own needs, as well as easily access thousands of AI applications available on Spaces. This meant making the MCP Server dynamic by adjusting users' tools on the fly.

We also wanted to make access simple by avoiding complicated downloads and configuration, so making it remotely accessible via a simple URL was a must.

Sources indicate that when building a remote MCP Server, the first decision is deciding how clients will connect to it. MCP offers several transport options, with different trade-offs. TL;DR: our open source code supports all variants, but for production we chose to go with the most modern one. This section goes through the different options in detail.

According to recent reports, since its launch in November 2024, MCP has undergone rapid evolution with 3 protocol revisions in 9 months. This has seen the replacement of the SSE Transport with Streamable HTTP, as well as the introduction and rework of authorization.

These rapid changes mean support for different MCP Features and revisions in Client applications varies, providing extra challenges for our design choices.

Here is a brief summary of the Transport Options offered by the Model Context Protocol and associated SDKs:.

Both STDIO and HTTP with SSE are fully bi-directional by default - meaning that Client and Server maintain an open connection and can send messages to each other at any time.

SSE refers to "Server Sent Events" - a way for HTTP Servers to maintain an open connection and send events in response to a request.

MCP Server Developers face a lot of choices when setting up the Streamable HTTP transport.

There are 3 main communication patterns to choose from:.

When using Request Scoped Streams with the official SDKs, use the sendNotification() and sendRequest() methods provided in the RequestHandlerExtra parameter (TypeScript) or set the related_request_id (Python) to send messages to the correct stream.

Industry observers note that an additional factor to consider is whether or not the MCP Server itself needs to maintain state for each connection. This is decided by the Server when the Client sends its Initialize request:.

The table below summarizes the MCP Features and their supported communication pattern:.

With Request Scoped streams, Sampling and Elicitation requests need a Stateful connection so that the mcp-session-id can be used for response association.

The Hugging Face MCP Server is Open Source - and supports STDIO, SSE and Streamable HTTP deployment in both Direct Response and Server Push mode. You can configure keep-alive and last activity timeouts when using Server Push Streams. There's also a built-in observability dashboard that you can use to understand how different Clients manage connections, and handle Tool List change notifications.

The following picture shows our MCP Server connection dashboard running in "Server Push" Streamable HTTP mode:.

For production, we decided to launch our MCP Server with Streamable HTTP in a Stateless, Direct Response configuration for the following reasons:.

Recent findings suggest that stateless For anonymous users we supply a standard set of Tools for using the Hub along with an Image Generator. For authenticated users our state comprises their selected tools and chosen Gradio applications. We also make sure that users ZeroGPU quota is correctly applied for their account. This is managed using the supplied HF_TOKEN or OAuth credentials that we look up on request. None of our existing tools require us to maintain any other state between requests.

Recent findings suggest that you can use OAuth login by adding ?login to the MCP Server url - e.g. https://huggingface.co/mcp?login. We may make this the default once the claude.ai remote integration supports the latest OAuth spec.

Direct Response provides the lowest deployment resource overhead - and we don't right now have any Tools that require Sampling or Elicitation during execution.

According to recent reports, future Support At launch, the "HTTP with SSE" transport was still the remote default in a lot of MCP Clients. However, we didn't want to invest heavily in managing it due to its imminent deprecation. Fortunately, popular clients had already started making the switch (VSCode and Cursor), and within a week of launch claude.ai also added support. If you need to connect with SSE, feel free to deploy a copy of our Server on a FreeCPU Hugging Face Space.

It has been revealed that in the future, we would like to support real-time Tool List Changed notifications when consumers patch their settings on the Hub. However, this raises a couple of practical challenges:.

First, users tend to configure their favourite MCP Servers in their Client and leave them enabled. This means that the Client remains connected whilst the application is open. Sending notifications would mean maintaining as many open connections as there were currently active Clients - regardless of active usage - on the chance the user updates their tool configuration.

Recent findings suggest that second, most MCP Servers and Clients disconnect after a period of inactivity, resuming when necessary. This inevitably means that immediate push notifications would be missed - as the notification channel will have been closed. In practice, it is far simpler for the Client to refresh the connection and Tool List as needed.

Unless you have reasonable control over the Client/Server pair, using Server Push Streams adds a lot of complexity to a public deployment, when lower-resource solutions for refreshing the Tool List exist.

Just before launch, @julien-c submitted a PR to include friendly instructions for customers visiting hf.co/mcp. This hugely improves the User Experience - the default response is otherwise an unfriendly bit of JSON.

According to recent reports, initially, we found this generated an enormous amount of traffic. After a bit of investigation we found that when returning a web page rather than an HTTP 405 error, VSCode would poll the endpoint multiple times per second!

Recent findings suggest that the fix suggested by @coyotte508 was to properly detect browsers and only return the page in that circumstance. Thanks also to the VSCode team who rapidly fixed it.

Although not specifically stated - returning a page in this manner does seem acceptable within the MCP Specification.

The MCP Protocol sends several requests during initialization. A typical connection sequence is: Initialize, Notifications/Initialize, tools/list and then prompts/list.

Given that MCP Clients will connect and reconnect whilst open, and the fact that consumers make periodic calls, we find there is a ratio of around 100 MCP Control messages for each Tool Call.

Some clients also send requests that don't make sense for our Stateless, Direct Response configuration - for example Pings, Cancellations or attempts to list Resources (which isn't a capability we currently advertise).

The first week of July 2025 saw an astonishing 164 different Clients accessing our Server. Interestingly, one of the most popular tools is mcp-remote. Approximately half of all Clients use it as a bridge to connect to our remote server.

MCP is rapidly evolving, and we're excited about what has already been achieved across Chat Applications, IDEs, Agents and MCP Servers over the last few months.

We can already see how powerful integrating the Hugging Face Hub has been and support for Gradio Spaces now makes it possible for LLMs to be easily extended with the latest Machine Learning applications.

Here are some great examples of things people have been doing with our MCP Server so far:.

We hope that this post has provided insights to the decisions that need to be made building Remote MCP Servers, and encourage you to try some of the examples in your favourite MCP Client.

Take a look at our Open Source MCP Server, and try some of the different transport options with your Client, or open an Problem or Pull Request to make improvements or suggest new functionality.

Let us know your thoughts, feedback and questions on this discussion thread.

Sending a document for signature is the easy part of an e-signature integration. One POST request and the signer gets an email. The work that actually breaks in production happens afterwards: knowing when the document was signed, trusting the notification that told you so, handling the same notification twice, and getting the final PDF into storage before the download link expires.

This tutorial builds that whole loop in Node.js with Express. An event in your app (a deal is approved, a client is onboarded, a task moves to "ready to sign") sends a contract from a template. When the signer finishes, a webhook arrives, your server verifies it, and the signed PDF plus its audit trail get saved without anyone touching them.

Recent findings suggest that the code uses Firma.dev, the e-signature API I work on, because I needed a real API to make the examples runnable. The patterns are not specific to it, though. Signature verification, idempotent handlers, short-lived download URLs, and reconciliation jobs show up in almost every webhook-driven integration, and the same structure applies whether you're receiving events from a payment processor, a CI system, or another signing provider.

There's a fifth part that tutorials usually skip: a reconciliation job that catches anything the webhooks missed. We'll build that too, because webhooks are a notification mechanism, not a delivery guarantee.

Set three environment variables:.

Recent findings suggest that before sending anything, wrap the HTTP calls in one place. This is where authentication lives, and it's also where you handle 429 Too Many Requests once instead of in every caller. Most APIs, this one included, return a Retry-After header on a 429, so the client should honour it rather than guessing a backoff.

Sources indicate that the 503 branch matters later. When a document has just been completed, the final PDF and its completion certificate take a moment to generate, and the download endpoint says so with a 503 and a Retry-After instead of handing you a half-built file.

In a recent development, the trigger depends on your product. It might be a route handler, a queue consumer, or a CRM automation calling into your service. What matters is that the function doing the sending is small and takes plain data:.

Two design choices are worth calling out.

Use a single create-and-send call when you can. Many signing APIs split this into "create a draft" and "send the draft." That's useful when a human needs to review the document first, but for automation it creates a window where your process can crash between the two calls and leave an orphaned draft. A combined endpoint makes the operation atomic from your side.

Store the provider's ID on your own record immediately. Webhook payloads reference the signing request, not your deal or customer. Without that mapping you'll end up searching by email address, which falls apart as soon as one client signs two documents.

It has been revealed that here's the first place integrations quietly go wrong. Webhook signatures are computed over the exact bytes the sender transmitted. If Express parses the body as JSON first, you lose those bytes, and re-serialising the object won't reproduce them (key order, whitespace, and number formatting can all change). Signature checks then fail intermittently, which is the worst kind of failure.

The fix is to use express.raw() on the webhook route only, so the handler receives a Buffer:.

Industry observers note that most webhook providers sign payloads with HMAC-SHA256 using a shared secret. The details vary, so read your provider's docs for the exact header format, but the scheme here is common: the header looks like t=1731456000,v1=5f2b..., and the signed string is the timestamp, a dot, and the raw body. Stripe uses a very similar format, and the Standard Webhooks spec describes the same idea as a vendor-neutral convention.

Each line here defends against something specific.

The OWASP guidance on cryptographic storage covers the other half of this: the secret belongs in an environment variable or secrets manager, never in the repository.

Every serious webhook system delivers at least once, not exactly once. If your endpoint is slow, returns a 5xx, or the network drops the response, the sender retries. Firma.dev, for example, makes up to three attempts per event (immediately, then after at least five minutes, then after at least an hour) and treats anything other than a 2xx as a failure, including redirects. Other providers retry more aggressively. Either way, your handler will eventually see the same event twice.

In a recent development, the defence is to record each event's unique ID and skip ones you've seen. In the server above that's alreadyProcessed and markProcessed. For a demo, a Set works:.

In production, use your database and let a unique constraint do the work, so two concurrent deliveries can't both pass the check:.

Also notice the order in the route: respond with 200, then do the work. Many providers time out deliveries after a few seconds (five, in this case). Downloading a PDF and uploading it to object storage can easily take longer than that, and a timeout counts as a failure, which triggers a retry, which triggers duplicate work. Acknowledging fast and processing asynchronously avoids that loop.

According to recent reports, setImmediate is fine for a tutorial, but it has a real weakness: if the process dies after sending the 200 and before finishing the work, the event is acknowledged and lost. In production, push the event onto a durable queue (BullMQ, SQS, a jobs table) before responding. Step 7 covers the safety net for whatever still slips through.

Sources indicate that now the actual business logic. You'll usually see several event types (sent, viewed, a signer signed, declined, expired, completed). Only one of them means "the document is final":.

Three things in here are easy to get wrong.

According to recent reports, don't treat "a signer signed" as "the document is done." With multiple signers, each one triggers its own event, and a per-signer "all complete" flag can be true on more than one of them. Key your storage logic off the single completion event.

It has been revealed that don't persist the download URL. Pre-signed URLs expire (this one carries an expires_at). Saving the link to your database and serving it to owners later produces broken links a few minutes or hours later. Download the bytes and store them in storage you control. Swapping the fs.writeFile calls for an S3 PutObject or a Google Drive upload is a drop-in change.

Industry observers note that store the audit trail, not just the PDF. If a signature is ever disputed, the PDF demonstrates what was signed, and the audit trail shows who signed it, when, and from where (timestamps, IP addresses, the sequence of views and signatures). That evidence is what makes an electronic signature defensible, which brings us to the legal side.

According to recent reports, retries are finite. Endpoints go down during deploys. Some providers auto-disable a webhook after enough consecutive failures, and events aren't guaranteed to arrive in order. Any one of these can leave a completed document sitting unsaved.

According to recent reports, A small scheduled job closes that gap. Keep a list of signing requests your app considers "pending," and periodically ask the API for their real status:.

Sources indicate that since storeSignedDocument overwrites by ID, running it twice for the same document is harmless. That's the property you want from every step in a webhook pipeline: doing it again shouldn't change the result.

None of this is legal advice, but a few facts shape how you build.

In the US, the ESIGN Act and the Uniform Electronic Transactions Act (adopted by 49 states) give electronic signatures the same legal standing as handwritten ones for most commercial documents. ESIGN also has requirements around consumer consent and record retention, which is part of why you store the final PDF yourself rather than relying on a third-party link.

In the EU, eIDAS defines three levels: simple (SES), advanced (AdES), and qualified (QES). SES and AdES cover most business contracts. QES requires a qualified trust service provider and certificate-based identity, and some documents (certain property transfers and court filings, depending on the country) require it or exclude e-signatures entirely. Check which level your document types need before you pick a provider, since not every API offers every level.

Across jurisdictions, the evidence that holds up is the same: who signed, how they were identified, when it happened, and proof the document hasn't changed since. That's the audit trail and the completion certificate, which is why Step 6 stores both.

If you're evaluating providers for a workflow like this, the questions that matter at the integration level are mostly not on the pricing page:.

The send call is one line. The reliability comes from everything around it: keeping the raw body for verification, checking timestamps and comparing in constant time, acknowledging fast and deduplicating by event ID, downloading files before their links expire, and running a reconciliation job for the events that never arrive. Get those right and contract signing becomes something your app does in the background, with no one chasing signatures or copying PDFs between folders.

For the Firma.dev-specific details used here (event names, header format, rate limits), see the webhooks guide.

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

The Nest app is officially dead, but it’s worth taking a step back and remembering that, while there are some rough edges, the Google Home app is a better smart home experience than Nest alone ever could have been.

The Nest app has been on life support for years now. Google has been migrating legacy products into the Home app for a while and the last few puzzle pieces came in Nest Protect support, the death of the earliest Nest Thermostats, and other assorted adjustments.

Realistically, even long-time Nest customers have had no reason to continue using the app over Google Home.

Having been personally, deeply invested in Google’s vision for the smart home over the past decade, I’ll say that the Google Home app we have today is better than the Nest app ever was or ever could be. A huge part of that comes from Google Home’s ability to pull together devices from third-party ecosystems. Being able to control your entire smart home from a single app is how the smart home always should have been, and between Google’s work and the Matter standard, we’re finally able to enjoy that pretty seamlessly for the most part. Automations, Google’s actually-useful AI features, and more only sweeten the deal. I’m also a major fan of what the Home app has become from a UX perspective. While there are always rough edges and bugs to clean up, the customizable homepage and well-organized sections make for a good – not perfect, but good – experience for the end user.

That mentioned, there is one thing that the Nest app’s limited scope benefitted from, and that’s a focus on making your own product great.

It has been revealed that google’s move to the Home app for Nest devices has been a 5-year run of trying to clean things up, improve on the app, and basically bring back the way things were in the Nest app as far as the first-party cameras and thermostats are concerned. It’s taken ages, but we’re finally up to speed, mostly. I still hate that you have to reset Nest Cams to change Wi-Fi when the Nest app just let you change it, and the Nest app’s settings were much less overwhelming, but I’d say the pros far outweigh the cons at this point.

In a recent development, the Nest app was good at its job, but the Google Home app is a worthy successor, finally, and now the Nest app can finally rest. I mostly think the same applies to Gemini vs Google Assistant, with the newer assistant a better overall experience, but it’s easier to poke holes in that argument.

Disagree? What do you think of the Google Home app, and were you still using the Nest app?

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Sources indicate that TL;DR: ScreenEnv is a powerful Python library that lets you create isolated Ubuntu desktop environments in Docker containers for testing and deploying GUI Agents (aka Computer Use agents). With built-in support for the Model Context Protocol (MCP), it's never been easier to deploy desktop agents that can see, click, and interact with real applications.

Industry observers note that imagine you need to automate desktop tasks, test GUI applications, or build an AI agent that can interact with software. This used to require complex VM setups and brittle automation frameworks.

ScreenEnv changes this by providing a sandboxed desktop environment that runs in a Docker container. Think of it as a complete virtual desktop session that your code can fully control - not just clicking buttons and typing text, but managing the entire desktop experience including launching applications, organizing windows, handling files, executing terminal commands, and recording the entire session.

ScreenEnv provides two complementary ways to integrate with your agents and backend systems, giving you flexibility to choose the approach that best fits your architecture:.

Perfect for custom agent frameworks, existing backends, or when you need fine-grained control:.

Ideal for AI systems that support the Model Context Protocol:.

This dual approach means ScreenEnv adapts to your existing infrastructure rather than forcing you to change your agent architecture.

In a recent development, screenenv natively supports smolagents, making it easy to build your own custom Desktop Agent for automation. Here’s how to create your own AI-powered Desktop Agent in just a few steps:.

Pick the backend VLM you want to power your agent.

Inherit from DesktopAgentBase and implement the _setup_desktop_tools method to build your own action space!

If you encounter acces denied docker error, you can try to run the agent with sudo -E python -m test.py or add your user to the docker group.

💡 For a comprehensive implementation, see this CustomDesktopAgent source on GitHub.

In a recent development, screenEnv aims to expand beyond Linux to support Android, macOS, and Windows, unlocking true cross-platform GUI automation. This will enable developers and researchers to build agents that generalize across environments with minimal setup.

These advancements pave the way for creating reproducible, sandboxed environments ideal for benchmarking and evaluation.

The Samsung Galaxy Watch Ultra 2 is worth spending more on if you want longer battery life, a brighter outdoor display, and specialized features for trail running and diving. The Galaxy Watch 9 is the better fit if you want Samsung’s latest everyday health tools in a smaller, lighter watch.

Both, however, are fantastic smartwatches with limitless potential. They share a Snapdragon Wear Elite processor and many of Samsung’s newest wellness features, so deciding between them is really about figuring out your priorities when it comes to buying a wearable this holiday season. We’re here to help you figure that out.

This post is sponsored by Samsung.

It has been revealed that as we covered in our Galaxy Watch 9 and Watch Ultra 2 comparison, both watches move to Qualcomm’s Snapdragon Wear Elite platform. Both also ship with Wear OS 7 and One UI 8 Watch.

Recent findings suggest that that shared foundation includes useful health insights. Vitals brings overnight measurements together to establish your personal baseline, while Daily Cardio Load helps you understand training demands and recovery. Hearing monitoring can flag potentially unsafe noise levels, whether you’re at a concert or somewhere unexpectedly loud.

Both also get five years of Wear OS updates and security patches, making either a useful long-term partner for your Samsung device, like the Galaxy S26 Ultra or Galaxy Z Fold8.

According to recent reports, the clearest differences are size, battery capacity, display brightness, and outdoor capabilities. Here’s how the lineup breaks down:.

As you can tell, the Galaxy Watch Ultra 2 is considerably bigger and heavier, but you get a lot more capability for that additional size.

The Galaxy Watch Ultra 2 makes its strongest case when your plans regularly take you beyond a desk, a gym, or a charger.

Samsung rates the Galaxy Watch Ultra 2 for up to 60 hours with the always-on display enabled, compared with up to 30 hours for the Watch 9, and that extra headroom is appealing when your day starts with a workout and finishes well into the evening.

Then there’s the screen. In our hands-on with both watches, the Ultra 2’s brightness stood out immediately, with a higher peak that gives it an advantage when checking workout information outdoors, even in the bright sun. And its titanium frame provides added durability.

According to recent reports, the Ultra 2 also adds Trail Run tracking for elevation and terrain impact, route guidance using compatible GPX files, and Nutrition Alert hydration guidance. These are tangible reasons to upgrade if your usual run involves trails instead of pavement.

Diving is another differentiator. Samsung specifies recreational diving support to depths of up to 40 meters, with automatic tracking of depth, dive time and water temperature — a remarkable feat for a piece of technology that lives on your wrist.

The best choice becomes clearer when you picture your own routine:.

In a recent development, choose the Galaxy Watch 9 for everyday wellness, a lighter fit, and strong value. Choose the Galaxy Watch Ultra 2 for longer adventures, more demanding outdoor activities, and greater freedom between charges.

Recent findings suggest that if you’re replacing an older Galaxy Watch, both offer a compelling new generation of health insights and long-term support. Both last a long time and look absolutely awesome with running shorts or a business suit. But the Watch Ultra 2 can take you that extra mile, literally and figuratively, and may be worth spending more on during Best Buy’s Holiday Deals event.

The pill-shaped container retains its Dynamic Color theming with just the text of the warning in red. This change also extends to the card on the city page. Google notes to “Submit a report if the weather conditions don’t look right.” Tapping “Submit a report” brings up a “Report weather in [city]” sheet. You can submit two pieces of information:.
