Asynchronous Robot Inference: Decoupling Action Prediction and Execution

📅 10 Jul 2025 | ⏱️ 10 min read (1959 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Hugging Face

⏱️ ~10 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • In a recent development, TL;DR Robotic policies are increasingly bulky, and predict chunks of future actions rather than a single next action.
  • Get started with async inference by following our tutorial.
  • Sequential inference (first) versus async inference (second).
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

In a recent development, TL;DR Robotic policies are increasingly bulky, and predict chunks of future actions rather than a single next action. This results in the robot being idle while awaiting latest actions to perform, introducing noticeable lags at execution, and lacking responsiveness. Asynchronous inference tightens the control loop, removing lags at runtime and resulting in more adaptive control by decoupling action prediction from action execution. In this blog post, we cover the basics behind async inference, and how it can be used to improve the performance of robotic policies in the real-world.

Get started with async inference by following our tutorial.

Sequential inference (first) versus async inference (second). Allowing for replanning and a tighter control loop, async inference results in (1) attempts at recovery, and (2) a ~2x speedup in task completion. Sequential inference keeps acting out the current action chunk even after failure to grasp the object, while async inference can replan and act the upcoming action chunk. Both setups use the same policy!

It has been revealed that with async inference, we decouple action execution from action prediction. This is particularly relevant considering the tendency of currently popular models like [ACT], [OpenVLA], [PI0], and [SmolVLA] to be outputting chunks of actions at:t+Ha_{t:t+H}at:t+H​ rather than single actions ata_tat​ given an observation oto_tot​. Convince yourself of this by running all these models using LeRobot.

It has been revealed that using chunks sequentially results in (1) lags at runtime, impacting task execution time and (2) lack of responsiveness, due to acting widely open-loop. Asynchronous inference mitigates both these limitations by decoupling action prediction from action execution. We introduced asynchronous inference in SmolVLA, and found it to result in a ~2x speed-up in task completion time with comparable task success rate.

In particular, we design a 2-component system where policy inference and action execution are performed in two different processes, possibly on two different machines connected through the network:.

Communication between PolicyServer and RobotClient relies on gRPC, which guarantees ~5× faster performance than a comparable REST API. The result of all of this is a robot that never waits for inference.

Asynchronous inference, highlighting: (1) The client sending the first observation for inference, receiving the first chunk shortly after; (2) The client sending another observation for processing while it has not yet exhausted the current chunk; (3) The client receiving an updated action chunk, which it aggregates with the remainders of the one it was previously executing.

In a recent development, suppose a policy π \pi π maps the current observation ot o_t ot​ to a sequence of H H H future actions. Formally, π:O  ↦  A,At=(at,at+1,…at+H)=π(ot)\pi : \mathcal{O} \;\mapsto\; \mathcal{A}, \mathbf{A}_t = \begin{pmatrix} a_{t}, & a_{t+1}, & \dots & a_{t+H} \end{pmatrix} = \pi(o_t)π:O↦A,At​=(at​,​at+1​,​…​at+H​​)=π(ot​).

A traditional control loop would therefore consist of the following steps:.

It has been revealed that during step 2 the robot is idle. The latency grows with the model size (and models tend to be increasingly bulky over time), and can quickly dominate interaction time (which is typically around 1/fps), as shown in the video below (coming from our Discord community 🤗):.

This directly results in (1) reduced performance in terms of task completion time---the robot needs to be waiting for the next action chunk to be computed---and (2) reduced responsiveness, due to (2.1) acting widely open-loop while actions are available and (2.2) complete idleness while waiting for the next action chunk.

(Left)Sequential inference with highlighted idle periods. (Right)Time to select an action showing spikes when inference is triggered due to local queue exhaustion (inference latency is around ~100ms---~3 frames at 30fps---using an ACT model on a 2021 MacBook Pro).

Our system removes the idle period by overlapping computation and execution:.

The key idea is that the robot already knows what to do for the next few timesteps, so it can keep moving while fresh actions are being computed on the server.

Asynchronous inference overlaps in time the execution of the current action chunk with the computation of the next one, by decoupling these two processes, possibly running them on entirely distinct machines connected through the network.

Industry observers note that this results in a tighter control loop, and a robot that never waits for inference. In turn, this results in ~2x speedup in task completion time with comparable task success rate, and more adaptive control coming from a tighter loop (see video below).

Because gRPC is HTTP/2-based and uses protocol buffers, it achieves low-latency binary messaging and bidirectional streams out of the box, which in turn helps us maintain a tighter control loop and sub-100ms round-trip latency (on our local network, and hosting SmolVLA on a NVIDIA RTX 4090).

Sources indicate that the RobotClient runs on-board, and streams observations to the PolicyServer through gRPC. The PolicyServer prepares the observations received for inference, and sends back to the RobotClient an action chunk.

Industry observers note that from the client's perspective, observations are streamed to the server according to the local queue status. Incoming chunks are aggregated on overlapping portions with the presently available action queue.

The RobotClient maintains a local action queue and follows a simple yet effective strategy: send a newly introduced observation when the queue length drops below a configurable threshold (\(g\) in the SmolVLA paper, chunk_size_threshold in the code). This threshold value, expressed as a fraction of the maximum chunk size, acts as a trigger condition that balances computational load with responsiveness.

The client streams observations to the server, according to the local queue status.

From the client's perspective, the process unfolds as follows:.

Sources indicate that queue monitoring: The client continuously monitors its action queue length against a chunk size threshold parameter. When the queue drops below this threshold, it signals that a new observation should be sent for processing.

It has been revealed that observation streaming: Once the threshold condition is met, the client captures the current observation and streams it to the PolicyServer via gRPC. Crucially, observations are streamed rather than being sent via a unary RPC because they typically exceed the maximum message size of 4MB (multiple camera captures at high resolution result in this).

Industry observers note that action chunk aggregation: When a new action chunk arrives from the server, the client merges it with any remaining actions in the current queue over the overlapping portion. This is where custom aggregators come into play, handling overlapping sections between the current and incoming chunks differently. As of now, we support flexibly aggregation between the chunks via the specification of a custom aggregate_fn(chunk1: torch.Tensor, chunk2: torch.Tensor) -> torch.Tensor function, which is called for each overlapping timestep and can be user-provided. The overlapping portions (shown in light blue in the diagram) require careful handling. We can design different aggregation strategies:.

According to recent reports, this system is highly configurable, as the chunk size threshold can be tuned based on network latency, model inference time, and desired responsiveness. A lower threshold means more frequent updates (and higher computational cost), while a higher threshold reduces communication overhead at the expense of potential queue starvation. Lastly, we typically receive actions from PolicyServer in a thread, and perform them in another one. This keeps the client listening for incoming chunks in a separate thread, without blocking execution and always consuming the current chunk until a new one becomes fully available.

Recent findings suggest that upon receiving observations from the RobotClient, the PolicyServer receives observations from the RobotClient, and performs the necessary observation cleaning to make received observations ready for inference. This process is illustrated in the image below:.

The observation cleaning pipeline running on the server, highlighting the three main steps related to (1) Keys matching (2) Preprocessing and (3) Preparation for inference.

Industry observers note that once the observation has been prepared, it is compared with the last observation used for inference. This avoids collapsing into a loop whereby very similar observations are processed, thus triggering unnecessary inference and similar actions being executed (which in turn, result in very similar observations being processed again). We compare observations in terms of their joint-space similarity, which provides us an approximate and quick way of measuring changes in the robot. Clearly, this metric is not adaptive to dynamic changes in the environment (an object changing its position, or disturbances being applied), but we found it to be a good trade-off for the majority of the cases, and to be very effective in avoiding unnecessary inference and state collapse. Critically, the RobotClient retains control over whether a given observation must be processed, to avoid deadlocks. Observations sent by the client and tagged with must_go=True are processed regardless of the similarity metric.

The policy workflow, in which incoming observations are compared to the last one used for inference, and processed only if different enough, or `must_go`.

Lastly, to ensure the PolicyServer always processes the latest available observation, we block incoming observations until the previous one has been successfully processed. In this, we leverage queues on the PolicyServer to ensure incoming observations are not enqueued until the server is ready to process them (see below).

The client pings the server every 1/fps seconds, but observations are not enqueued for processing until the previous one has been successfully processed.

Critically, ccc influences the number of available actions in the queue at any given time. To avoid the aforementioned sequential limit control, one can:.

Experiments (see plots below) show that g≈0.7g\approx0.7g≈0.7 offers a good trade-off when observations sent are not filtered out (they are all must-go). We recommend setting g=0.5g=0.5g=0.5 and following our documentation to tune this parameter to your needs.

It has been revealed that the number of available actions in the queue at any given time, as a function of g. Larger values of g result in more frequent updates, and more computational cost. Values of g closer to 0 reproduce sequential inference (empty queue, wait). We found g~0.7 to be a good trade-off in our experiments.

It has been revealed that async inference is a simple yet effective way to improve the performance of robotic policies. In our experiments using SmolVLA, async inference results in a ~2x speedup in task completion time with comparable task success rate, and more adaptive control coming from a tighter loop.

To run your policy using async inference, you just need to follow our tutorial with your own custom parameters (e.g., the policy path or the chunk size threshold). Async inference comes with support for policies supporting action chunking!

Recent findings suggest that we have introduced async inference, a simple yet effective way to improve the performance of robotic policies. In our experiments using SmolVLA, async inference results in a ~2x speedup in task completion time with comparable task success rate, and more adaptive control coming from a tighter loop.

We are excited to share this work with the community, and to see how it can be used to improve the performance of robotic policies. We welcome PRs to improve and extend the async inference framework at huggingface/lerobot, and are available to discuss this further in our Discord community, 🤗.

Deadline-aware scheduling scores requests across cadence urgency (EMA-tracked), robot-reported priority, anti-starvation age, trajectory progress, and static priority. ZMQ ROUTER/DEALER transport with protobuf+numpy wire format -- under 1ms serialize-transmit-deserialize vs ~100ms over gRPC.   • Samsung has three foldables in its lineup this year, two of which are pretty familiar.
  • Each one serves a different need, but they all share similar performance and core specs.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

It has been revealed that folding phones are entering a new chapter and, if you’re looking to try one for the first time, you might not know exactly where to start. In this guide, we’ll take a look at some of the most vital questions to answer when buying a foldable, and dissect how Samsung’s Galaxy Z Fold 8, Galaxy Z Fold 8 Ultra, and Galaxy Z Flip 8 fit the bill to figure out which is the best for you, especially if you’re interested in one this holiday season.

This post is sponsored by Samsung.

Samsung has three foldables in its lineup this year, two of which are pretty familiar. The Galaxy Z Flip 8 continues the lineup of clamshell-style foldables, offering a form factor similar to that of a classic flip phone. The Galaxy Z Fold 8 Ultra, meanwhile, is designed to be a normal smartphone on the outside, hiding a tablet within. Finally, the Galaxy Z Fold 8 is the new kid on the block, offering a compact outer display that opens up to a media-friendly, wider inner panel.

Each one serves a different need, but they all share similar performance and core specs. Here’s a quick rundown of the key details on each device:.

It has been revealed that starting with the displays, the book-style Galaxy Z Fold 8 and Fold 8 Ultra both provide outer displays that are fully usable as standard smartphones, while the inner display is useful for multitasking, media, or just getting more space for reading a website or e-book. Samsung’s top-tier specs deliver performance for everything you’d need, with Snapdragon 8 Elite Gen 5 for Galaxy powering everything from demanding games or media-editing apps to day-to-day use.

With each Samsung foldable, you’re getting a fully capable smartphone, but finding the one that’s best for you is a matter of picking your most important priorities. Cameras, battery life, content consumption, and size are some of the most important points to consider, so let’s take a look one-by-one.

Sources indicate that when it comes to cameras, foldables have a tough time. There’s only so much physical space to fit the camera sensors and, with cameras, having more space generally results in a battery overall camera.

That said, the best camera on a Samsung foldable is undoubtedly on the Galaxy Z Fold 8 Ultra.

Industry observers note that the Galaxy Z Fold 8 Ultra has a 200MP main camera that’s similar to the Galaxy S26 Ultra, while it also packs a 50MP ultrawide and something neither of the others offer, a telephoto lens. The 10MP telephoto shooter captures faraway subjects at 3x optical zoom, meaning you’re not giving up on quality when you zoom in. Two 10MP cameras can be found on the displays, with neither sacrificing quality for an under-display look.

Runner-up here is the Galaxy Z Fold 8, which offers a pair of 50MP cameras for wide and ultrawide shots. You can get 2x optical-quality zoom out of the main sensor to still get a good zoom shot, while the main camera still offers good quality and Samsung’s best camera features including 2x optical-quality zoom and the subject-tracking My FanCam.

The Galaxy Z Flip 8 may not have the best camera hardware, but what it lacks in hardware it makes up for in flexibility. This is definitely the best form factor of the bunch for using the foldable design as a tripod for capturing clips. All three devices also use their foldable nature to let you capture full-quality selfies using the rear cameras, which always have better quality than the 10MP dedicated front-facing cameras.

Here’s where specs on paper can tell a different story compared to real life.

The Galaxy Z Fold 8 Ultra may offer the biggest battery of the bunch at 5,000 mAh, but its battery life is on par with the smaller Galaxy Z Fold 8. Both foldables are designed to last you through a full day, though sticking to the outer display only on the Fold 8 Ultra may bring you slightly better battery life overall.

In a recent development, in either case, you’re also getting 45W fast charging over USB-C, granting you speedy recharging if your device happens to get low through the course of a busy day. These are also “Qi2 Ready,” meaning you can use magnetic wireless chargers if you use a compatible magnetic case.

One of the most key things you’ll want to ask yourself when buying a foldable phone is why you want to opt for a foldable in the first place, and each of these devices gives a different answer.

The Galaxy Z Fold 8 Ultra is a productivity powerhouse, delivering more space on its inner display for you to get work done through the web, apps, and more. You can run up to three apps at once on the Galaxy Z Fold 8 Ultra’s display, as well as floating apps, and more.

According to recent reports, galaxy Z Fold 8 is great for media consumption. The wider aspect ratio is perfect for watching videos, playing games, reading books, and more, all while still giving you plenty of space for productivity just like the Ultra.

In a recent development, galaxy Z Flip 8, meanwhile, is all about giving you a more compact device. The outer display lets you quickly reply to messages or keep up with directions, while you can unfold it to do everything you want to on a normal phone. Close it up to more easily stow it away in your pocket or your bag.

Recent findings suggest that if you are moving into a latest Galaxy foldable, the good news is that you don’t have to start from scratch. Thanks to Samsung’s Smart Switch app, you can easily transfer supported content including pictures, contacts, messages, and more from an older Galaxy phone, another Android phone, or even an iPhone over to a Galaxy foldable. Apps, messages, photos, and more can all make the move wirelessly, without the need of a cable.

You can get the Galaxy Z Fold 8, Fold 8 Ultra, and Flip 8 from your favorite carriers and retailers, but Best Buy is one of the best places to score a great deal with solid trade-in values and deep discounts around Black Friday and throughout the holiday season.

The new schedule will apparently see new Galaxy Watch releases every other year, pushing the next release into 2028. Apparently, Samsung intends fresh Galaxy Watch software updates next year as well as “enhancement of healthcare features.” The Galaxy Fit 4 fitness tracker is also expected in 2027, with Dealabs reporting that the tracker will be priced at €79.90 in Europe, a slight price hike over the previous release.

Kimina-Prover: Applying Test-time RL Search on Large Formal Reasoning Models

📅 10 Jul 2025 | ⏱️ 12 min read (2413 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Hugging Face

⏱️ ~12 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Sources indicate that we're excited to announce the release of Kimina-Prover-72B, our state-of-the-art theorem proving model trained with the Kimi k1.5[1] RL pipeline based on Qwen2.5-72B [2].
  • Test-Time Reinforcement Learning Search: A trainable agentic proving framework that enables the model to recursively discover, combine and apply multiple lemmas to construct complex proofs, building on a novel lemma-enabled pattern.
  • Error-Fixing Capability: Kimina-Prover can read and interpret Lean’s error messages and propose targeted fixes, demonstrating significantly higher sample efficiency compared to regenerating proofs from scratch.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Sources indicate that we're excited to announce the release of Kimina-Prover-72B, our state-of-the-art theorem proving model trained with the Kimi k1.5[1] RL pipeline based on Qwen2.5-72B [2]. Alongside it, we are also releasing two distilled variants: Kimina-Prover-Distill-8B and 1.7B (based on Qwen3-8B and Qwen3-1.7B[3] respectively).

Test-Time Reinforcement Learning Search: A trainable agentic proving framework that enables the model to recursively discover, combine and apply multiple lemmas to construct complex proofs, building on a novel lemma-enabled pattern.

Error-Fixing Capability: Kimina-Prover can read and interpret Lean’s error messages and propose targeted fixes, demonstrating significantly higher sample efficiency compared to regenerating proofs from scratch.

These advancements enable Kimina-Prover to solve challenging mathematical problems and surpass prior methods. As shown in Figure 1, on the widely used miniF2F benchmark, Kimina-Prover achieves a state-of-the-art pass rate of 92.2%.

It has been revealed that we focus on automated theorem proving (ATP) in the Lean 4 language, aiming to automate the construction of formal mathematical proofs. Recent advances in neural theorem proving have significantly improved the ability of AI systems to assist with or automate this process. Notable progress includes AlphaProof[4] from Google DeepMind, which demonstrated strong performance on problems at the level of the International Mathematical Olympiad. Open-source systems such as DeepSeek-Prover-V2[5], which incorporates reinforcement learning, have also achieved state-of-the-art results. In addition, neuro-symbolic agentic approaches like DSP+[6] have shown that competitive performance is possible without large-scale training by leveraging off-the-shelf models in a modular framework.

Our earlier work of Kimina-Prover Preview[7] introduced a large language model for formal theorem proving in Lean, establishing a upcoming performance baseline on the miniF2F benchmark. Trained with a large-scale reinforcement learning pipeline, the model adopted a reasoning-driven exploration paradigm and demonstrated that larger models can serve as stronger formal reasoners. Its structured reasoning pattern enabled efficient proof search and emulated human-like problem-solving strategies.

Industry observers note that following this initial success, we continued to improve the model through further iterations of reinforcement learning. However, single-step reasoning remains insufficient for solving complex problems that require long, multi-stage proofs. To address this limitation, we introduce the Test-Time Reinforcement Learning (TTRL) search framework, which enables the model to discover, combine, and reuse multiple intermediate lemmas autonomously. This framework supports deeper, long-horizon reasoning by decomposing hard problems into reusable subcomponents.

A key ingredient of TTRL search is the lemma-enabled pattern, which allows the model to identify and apply intermediate lemmas as part of its proof construction process. This structured reuse of intermediate results significantly expands the model’s problem-solving capability beyond single-step generation.

To further enhance robustness, we also integrate an error-fixing mechanism that interprets Lean’s error messages and proposes targeted corrections. This allows the model to refine its outputs through iterative feedback, improving proof reliability and overall sample efficiency.

Industry observers note that as the combination of the proposed techniques results in significant improvements in formal theorem proving performance. On the miniF2F benchmark, Kimina-Prover achieves a pass rate of 84.0% with pass@32 and 86.4% with the addition of a single round of error correction. With pass@1024, the pass rate reaches 87.7%. Applying the full Test-Time Reinforcement Learning (TTRL) search framework yields a final pass rate of 92.2%, with an estimated pass upper bound of approximately 42,000. However, this pass budget can be substantially optimized in future versions, as a large portion of the current sampling is spent on proving unhelpful or redundant lemmas.

It has been revealed that notably, these results indicate a shift in the scaling behavior of the prover. While earlier versions exhibited approximately linear improvements in log scale with increasing sampling budget, the current system shows diminishing returns beyond pass@1024. This suggests that further gains are less dependent on increased sampling and instead require more sophisticated search strategies, such as those introduced by TTRL.

Industry observers note that the lemma-enabled pattern is designed to equip the model with the ability to identify and utilize useful lemmas provided in the input. To support this capability, during reinforcement learning (RL) training, a random subset of one to three formal lemmas is prepended to the problem context, exposing the prover to potentially useful intermediate results that can aid in constructing the final proof. These lemmas are prepared through a two-step pipeline: (1) a general-purpose LLM generates candidate lemmas in natural language; (2) these are then translated into formal statements using our Kimina-Autoformalizer-7b.

Recent findings suggest that initial observations revealed that the model had a low tendency to incorporate the provided lemmas. To address this, we introduced a preference-based reward shaping strategy within the RL framework. When a theorem could be proven through multiple trajectories, solutions that successfully leveraged a provided lemma were assigned a higher reward, while those that did not were penalized. This approach proved effective, increasing the lemma utilization rate to a stable 30–40% after training. Importantly, this method not only encouraged lemma usage but also promoted selectivity: the model learned to apply lemmas strategically when they were useful, while ignoring irrelevant ones, demonstrating more efficient and human-like reasoning behavior.

In a recent development, the lemma-enabled pattern allowed the model to incorporate pre-generated lemmas as intermediate steps in constructing proofs. However, we observed that randomly sampling and inserting lemmas was insufficient for solving complex problems requiring highly structured and deeply nested reasoning. To address this limitation, we developed the Test-Time Reinforcement Learning Search framework—a trainable, agentic approach that systematically organizes, filters, and composes a large set of candidate lemmas to build complete proofs. This framework transitions the process from random exploration to a more strategic, goal-directed search.

As illustrated in Figure 2, we define the search scope of each problem as the problem itself along with its associated candidate lemmas. TTRL Search tracks a lemma utilization score within each search scope to measure how frequently and effectively each lemma contributes to the final proof. At the beginning of each RL training iteration, for each problem (i.e., search scope), we construct K = 10 input variants by prepending different combinations of lemmas. To balance exploration and exploitation, 60% of the inputs are built using the top-ranking lemmas—those with the highest utilization scores—focusing the model on the most promising proof paths. The remaining 40% are formed by including these top lemmas alongside one to four randomly selected additional lemmas, encouraging exploration of novel and potentially useful lemma combinations.

To ensure quality, a filtering mechanism prunes lemmas that consistently fail to contribute meaningfully: any lemma that fails to achieve a utilization score of at least τ=0.10 after 50 insertion attempts is removed from the search pool.

A key feature of TTRL is its recursive search mechanism. The search scope is not limited to the original theorem but is also maintained for each lemma, allowing the framework to recursively decompose the problem into smaller subproblems. A parallel sublemma generation process runs throughout, and whenever a theorem or lemma fails to find a proof after N = 128 attempts, newly introduced candidate sublemmas are generated. This recursive strategy enables test-time scaling of reasoning depth, significantly extending the model’s effective problem-solving capability.

To maintain logical soundness, we address a failure mode wherein incorrectly formalized lemmas could lead to trivial or invalid proofs. In such cases, the model may exploit inconsistencies to construct seemingly valid but unsound solutions. To prevent this, we introduce a negation proving process: for each newly generated lemma, we attempt to prove its logical negation. If the negated statement is provable, it indicates that the original lemma is logically inconsistent and is immediately discarded. This step ensures the reliability and soundness of the overall proof construction process.

Recent findings suggest that A critical limitation of recent advanced theorem proving models is their lack of the ability to correct proofs based on feedback from the proof assistant—capabilities that human customers routinely leverage. To address this gap, we developed a dedicated framework to integrate error-fixing capabilities into Kimina-Prover.

It has been revealed that SFT Data Generation for Error Correction. General-purpose large language models exhibit a low success rate when interpreting Lean’s error messages and proposing valid corrections. To overcome this, we constructed a specialized Supervised Fine-Tuning (SFT) dataset tailored for error correction. This dataset consists of triplets in the form of (incorrect proof, Lean feedback, correct proof). To enrich the supervision signal, we prompted Claude 3.7 sonnet[8] to synthesize step-by-step reasoning chains explaining how the incorrect proof can be transformed into the correct one using the provided feedback. The result is a high-quality dataset that includes not only the initial and corrected proofs but also the intermediate reasoning, facilitating more effective learning.

Industry observers note that batched Failure Replay Strategy. Integrating error correction directly into the reinforcement learning (RL) loop initially proved ineffective due to the low success rate (~1%) of the SFT model in fixing errors, resulting in sparse rewards and unstable training. To address this, we designed the Batched Failure Replay strategy. Rather than attempting to correct errors immediately during an RL iteration, all failed proof attempts from iteration N are collected. In the subsequent iteration N+1, the training batch is composed of a fixed-size union of these prior failures (e.g., 500 samples) and standard problems from the prompt set (e.g., another 500 samples). This ensures consistent and high-volume exposure to error correction tasks in each training step, enabling the model to gradually learn effective error-handling behaviors in a stable and data-efficient manner.

This training approach led to measurable improvements in the model’s ability to recover from failure. The model advanced from correcting basic syntax errors to resolving complex logical mistakes and, eventually, discovering alternative proof strategies when initial attempts failed. Crucially, this capability improved sample efficiency. As shown in Table 2, we compared different strategies under fixed computational budgets. The 16+16 attempt-and-fix strategy—consisting of 16 initial proof attempts, each followed by one error-fixing attempt—achieved a success rate of 35.6%, outperforming the 32×1 brute-force baseline, which reached 28.8% with 32 independent attempts. Further increasing the sample budget to 32+32 with error correction yielded a success rate of 44.1%. These results demonstrate that enabling the model to correct its own errors is a more efficient use of computational resources than repeated trial-and-error.

In addition to our core TTRL search and Error fixing, we developed several other novel techniques to enhance the model's learning process and problem-solving capabilities.

It has been revealed that prompt Set Curation and Iteration. Effective data curation is critical for reinforcement learning (RL) efficiency. Our initial prompt set of over 300K problems was refined to a competition-focused subset of approximately 90K, with an emphasis on problems from sources such as the olympiads-ref subset of NuminaMath 1.5[9]. During RL, we applied dynamic filtering: problems with consistently high success rates were removed to maintain challenge, while persistently difficult problems were decomposed into simpler subproblems or variations using a general-purpose LLM. The final prompt set combines auto-formalized statements for broad coverage, human-annotated problems for quality, and augmented variations for targeted skill development. The curated prompt set will be open-sourced.

Recent findings suggest that continuous Pre-training on Lean Data. To address the limited Lean proficiency in most base models, we applied Continuous Pre-training (CPT). A 6-billion-token CPT dataset was constructed from multiple sources: 260M tokens from online platforms such as GitHub, 5.5B tokens of compiler-validated rollout data from our RL pipeline, and additional structured data in state–tactic–state and state–tactic–error formats to enhance diversity. These structured data supplements the base model with additional domain knowledge.

Random Proof Cut Data Augmentation. To better utilize high-quality, human-annotated proofs that lack intermediate reasoning steps, we developed the Random Proof Cut technique. This method augments such data using two variations:.

This strategy allows the model to learn how to extend existing lines of reasoning and to fill in logical gaps, effectively integrating human-generated content into the training process.

Recent findings suggest that non-proof Problem Solving. Many problems are presented in the form of requiring a final answer, which cannot be naturally framed as a traditional proof task. Inspired by the CombiBench[10] evaluation methodology, we introduced a capability for non-proof problem solving to unify answer generation with proof construction. In this setting, the model is given a problem with the final answer field left blank. It performs a two-stage process within a single inference: it first deduces the correct answer and then generates a complete formal proof to justify that answer. This approach ensures the model’s reasoning is explicitly conditioned on reaching the correct solution.

Here we provide some proof cases found by our newest Kimina-prover model. The complete list of solved miniF2F problems is available on GitHub.

In a recent development, the system recursively decomposed the problem into four layers of lemmas using a TTRL search approach, ultimately generating a 520-line formal proof. During this recursive proving process, initially, only one lemma, sum_cexp_div_pow_ne_zero, remained to be solved. While this conclusion seems straightforward to prove informally, it would still require a lot of steps to prove it rigorously in Lean 4. Our system recursively generated two extra layers of lemmas and obtained a 260-line formal proof for sum_cexp_div_pow_ne_zero. This proof is valid under Mathlib v4.15.

In the following example, the initial proof timed out because directly applying simp to ((Real.sqrt 3 / 2 : ℂ) + (1 / 2) * Complex.I) ^ 12 resulted in excessive search complexity. Breaking down the proof by step-by-step calculating intermediate powers like $z^3$, then $z^6$, and finally $z^{12}$ significantly reduced the computational burden on the compiler.

If you'd like to cite Kimina-Prover, please feel free to reference our preview paper for now. A full paper is right now in preparation and will be available soon.

A frontend application can compile successfully and still fail when it communicates with the backend.

Imagine a backend developer changes an API response from:.

The backend works correctly. The frontend also builds without errors. However, a component expecting user.name now receives undefined.

This is an example of API contract drift: the frontend and backend no longer agree on the structure or behavior of an API.

The problem becomes more difficult when several developers or teams work on different parts of an application. A change made by one team may affect another team's assumptions without producing an obvious error during development.

Industry observers note that typeScript helps catch many programming mistakes, but its types do not automatically validate data received over HTTP. A type declaration can describe what the application expects without proving that the server actually returns it.

In this tutorial, we'll look at a practical way to make API contracts more reliable.

Consider a typical frontend API function:.

At first glance, this looks reasonable.

The function promises to return a User, so TypeScript allows the application to access properties such as name and email.

Recent findings suggest that the return value of response.json() is not automatically checked against the User interface. The interface only provides compile-time information; it does not validate the actual JSON received from the server.

the frontend may still treat the response as a User even though the data has a different structure.

This is particularly important when working with:.

Independently deployed frontend and backend applications.

APIs maintained by different engineering teams.

The solution is to validate data at the boundary where it enters the application.

It has been revealed that zod is a TypeScript-first schema validation library. It allows developers to describe expected data structures and validate actual values against those definitions.

Now create a schema for the user response:.

There are two important parts here.

First, UserSchema describes the structure that the application expects at runtime.

Second, z.infer generates the corresponding TypeScript type from the schema.

This means developers do not need to maintain a separate interface and validation definition for the same data structure.

The response is initially treated as unknown, which prevents the application from assuming that untrusted data already has the expected structure.

UserSchema.parse() validates the actual response.

If the backend returns an unexpected property type or misses a required field, Zod throws a validation error instead of allowing invalid data to move silently through the application.

You can also use safeParse() when you prefer to handle validation errors without exceptions:.

This approach is useful when API responses are external or when a frontend must provide more controlled error handling.

One common mistake is placing API validation logic directly inside React components.

In a recent development, for a small application, this may seem convenient. As the project grows, however, it becomes difficult to reuse validation rules and identify where data transformations happen.

A better approach is to separate API schemas, service functions, and UI components.

The responsibilities are straightforward:.

schemas/user.ts defines the expected user data.

api/client.ts handles common HTTP configuration.

api/users.ts contains user-related API requests.

hooks/useUser.ts manages data fetching for React.

components/UserProfile.tsx displays the validated data.

This structure makes it easier to change an API implementation without rewriting the UI.

It also makes testing more manageable because validation logic can be tested independently of React rendering.

For more ideas on organizing application code, see SitePoint's guide to modern JavaScript modules.

Runtime validation protects an application when data arrives. However, teams also need a shared description of what an API is supposed to accept and return.

This is where OpenAPI becomes useful.

OpenAPI provides a standard format for describing HTTP APIs, including:.

Request and response structures.

Data types and validation constraints.

For example, an endpoint can be described using an OpenAPI document:.

This document describes what the endpoint should return.

Both frontend and backend developers can refer to the same contract instead of relying on separate assumptions or outdated documentation.

Swagger Editor helps developers write and validate OpenAPI documents. It also provides a convenient way to inspect API definitions.

Swagger UI turns an OpenAPI document into interactive API documentation, allowing developers to explore endpoints and test requests.

Redoc provides another way to generate readable API documentation from an OpenAPI specification.

These tools are particularly useful when APIs are maintained by multiple developers or consumed by several applications.

Maintaining API types manually across frontend and backend repositories creates opportunities for inconsistencies.

For example, a backend developer might add a upcoming optional property while the frontend continues using an older interface.

One way to reduce this duplication is to generate TypeScript definitions and API clients from an OpenAPI specification.

Orval is a useful tool for this workflow.

It can generate TypeScript clients and types from an OpenAPI document, helping frontend developers work with consistent endpoint definitions.

A simplified workflow looks like this:.

A typical configuration might look like this:.

The exact configuration depends on the Orval version and the structure of the OpenAPI document.

Once configured, the client can be regenerated when the API specification changes.

This reduces the amount of repetitive code developers need to maintain manually.

However, generated types should not be confused with runtime validation. They improve consistency during development, but an application may still need to validate responses received from external systems or services that cannot be fully trusted.

Frontend developers often need to build or test features before the corresponding backend endpoint is ready.

Waiting for a complete backend implementation can slow down development, particularly when multiple teams work independently.

Mock Service Worker (MSW) helps solve this problem by intercepting network requests and returning controlled responses.

You can define a mock handler for the user endpoint:.

The frontend can now make normal HTTP requests while MSW supplies predictable responses during development or testing.

You can also simulate an invalid response:.

This makes it possible to check whether the application's validation and error-handling logic behave as expected.

MSW is particularly valuable because it allows frontend tests to run without requiring a live backend environment.

Runtime validation and generated clients improve reliability, but they do not automatically guarantee that independently developed services remain compatible.

For systems with multiple services, contract testing can provide another layer of protection.

Pact is a contract-testing tool that allows consumers and providers to verify their expectations about API interactions.

Consider a frontend application that expects the user endpoint to return:.

The consumer defines the expected interaction.

The backend provider can then run verification against that contract to check whether its actual response satisfies the consumer's expectations.

This helps identify breaking changes before they reach production.

According to recent reports, these tools solve different problems. A project does not necessarily need all of them, but larger applications can benefit from combining the approaches that match their architecture.

A contract is only useful if developers consistently check it when making changes.

A practical approach is to run validation and tests automatically whenever someone opens a pull request.

For example, a GitHub Actions workflow might look like this:.

The api:validate script should be configured to validate the project's OpenAPI document or run the relevant contract checks.

The test command should execute the application's automated tests.

For a production project, you may also want to include:.

Generated-client consistency checks.

Consumer-provider contract verification.

The objective is to detect incompatible changes before they are merged.

A failed pipeline gives developers an opportunity to investigate the change while the context is still fresh.

API contracts become harder to maintain when several teams contribute to the same system.

For example, a company might have separate teams responsible for:.

Customer-facing frontend applications.

If nobody owns an API contract, small changes can create unexpected problems for other teams.

Assigning clear ownership helps establish who reviews changes, maintains documentation, and coordinates breaking updates.

It has been revealed that this becomes particularly vital when an organization expands its engineering capacity across locations or adds several specialized teams. Companies planning that kind of growth may also need to consider enterprise IT recruitment as part of their wider engineering workforce strategy.

Regardless of how a team is assembled, its development process should establish clear responsibilities for API design, versioning, testing, and release coordination.

A few practical conventions can make a significant difference:.

Assign an owner to every important API or service.

Document breaking changes before implementation.

Require contract-related tests in pull requests.

Keep generated clients synchronized with the API specification.

Communicate deprecations before removing existing fields.

Monitor production errors after deploying API changes.

These practices help prevent a growing engineering organization from becoming a collection of disconnected services.

In a recent development, API contract drift is not simply a TypeScript problem. It is a coordination problem that becomes visible when applications and services develop different expectations about the same data.

TypeScript provides useful compile-time checks, but it cannot guarantee that an HTTP response matches a declared interface.

A more reliable approach combines several techniques:.

Use Zod to validate incoming data.

Use OpenAPI to document API expectations.

Generate TypeScript clients with tools such as Orval.

Use MSW to test frontend behavior without a live backend.

Use Pact when consumer-provider contract verification is appropriate.

Run validation and tests automatically in CI/CD.

You do not need to introduce every tool at once. Start by validating external API responses, document important endpoints, and gradually automate contract checks as the application grows.

The result is a codebase where developers can make changes with greater confidence and where frontend and backend teams have a shared understanding of how their systems communicate.

You’ll also only need to think about charging around 2 times per month thanks to the impressive 14-day battery life. 📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

In January of this year, Hugging Face's Xet Team deployed a upcoming storage backend, and shortly after shifted ~6% of Hub downloads through the infrastructure. This represented a significant milestone, but it was just the beginning. In 6 months, 500,000 repositories holding 20 PB joined the move to Xet as the Hub outgrows Git LFS and transitions to a storage system that scales with the workloads of AI builders.

Today, more than 1 million people on the Hub are using Xet. In May, it became the default on the Hub for latest customers and organizations. With only a few dozen GitHub problems, forum threads, and Discord messages, this is perhaps the quietest migration of this magnitude.

How? For one, the team came prepared with years of experience building and supporting the content addressed store (CAS) and Rust client that provide the system's foundation. Without these pieces, Git LFS may still be the future on the Hub. However, the unsung heroes of this migration are:.

Sources indicate that together, these components have allowed us to aggressively migrate PBs in the span of days without worrying about the impact to the Hub or the community. They're giving us the peace of mind to move even faster in the coming weeks and months (skip to the end 👇 to see what's coming).

In the early days of planning the migration to Xet, we made a few key design decisions:.

Sources indicate that driven by our commitment to the community, these seemingly straightforward decisions had significant implications. Most importantly, we did not believe customers and teams should have to immediately alter their workflow or download a latest client to interact with Xet-enabled repositories.

Industry observers note that if you have a Xet-aware client (e.g., hf-xet, the Xet integration with huggingface_hub), uploads and downloads pass through the entire Xet stack. The client either breaks up files into chunks using content defined chunking while uploading, or requests file reconstruction information when downloading. On upload, chunks are passed to CAS and stored in S3. During downloads, CAS provides the chunk ranges the client needs to request from S3 to reconstruct the file locally.

Industry observers note that for older versions of huggingface_hub or huggingface.js, which do not support chunk-based file transfers, you can still download and upload to Xet repos, but these bytes take a different route. When a Xet-backed file is requested from the Hub along the resolve endpoint, the Git LFS Bridge constructs and returns a single presigned URL, mimicking the LFS protocol. The Bridge then does the work of reconstructing the file from the content held in S3 and returns it to the requester.

To see this in action, right click on the image above and open it in a newly introduced tab. The URL redirects from https://huggingface.co/datasets/huggingface/documentation-images/resolve/main/blog/migrating-the-hub-to-xet/bridge.png to one that begins with https://cas-bridge.xethub.hf.co/xet-bridge-us/.... You can also use curl -vL on the same URL to see the redirects in your terminal.

It has been revealed that meanwhile, when a non-Xet-aware client uploads a file, it is sent first to LFS storage then migrated to Xet. This “background migration process,” only briefly mentioned in our docs, powers both the migrations to Xet and upload backward compatibility. It is behind the migration of well over a dozen PBs of models and datasets and is keeping 500,000 repos in sync with Xet storage all without missing a beat.

Recent findings suggest that every time a file needs to be migrated from LFS to Xet, a webhook is triggered, pushing the event to a distributed queue where it is processed by an orchestrator. The orchestrator:.

These migration workers then pick up the jobs and each pod:.

In a recent development, in April, we tested this system's limits by reaching out to bartowski and asking if they wanted to test out Xet. With nearly 500 TB across 2,000 repos, bartowski's migration uncovered a few weak links:.

It has been revealed that fixing this three-headed monster meant touching every layer - patching xet-core, resizing CAS, and beefing up the worker node specs. Fortunately, bartowski was game to work with us while every repo made its way to Xet. These same lessons powered the moves of the biggest storage owners on the Hub like RichardErkhov (1.7PB and 25,000 repos) and mradermacher (6.1PB and 42,000 repos 🤯).

CAS throughput, meanwhile, has grown by an order of magnitude between the first and latest large-scale migrations:.

When we began replacing LFS, we had two goals in mind:.

Designing with our initial constraints and these goals allowed us to:.

In a recent development, instead of waiting for all upload paths to become Xet-aware, forcing a hard cut-over, or pushing the community to adopt a specific workflow, we could begin migrating the Hub to Xet immediately with minimal user impact. In short, let teams keep their workflows and organically transition to Xet with infrastructure supporting the long-term goal of a unified storage system.

Industry observers note that in January and February, we onboarded power users to provide feedback and pressure-test the infrastructure. To get community feedback, we launched a waitlist to preview Xet-enabled repositories. Soon after, Xet became the default for fresh users on the Hub.

We now support some of the largest creators on the Hub (Meta Llama, Google, OpenAI, and Qwen) while the community keeps working uninterrupted.

Starting this month, we're bringing Xet to everyone. Watch for an email providing access to Xet and once you have it, revision to the latest huggingface_hub (pip install -U huggingface_hub) to unlock faster transfers right away. This will also mean:.

If you upload or download from the Hub using your browser or use Git, that's fine. Chunk-based support for both is coming soon. In the meantime use whichever workflow you already have; no restrictions.

Industry observers note that next up: open-sourcing the Xet protocol and the entire infrastructure stack. The future of storing and moving bytes that scale to AI workloads is on the Hub, and we're aiming to bring it to everyone.

If you have any questions, drop us a line in the comments 👇, open a discussion on the Xet team page.

Perhaps a dumb question: Xet is supposed to not only drive some speed ups but also provide a significant storage advantage in that only the diffs of a given object need to be uploaded/stored right?

Recent findings suggest that I ask as my account migrated to xet, but I don’t see any reduction in the amount of storage quota anything created after migration. For example, as far as I’ve seen, if I create a dataset repo that is 1 GB, change a handful of rows and re-push, the storage usage is going to say 2+ GB. Am I missing something?

Not a dumb question at all. The Hub reports storage based on the logical size of each new object; what you're seeing is expected.

For the use-case that you're describing, Xet still provides faster file transfers as there is less to push and pull, so changes finish faster and uses less bandwidth/compute.

This enables and strengthens our commitment to provide free public storage to the open source community. Of course, we're always evaluating ways to surface this transparently and support the community, so let me know if any of this is confusing.

Gotcha, didn’t realize it was global deduplication, that makes sense (btw - is the deduplication done after upload then, or xet somehow compares diffs vs 20+ PB of data prior to upload?).

Industry observers note that I’m not in the position where this impacts me at the moment (thankfully 🙏) and not my call but if the private storage is handled the same way it has some interesting.. implications. For example if people are paying for extra private storage, and their storage is being counted “full size” against limits whilst being deduplicated against the rest of the hub and therefore a fraction of that in reality, is that fair? Etc.

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Google’s Fitbit Air is a simple screenless fitness tracker, but it can do a bit more, and now someone has built an app that lets the Air buzz your wrist when phone notifications come through.

The era of vibe-coding has been very quickly bringing ideas to reality, and these new Fitbit Air notification apps are a great example.

It has been revealed that “Air Relay” is the result of a developer managing to reverse-engineer a way to control haptics on the Fitbit Air via Bluetooth without affecting Google Health sync. “Cuff” uses the same method while also showing health stats if you don’t want to use Google Health.

It has been revealed that the idea here is pretty simple. You can have apps on your phone ping your Fitbit Air as you choose. “Air Relay” lets you pick select apps and even change the vibration pattern or strength based on the app. You can set “Quiet hours” to prevent notifications while you’re sleeping, and there’s a WhatsApp-specific setting that lets you only get notifications from specific groups or people. A “Find My Air” setting uses Bluetooth strength you help you track down a lost tracker.

While a massive part of the appeal of Fitbit Air is its screenless, disconnected nature, having the option to set up alerts for vital apps or contacts is certainly a useful option.

“Air Relay” is free on Google Play, and Fitbit Air is available for $99.

The Binding of Isaac: Repentance Plus has spent the last few days getting review-bombed on Steam after it was discovered that a particular segment of the game used AI music. Reddit user ShweetsStuff discovered the songs used during a Grand Theft Auto-themed section. They found several audio files with Suno metadata that pointed back to the tracks on Suno’s site.

Creator Edmund McMillen took to X to apologize and claimed he “had no idea” the in-game GTA parody used generative AI music. Adding to the drama, Valve requires developers to disclose how and when they use generative AI in the development process, and Nicalis, Inc., the studio behind Repentance Plus, doesn’t appear to have mentioned the AI music anywhere.

In a recent development, within hours of the discovery, Nicalis shared on X that Repentance Plus had been updated and the generated music files had been removed. While reviews on Steam have yet to rebound, and the game is still rated as “overwhelmingly negative,” owners on X seem to be giving McMillen the benefit of the doubt, likely because he’s been quite outspoken on AI in game development, calling it “uninspired and bland” in a TikTok from 2024.

📅 16 Jul 2025 • ⏱️ 5m • 📚 Deep Dive (1068 w)
📖 Baca
General ⚖️ Neutral 🌐 Hugging Face ↗ Open Full Page

Ettin Suite: SoTA Paired Encoders and Decoders

📅 16 Jul 2025 | ⏱️ 5 min read (1068 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Hugging Face

⏱️ ~5 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • According to recent reports, what would happen if you took the ModernBERT recipe and applied it to a decoder-only model?
  • According to recent reports, we introduce a newly introduced open-data training recipe to reproduce the encoder-only ModernBERT model (and actually beat it!).
  • This blog post introduces Ettin, the first suite of SoTA paired encoder-only and decoder-only models (17M-1B params) trained with identical data (2T tokens), architecture, and training recipes.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

According to recent reports, what would happen if you took the ModernBERT recipe and applied it to a decoder-only model? Turns out, a state-of-the-art decoder language model that beats Llama 3.2 1B and SmolLM2!

According to recent reports, we introduce a newly introduced open-data training recipe to reproduce the encoder-only ModernBERT model (and actually beat it!). We then apply the exact same recipe to decoder-only models. For the first time, we have two state-of-the-art models trained in the same setup but with two different training objectives: masked language modeling (MLM), and causal language modeling (CLM).

This blog post introduces Ettin, the first suite of SoTA paired encoder-only and decoder-only models (17M-1B params) trained with identical data (2T tokens), architecture, and training recipes. Ettin enables true apples-to-apples comparisons between architectures and delivers state-of-the-art performance for open-data models in both categories. We then further explore whether it is possible to get a competitive encoder starting from the decoder and vice-versa.

If you are interested in trying out the models, some boilerplates are available at the end of this blogpost!

The LLM community has largely converged on decoder-only models like GPT, Llama, and Qwen. Their generative capabilities are impressive, but this focus is detracting attention from other categories, such as encoder-only models like BERT.

However, encoder BERT-like models remain the workhorses of production systems for classification, retrieval, and embedding tasks. They're faster, more memory-efficient, and often more accurate for discriminative tasks. The key difference lies in their attention patterns:.

While decoder models have seen rapid innovation, encoder model development had stagnated – until recently, with efforts like ModernBERT modernizing them. But which architecture is better? Previous comparisons between encoders and decoders used different datasets, architectures, and training recipes, so it was hard to tell.

According to recent reports, named after the two-headed Norse giant, Ettin provides a controlled comparison by training with both architectures on identical data, identical model shapes, and identical training recipes. They only differ in attention patterns and training objectives!

Sources indicate that we build on the ModernBERT recipe, which borrowed modern techniques from decoder-only models and brought them to encoder training. This provides a strong base for training both architectures.

We train six different sizes, ranging from 17M to 1B parameters. This allows us to test the effects of scale, and provides a wide variety of models for you to use! No matter if you need a blazing fast on-device model or a powerful but slower model, we got you covered!

We use a comprehensive three-phase training approach to maximize performance:.

Phase 1 - Pre-training (1.7T tokens): We start with a diverse mixture of high-quality data sources, training on shorter contexts (1024 tokens) to establish strong foundational knowledge.

Phase 2 - Context Extension (250B tokens): We increase context length to 8K tokens using higher-quality filtered data, allowing models to understand longer documents and more complex relationships.

Phase 3 - Decay (100B tokens): We finish with premium data sources including scientific papers, textbooks, and curated content while gradually reducing the learning rate.

Our encoder models gain all the benefits of ModernBERT's speed, allowing them to be significantly faster than the previous generations of encoders.

Unlike ModernBERT, all our training data is public and reproducible:.

You can continue to train these models on newly introduced data or propose a new recipe to further improve results!

It has been revealed that our encoder models outperform ModernBERT across all tasks and model sizes, while using completely open training data. Since we provide a large range of sizes, you can now use ModernBERT-style models in smaller sizes (great for on-device or for fast-inference), or power up with a 1B-sized encoder that crushes the competition.

Applying the same recipe to decoder models yields equally impressive results, with our models outperforming or matching established baselines such as Llama 3.2 and SmolLM2:.

The gains are particularly strong on knowledge-intensive tasks like SciQ, reflecting the benefits of our high-quality training data mixture. These results demonstrate that our training recipe creates genuinely strong models in both architectural paradigms.

Industry observers note that for the first time, we can fairly compare encoder and decoder architectures trained with identical data and recipes. The results reveal fundamental architectural advantages that persist even when all other factors are controlled:.

The results show clear patterns:.

Encoders dominate classification and retrieval: On MNLI classification, even a 150M encoder (89.2) outperforms a 400M decoder (88.2). For retrieval tasks, the gap is smaller but still noticeable - especially when decoders are not trained with MNTP.

Decoders excel at generation: On generative tasks, decoders maintain consistent advantages, with the performance gap actually widening at larger model sizes.

Size doesn't always matter: A 400M encoder beats a 1B decoder on classification tasks, while a 400M decoder beats a 1B encoder on generation tasks.

Recent findings suggest that due to the lack of new encoder models, works like LLM2Vec have proposed to continue pre-training decoders with MLM. We can now test the effectiveness of this strategy!

Recent findings suggest that we switched the objective and continued to train our models with the opposite objective for 50B additional tokens. This is what we found:.

This suggests the architecture choice matters fundamentally, not just the training objective.

With identical training data, we can study how different objectives affect learning. For example, analyzing gender bias using the WinoGender benchmark reveals:.

This opens doors for systematic studies of how training objectives influence model behavior beyond just accuracy metrics.

You can use these models with just a few lines of code!

For classification and retrieval tasks, use encoder models: You may want to use a fine-tuned version for these tasks as well.

For text generation tasks, use decoder models:.

The complete Ettin suite includes models at six different scales (for both encoders and decoders):.

Recent findings suggest that any chance you can add the trained sentence transformer versions of these models? It'd be very useful (And I lack compute for training from scratch :)).

According to recent reports, yes, we’re working with some people to get some trained embeddings versions. Hopefully you won’t have to wait too long :).

Recent findings suggest that softr gets used a lot by operations and business teams as their AI app builder for secure client portals, internal tools and other business apps, none of which require code. Write a short brief in your own words, and the AI Co-Builder turns it into a database plus the core app that sits on it: tables, pages and layouts, the data connections behind them, plus user groups and permissions, so real users can sign in from day one. Workflows come as the next step, either by prompting the Co-Builder again or by adding them in the visual editor.

In a recent development, the Free strategy is $0 for unlimited apps, with room for 5 app users, 3 builders, 5,000 records and 5 AI credits each month. Basic runs $19 per month, Pro $99 and Business $329, all on annual billing. Enterprise pricing is custom and includes SSO and SCIM for organizations managing access at scale. The full plan table sits on Softr's pricing page.

Lovable builds full-stack web apps through conversation, writing React code while it takes care of hosting, SSL and the backend. It's designed to move a founder or product team from a prompt to a shareable prototype, and the preview updates as the agent works.

Base44 calls itself a no-code AI platform: you explain the app, and it generates the structure, design and logic while running the backend itself. Authentication, a database and analytics come on every blueprint, Free included.

According to recent reports, base44 is free for 25 message credits a month. Starter costs $16 per month and Builder $40 per month, both on annual billing, with Pro at $80 and Elite at $160.

According to recent reports, bolt is a coding agent that writes full-stack projects in the browser and runs them on Bolt Cloud, which supplies hosting, databases and integrations. It suits people who want to watch the code take shape and edit it themselves.

The questions buyers ask have turned plainer since then: what each edit costs, who keeps the app running, and whether a client can sign in and see their own records alone. A generated front end makes a good demo, and a team using it every day needs permissions and a predictable bill for the next hundred edits.

Industry observers note that softr is now my default when recommending AI app builders. It handles teams, auth, and real company data better than any other product. The AI Co-Builder drafts tables, pages and user groups, workflows follow as the next step, and the app keeps running on maintained platform components with no codebase to patch. App-user pricing and an editor that works without AI credits keep later changes from turning into a running meter.

Sources indicate that three situations call for a different tool. Glide makes a better mobile-first choice when the app spends its days on phones in the field. Bubble gives more front-end design freedom when a project calls for bespoke layouts, interactive animation or heavy brand styling. If your engineers want version control and audit logs and can handle a technical setup, Retool covers that need.

Recent findings suggest that agents are moving inside the apps these tools produce. Gartner expects task-specific AI agents inside 40% of enterprise applications by the close of 2026, against under 5% in 2025, so a 2027 app builder will need to host agents that respect the same permissions as human consumers.

Building is also leaving the builder's own window. The Model Context Protocol now sits under the Linux Foundation's Agentic AI Foundation and reports more than 97 million SDK downloads a month, with client support in ChatGPT and Claude, among others. Softr's changelog dates its official Claude and ChatGPT connector to October 6, 2026, and I expect more teams to start an app from the chat assistant they already use.

The caution comes from Gartner too: it predicts organizations will scrap upward of 40% of agentic AI projects before 2028, citing escalating costs, unclear business value and inadequate risk controls. Going into 2027, I'd judge any builder on whether it keeps agent costs and access rules visible to the team running the app.

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Agent Anomaly Detection is in Private Preview, including monitoring for agents that run outside Google Cloud. To request access, see the Agent Anomaly Detection overview.

According to recent reports, our launch post introduced Agent Anomaly Detection, which helps you understand and act on agent behavior that drifts outside its intended boundaries. It covered agents on Google Cloud, such as Agent Runtime, Cloud Run, and Google Kubernetes Engine (GKE). Many teams also run agents on other clouds: on AWS Lambda next to an inventory database, as a hosted agent in Microsoft Foundry, or on-premises next to a system that can't move. Those agents carry the same behavioral risks, and until now Agent Anomaly Detection couldn't review them.

Agent Anomaly Detection works from an agent's traces and logs, so it doesn't need access to the agent's runtime. If those traces and logs reach your Google Cloud project, it can detect anomalous behavior wherever the agent runs. In this post, we explain what Agent Anomaly Detection needs from an agent on other cloud, then show what it found for an agent on AWS Lambda and an agent on Microsoft Foundry.

Agent Anomaly Detection reads the logging and observability buckets that you choose when you enable it. Telemetry from anywhere works when:.

Agents built with the Agent Development Kit (ADK) for Python, version 2.12.0 or later, can produce this telemetry with ADK's Google Cloud exporters and a few environment variables, which the next section shows.

AirTag-like trackers for Android and iPhone are everywhere nowadays, but Kodak’s latest SlideTag steps it up with a built-in E-Ink display that can show off your photos, widgets, and more along with being able to track down your items.

Compatible with both the Android Find Hub and Apple Find My networks, the Kodak SlideTag is a tracker inspired by the golden era of Kodak photography. The tracker is built by Reto, the same company that built the Kodak Chamera keychain digital camera.

SlideTag’s premise is relatively simple. You get a tracker with an E-Ink display and a frame in one of eight styles inspired by classic 35mm slides. Those styles are sold in a blind box format, meaning you don’t know what you’re getting until you open the box (unless you buy the full set). There’s also a ninth style that only shows up in one out of every 64 boxes.

The E-Ink display can show six-color versions of your photos, or it can display things like lists, calendars, and more. There’s enough storage on the tracker for a 12-photo slideshow, synced through the Kodak Memory Link app on Android and iOS.

Connect instantly via Bluetooth to the KODAK Memory Link App. From live slideshows and custom QR codes to countdowns and dual-network tracking with Apple Find My and Google’s Find Hub, the KODAK SlideTag seamlessly integrates retro aesthetics into your everyday carry.

Kodak SlideTag is available today from Amazon.

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Recent findings suggest that gradio is an open-source Python package for creating AI-powered web applications. Gradio is compliant with the MCP server protocol and powers thousands of MCP servers hosted on Hugging Face Spaces. The Gradio team is betting significant on Gradio and Spaces being the best way to build and host AI-powered MCP servers.

To that end, here are some of the massive improvements we've added to Gradio MCP servers as of version 5.38.0.

If you've tried to use a remote Gradio MCP server that takes a file as input (image, video, audio), you've probably encountered this error:.

This happens because the Gradio server is hosted on a different machine, meaning any input files must be accessible via a public URL so they can be downloaded remotely.

While many ways exist to host files online, they all add a manual step to your workflow. In the age of LLM agents, shouldn't we expect them to handle this for you?

It has been revealed that gradio now includes a "File Upload" MCP server that agents can use to upload files directly to your Gradio application. If any tools in your Gradio MCP server require file inputs, the connection documentation will now show you how to start the "File Upload" MCP server:.

Learn more about using this server (and notable security considerations) in the Gradio Guides.

Sources indicate that depending on the AI task, getting results can take some time. Now, Gradio streams progress notifications to your MCP client, allowing you to monitor the status in real-time!

In a recent development, as an MCP developer, it's highly recommended to implement your MCP tools to emit these progress statuses. Our guide demonstrates you how.

Recent findings suggest that if you want to integrate an existing backend API into an LLM, you have to manually map API endpoints to MCP tools. This can be a time-consuming and error prone chore. With this release, Gradio can automate the entire process for you! With a single line of code, you can integrate your business backend into any MCP-compatible LLM.

In a recent development, openAPI is a widely adopted standard for describing RESTful APIs in a machine-readable format, typically as a JSON file. Gradio now features the gr.load_openapi function, which creates a Gradio application directly from an OpenAPI schema. You can then launch the app with mcp_server=True to automatically create an MCP server for your API!

Find more details in the Gradio Guides.

It has been revealed that A common pattern in MCP server development is to use authentication headers to call services on behalf of your people. As an MCP server developer, you want to clearly communicate to your users which credentials they need to provide for proper server usage.

Sources indicate that to make this possible, you can now type your MCP server arguments as gr.Header. Gradio will automatically extract that header from the incoming request (if it exists) and pass it to your function. The benefit of using gr.Header is that the MCP connection docs will automatically display the headers you need to supply when connecting to the server!

In the example below, the X-API-Token header is extracted from the incoming request and passed in as the x_api_token argument to make_api_request_on_behalf_of_user.

You can read more about this in the Gradio Guides.

Recent findings suggest that gradio automatically generates tool descriptions from your function names and docstrings. Now you can customize the tool description even further with the api_description parameter. In this example, the tool description will read "Apply a sepia filter to any image.".

It has been revealed that want us to add a new MCP-related feature to Gradio? Let us know in the comments of the blog or on GitHub. Also if you've built a cool MCP server or Gradio app let us know in the comments and we'll amplify it!
